div.head: CARRIED HOME FOR DEAD.
div.p: CARRIED HOME FOR DEAD.
Boy's Wounds Wonderfully Healed By
Zam-Buk.

"Whilst playing on the railway foot-bridge," said Mrs. Tack, of 12, Fairleigh-terrace, Downs- road, Enfield, to a London reporter, "my son, Bertram, then nearly 8 years old, fell down some twenty steps, and was carried ,home for dead. Happily he proved to be alive, but suffering badly from concussion of brain. Subsequently an abscess formed on the back of his head.

"Despite treatment by two doctors, the abs- cess grew till it was nearly as large as another head. It was feared that the skull was diseased so he had to have an operation. This released a great quantity of corruption, yet the place •would not heal for any length of time, but kept on discharging. "In despair we stopped the doctor's treat- ment, and tried homely remedies, but in vain. "Seeing Bertram's miserable plight a nurse advised me to try Zam-Buk. I did so, getting a box from the chemist. The first application of Zam-Buk brought away a vast amount of evil matter, and the next two or three dressings cleansed the place thoroughly.

"Marvellous as it may -seem, simply one boil of Zam-Buk completely cured that boy's head. The wound healed, and where the large bald place used to be is now covered with hair justi as before the accident. "Scores of people know of the cure Zam-Buk effected. The facts are well-known, as just be- fore I began to use Zam-Buk there was a rumour about that the boy had died from his sufferings. "At various times Zam-Buk has saved me many a bright pound, and my faith in its heal- ing power is unlimited." Every home should keep a box. of Zam-Buk handy, because daily mishaps make Zam-Buk a daily need. As a certain remedy for piles, and a soothing and lasting cure for eczema, ulcers, ringworm, chilblains, chapped hands, and other skin troubles, Zam-Buk has no equal. Its purely herbal composition, its compactness and con- stant reliability, make Zam-Buk a priceless boon to the families at home and the soldiers in the trenches. div.head: MUNITIONS TRIBUNAL.
div.p: MUNITIONS TRIBUNAL.
Sixteen Men Who Got Their
Certificates.

In one batch sixteen workers applied to the local Munitions Tribunal on Monday for cer- tificates entitling them to leave the works at which they had been employed and go else- where. The whole sixteen did not turn up be- fore the Tribunal, but delegated the task of presenting their case to two of their number."

The Tribunal consisted of Mr., T. J. Ridgway (president), the Hon. E. H. Cozens-Hardy (sitting as assessor for the masters) and Mr. J. Bradbury (assessor for the men). The sixteen men contended, through the medium of a written statement, that they had made application for the district rate of wages and had been refused. Further they urged that they had given six days' notice and that the same was accepted and "back time" was paid to them. Their insurance cards and unem- ployment books were refused them, although they had tendered the required notice for the de- livery of 'the same; in fact, the cards and books were withheld until the Tuesday after the men terminated their employment on October 23rd. The majority of the men concerned, it was stated, were fitters, most of the remainder being turners and machinemen, and one a labourer.

div.head: DID NOT KNOW WHY.
div.p: DID NOT KNOW WHY.

One of the representatives of the men said they did not know why their certificates had been withheld; they got no sufficient reason why. When they asked for them they were told by a representative of the firm that he was " rather inclined to follow legal 'advice in the matter."

The firrca representative contended-- that t' men had no right to stop work, and added that he told them so in the course of a friendly chat, that they had all made application to be employed on munitions, that the firln had been in correspondence with the War Department, and that the men had been allotted to them.
The President: Do you allege that you come within the terms of the Order?

The Representative: We have among our customers firms who do engineering work for the Government; we have undertaken some work in connection with guns, such as giving them a rough turning. The President: For private firms? The Representative: For firms working for the Government. Moreover, we are working for a firm who are making shells. The speaker added that mainly his firm were concerned with colliery repairs. It was true that the men did ask for their insurance cards, and he said "No ; I don't think I can give them to you. I am entirely in the hands of my legal adviser." The question of certificates was never men- tioned.

One of the men's representatives said that the workers mentioned the question of certifi- cates to the chief engineer before they went to see the manager. The Tribunal decided that the men were entitled to their certificates.
The firm's representative asked whether he had any right of appeal against that decision, and was told that he had not.

div.head: INJURED IN FRANCE.
div.p: INJURED IN FRANCE.

In another case which came before the Tribunal, it was contended by the worker, through the medium of a letter, that his cer- tificate had been unreasonably withheld. The man added that he was a discharged soldier, that he had a wife and three children, and that his wage of 225. a week was not enough. He desired to leave the .firm for whom he had been working in order that he might get more money. He was often "laid up" owing to an injury he received whilst in France. The man's certificate was refused.

div.head: Cljurrli Ocius.
div.p: Cljurrli Ocius.
TO THE FALLEN.
Special Memorial Service At
St. Peter's.

A special service to the memory of those who have fallen in the war, was held in St. Peter s Church, Birchall-street, on Sunday evening. The service opened with the singing of the first verse of the National Anthem, whilst suitable hymns were also rendered, one of which, "Heavenly Father, in Thy Mercy," was sung by the choir and congregation kneeling. Special prayers were also offered. A celebration of the Holy Communion was a fitting end to a solemn service.

In the church vestry, before the service com- menced, the Vicar, the Rev. B. Percival, took the opportunity of presenting a New Testa- ment to Mr. E. Walker, a member of the choir, who is departing to take up military duties. The Vicar wished him good luct and a speedy return. He also expressed the desire that the communicants in the choir would stop and par- take of Holy Communion with Mr. Walker, for it would be the last occasion on which they would do so for a considerable time.

div.head: WHAT WE CAN DO FOR INDIA.
div.p: WHAT WE CAN DO FOR INDIA.
Cause Of Foreign Missions Pleaded in Warrington.
WAR'S EFFECT ON FUNDS.

The annual meeting in support of Foreign Missions, organised by various local societies of the Church of England, was held at the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, on Tuesday night. Colonel Mocatta was in the chair and on the platform were many of the local clergy, including the Rector of Warrington (Canon Willis). A large number of people were pre- sent.

div.head: WORK THAT MUST GO ON.
div.p: WORK THAT MUST GO ON.

After the hymn "Thy Kingdom Come, 0 God," had been sung, The Chairman said that they were all inter- ested in the great war; at the present time the war overwhelmed all other topics and their thoughts were specially with their sailors and soldiers and those who were ministering .to them in the gigantic struggle. In spite of this the work of the Church in the Mission Field must be carried on. The war would not last for ever, but the work of the Church must go on for ever. The task of the missionaries would be greatly increased by this war and it would be hard to make the natives of foreign lands accept the advantages of the Catholic Faith when they knew of the terrible conflict that was going on in Europe, which professed Christianity. The object of that meeting was to rekindle the flame of enthusiasm in Foreign Missions, and on behalf of the laity present he promised sympathy and support.

div.head: GREAT REVIVAL NEEDED.
div.p: A GREAT REVIVAL NEEDED.

The Rev. Prebendary Burn, Vicar of Hp who was received with loud applause, said that though the war absorbed their thoughts, they must make more time to pray about the work of the Church in foreign lands. The men in the trenches were praying, and they needed a great revival in England to be worthy of the men when they came back. The men had gone out to give their lives for those at home. How much sacrifice had we made? Faith was not resignation; it was more like an explosion. The funds of the S.P.G. were down £17,000 on the year, and unless a great effort was made some of the work of the Society would have to be curtailed. This would be a disastrous thing. If they were all to pray, the money would soon be forthcoming. The speaker went on to give some examples of the benefits accruing from mission work in India, and in conclusion pointed out the great need for selt- sacrifice. INDIAN VIEW OF THE WAR.

The Rev. C. E. Tyndale Biscoe, a missionary from the Punjaub, spoke of the opinions on the war of the Brahmins and Mohammedans in his school. His boys were of the opinion that the Germans could not be Christians, for if they had been they would not have mur- dered the women and children of Belgium. Giving a short history of the mission work in Kashmir, the speaker described that province as one of. the most beautiful in India. He spoke of the work of the medical missionaries and also of the educational work. The motto of his school was "In all things be a man." Mr. Biscoe gave the following definition of a man: "A man must have kindness and strength. If these are not together you will have either a kind fool or a strong brute." In this war India had done much for the Old Country. What could England do for India? They could give India the knowledge of the Lord Jesus Christ. (Loud applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chair- man and speakers, on the proposition of the Rev. and Hon. C. F. Cross, seconded by Canon Willis.

div.head: PRESBYTERIAN FESTIVAL.
div.p: PRESBYTERIAN FESTIVAL.
Anniversary Of The Dedication Kept At St. John's.
The dedication festival of St. John's Presby- terian Church, Warrington, was observed on Sunday, and on Monday evening the annual tea and concert were held.

The special preacher at both the Sunday ser- vices was the Rev. Sydney 0. Morgan, of Roy- lake. The soloist at the evening service was Madame Sanders, who rendered "Sun of my soul." The choir gave fine renditions of the anthems "God so loved, the world" (Stainer) and "Glory to Thee, my God, this night" (Gounod). Mr. Lewsey presided at the organ and Mrs. Snailham_was at the piano. The Mayor and the Old Church.

On Monday a large number of people were present at the tea, after which the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Peter Peacock) took the chair for the concert. In his remarks his Worship, said that he remembered the old church of St. John. He once paid it a visit and well recollected the cold, clammy feeling of the place. (Laughter.) He was glad to see such a warm building as the present one and such a large congregation. Whenever it was possible he made a point of attending the ser- vices at the existing church. In Warrington the Presbyterian body were very fortunate in having the Rev. William Reid amongst them. (Loud applause.) At intervals in the programme speeches were made by the Rev. J. Yonge and the Rev. J. J. Glover.

In his remarlis the Rev. John Yonge 'said that that gathering reminded him very powerfully of the old idea of a Lancashire tea. He was very glad to be present in order to testify as to his good feeling towards the Church and its minister. (Applause.) He remembered preach- ing in the old church some years ago, to 25 people, and he was glad when he had finished the sermon. (Laughter.) He was glad to notice that Mr. Reid did not publish the sub- jects of his sermons in the newspapers. He was sorry- to see . the apparent -preaching matches which went on week by week and all . the ministers publishing, the .subjects • of their ser- thons, leaving it to the public to decide which was the brightest and most interesting. He thought that they had a grand theme in their ministry, and that it was much better that people should come to the church to hear the Gospel. In Mr. Reid they had a man whom it was a pleasure to follow. He hOped that the membership, of the new St. John's Church would increase and multiply. The Faith-Testing War.

The Rev. J. J. Glover observed that the people were living in momentous times. What was going on around them was probing the founda- tions of the faith of many men and many women. Men wondered if it were possible to believe in God when such things were happen- ing. Yet he believed that there were men and women who were being thrown back to a new faith and a new trust ih God. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDA f, NOVEMBER 6, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA f, NOVEMBER 6, 1915.
By permission of the Proprietors of "P
FEEDING TIME.
JOCK (accustomed to the formula of orderly officers): "Any compla

Land "; South Africa came to us from our conflict with the Dutch; Canada from our con- tentions with France; and India at first in the same •• way; while our further conquests there were caused by interference with our trade and the internecine .strife which had been India's curse for ages till the Pax Britannica brought order out of chaos. We have often fought for the right to trade, never for the extension of territory, and therefore our Empire is a phenomenon not to be matched by my other, ancient or modern, Assyrian or Per- 3ian, Greek or Roman. True, a corrupt King ind an equally corrupt Prime Minister ill- ,reated and alienated what are now some of ,he -United States of America, but the precent oyalty and splendid support of the Colonies tnd India bear witness to the wisdom and mildness and justice of our rule. In whatever way the Empire has been won, it is a magnifi- 3ent inheritance, an unrivalled trust we .are bound to discharge, and cannot surrender through "the craven fear of being great." Our literature is perhaps a stronger bond of union and a greater inspiration to patriotism. It mirrors our genius and aims and affections, and enshrines the soul of England. Historians and essayists, poets and dramatists and novelists, dreamers and thinkers, the "Pilgrim's Pro- gress" and the authorised version of the Bible, are one of the glories of our name, a common source of instruction and strength wherever our race is found. Our most priceless treasure and our chief contribution to the world's wel- fare had been our devotion to liberty, our example of constitutional freedom. It cost us sore struggles and the dethroning of two Sovereigns, and we have proved that "The price of liberty is eternal vigilance." What we have learnt we have taught to others, and France, Italy, America, Portugal, Switzeiland, and Holland are nations acknowledging their indebtedness. Once motTwe are summoned to defend the freedom of 'our Emiiire and of Europe, and in the Council Chamber and the battlefield our Statesmen and our sons are proving worthy of their ancestry and tradi- tions.

"In our halls is hung Armoury of the invincible knights of old; We must be free or die, who speak the 1-ongue That Shakespeare spake, the faith and morals hold Which Milton held. In everything we are sprung Of earth's first blood, have titles manifold." Christ and Individual Character.

And there (is Christian patriotism. The others are not wrong or un-Christian, but non- Christian patriotism includes the other two, but tests them by Christ's teaching and spirit, and adds the sanction of His religion. The ancient world put the State first, and judged a man by his relation to the community, not by his moral character or his fidelity to his family. Germany, with its "will to power," has sub- ordinated the welfare and conscience of the citizen to the greatness of the State, and holds a creed outworn; for Amiel is right and Chris- tian when he writes in his journal: "The test of every religious and .political and educational system is the man which it forms." Christ taught that the man himself came first, that individual character was what mattered-most, and that being right would rectify all his relations to others. When Christ gave the two commandments of love to God and man, He showed that when a man got right with God, he got right with all mankind. Thus the best Christian is the best church-member, the best parent, the best patriot, animated by the high- est and most inspiring motives. The common patriot is apt to say: "My country right or wrong." The Christian patriot says, to quote General Schurz, a gallant soldier and politician of .the American War of Secession: "My country right or wrong! If right, to be kept right; if wrong, to be set right." When Christ said: "Whosoever would be first among • you shall be your servant, even as • the Son of Man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister and to give His life a ransom for many," He proclaimed that the true ruler,. the perfect patriot, is the man who gives most to his country, not the man who gets most from it in position and applause, in honour and reward. Christ was Himself a patriot, constantly quot- ing the great names on His country's Scroll, asserting that He came for the salvation of His nation first, lamenting His city's fate in moving, memorable' words, and after His resur- rection commanding "That repentance and remission of sins should be preached in His name unto all the, nations, beginning from Jerusalem." By example and precept both, He made it clear that while all mankind have a claim upon us, our country was to come first.

div.head: WESLEYAN WAR SERVICES.
div.p: WESLEYAN WAR SERVICES.
Solemn Intercession And Thanksgiving in Local Churches.

div.head: WARRINGTON'S PART IN NATIONAL PRAYER DAY.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S PART IN NATIONAL PRAYER DAY.

Sunday was set apart by the Wesleyan Con- ference for solemn war services of intercession and thanksgiving and, in common with the rest of the churches of the denomination through- out the length and breadth of the country, those of the Warrington circuit were specially given over to prayerful and thoughtful services, such as befit the days of crisis through which the nation is passing. The local ministers ex- changed pulpits and had the assistance of brethren from outside the circuit, as well as of well-known local preachers. The full list of preachers was as follows : Bewsey-road.—Rev. P. meson, Rev. W. T. Derry. Sankey Bridges.—Mr. E. W. Evans, Mr. J Upson. Latchford.—Rev. E. May. Lymm.—Rev. A. J. Morton, Mr. J. E. Pass- more. Penketh.—Rev. W. T. Derry, Rev. H. T. Dixon. Moore.—Rev. H. T. Dixon, Mr. R. H. Sutton. Padgate.—Mr. M. H. Llewellyn, Rev A. J. Morton. Stockton Heath.—Mr. F. Wright, Rev. P. meson.

div.head: CALL OF PATRIOTISM.
div.p: CALL OF PATRIOTISM.
Our Magnificent Inheritance
And Unrivalled Trust.
TnE BOND OF EMPIRE.

The Rev. W. T. Derry preached on Sunday evening at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church from Psalm cxxxvii. 5,6: "If I forget thee, 0 Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cun- ning," &d. After describing the text as the perfect ex- pression of a passionate patriotism, the reverend gentleman spoke of the way in which the Jewish nation looked upon patriotism as sacred, with the result that it was associated with religion. wherever their Scriptures were read. Referring to the German attempt to impose its culture on others on the ground of its supe- riority, he said that an enlightened patriotism denied that superiority and contended that, if it existed, it could not be imposed by force, and asserted the value of its own nationality.
Love Of Native Land.

There are three kinds of patriotism, lict con- tinued. In most people it is instinctive. Self- preservation is the first law of Nature. To de- fend ourselves, our families, our neighbours, our native land from violence and injustice is bred in the bone, and we feel that the protec- tion of these others is only an extension of self-defence. "God setteth the solitary in families," and also in nations, for ou, mutual comfort and help. The love of country is inherent and the exceptions to it are decadent and are few. There are lands with higher mGuntains and broader rivers, with bluer skies and brighter flowers, but the green fields and verdant spring and summer Pomp of England are incomparable to us because they recall the days of childhood and speak to us of home. It is as natural for us to love the sons and daugh- ters of our Fatherland- more than those of others as it is for us to love our own children more than other people's. Our fellow-country- men are more to us than foreigners just as our friends are more to us than strangers. It is true that all men are brethren, but in a large family there is not the same intimacy and sym- pathy among all the brothers. The progress of the world from barbarism has been depend- ent upon the principle of " nationality, and where it has been strongest and unchecked civilisation has made its- greatest strides. :In the King's last rappeal. to the people he calls upon us- to hold our own: "I feel pride in the voluntary response from my subjects all over the world, who have sacrificed home, fortune and life in order that another may not inherit the free Empire which their ancestors and mine have built. I ask you to make good these sacrifices." "The land we from our fathers had in trust And to our children will transmit or die; This is our maxim, this our piety; And God and Nature say that it is just." Proud Of Our History.

So there is an intelligent patriotism. The humour and good humour, which mean so much to our soldiers in :trend' and ship and hos- pital, is one of the characteristics which endear us to each other. The sense of honour is an- other. When a captured German officer ex- claimed: "You will always be fools, and we shall never be gentlemen," he , complimented our hearts, though at the expense of our heads. But we find this feeling for -fair-play; 'for 'play ing the game, permeating, all parts "of our Population and every department of our life. The order which marks our households and is a feature of our institutions, an order which results from education and training, and not from drilling and dragooning, makes us prize our English privileges. We are proud of our history. We do not hold that all our laws have been just and all our warsluStifiable, but we do claim that our legislation has gradually grbtivn 'More just, and that we curbed the tyranny of Spain in the .sixteenth cenbiry and broke the despotism of Napoleon in the nine- teenth. Our enemies, without and within, allege that. our Empire is , our - condemnation, because it is the product of plunder and piracy; but they put their fanciful fiction in place of history. Australasia was "No Man's

pened 'all over the land, they were on the eve of a new age. (Applause.) The Rev. William Reid expressed his thanks to the Mayor for his presence; to the artistes; and to the ladies who had arranged the tea.

div.head: Entertainers.
div.p: The Entertainers.

The programme, which WAS greatly enjoyed by the large audience, was contributed to by Mesdames Sanders and Miller, Miss Emily Tay- lor, and Messrs. Walter Clay and R. Mungall. Mrs. Hutton and Mrs. Snailham were the accompanists.

div.head: Demand of Christian Patriotism.
div.p: The Demand of Christian Patriotism.

The patriotism we approve is Christian pat- riotism, and •we ask what demand it makes on us to-day? The patriot* of. peace means that we take an interest in public affairs, use our influence in the right direction, and pay our taxes honestly. The patriotish, of war-time, When we are engaged in a just and inevitable strife, requires of us effort and self-sacrifice. It calls us to intercession, service and courage. We have been praying for victory, and we are warranted in doing so, because our cause is that of truth and right and freedom. Apart from the origins of the war, the frightfulness with whidh it has been *aged by the enemy— Louvain and the Lusitania, the poisoning of air and water, the useless shelling of unde- fended towns, and the execution of a .noble woman, who had nursed their own wounded— all this reveals the unscrupulousness and cruelty of unbridled militarism. A patched-up peace with a Power so lacking in conscience would be virtual defeat and worse than war, .and would mean that. the sacrifices of .our sons had been made in vain. We pray for victory first, then peace, with a wisdom which is first pure, then peaceable! And our prayers •must be public and private and persevering._

Those who can are called to serve in arms. Surely the heroic example of Nurse Cavell— "l willingly give my life for my country; I have no fear or shrinking "—will not shame, but rouse the laggard. After millions of our young men from the heart and extremities of the Empire have offered themselves willingly and enrolled in a crusading spirit, it would be a great misfortune if the Government had to fall back upon Conscription. Those who can- not take up arms and serve abroad are called
to take up work at home for the nation, and the response which has been so splendid and wide- spread should be universal throughout the land.

div.head: Courage and Encourage.
div.p: Courage and Encourage.

We are called to courage and encourage. Our Fleet is stfonger than ever; our numbers and munitions and those of our Allies are increas- ing and will increase, and our enemies' cannot; our finance is less difficult to raise than theirs; and our cause, the neutral countries being our judges, remains the cause of civilisation and humanity. If we have made mistakes, so have our opponents; and Napoleon said that• victory is given not to those who make no mistakes, but to those who make fewest; and those who read history know that no war can be waged with- oullhem. In the King's appeal to the nation the most stirring words are these: "In ancient days the darkest moment has ever produced in men of our race ,the sternest resolve." If the courage with which we commenced is the cour- age with which we continue, it will be the courage in which we conquer; and the greater our courage the less our rancour and revenge. Let us make sure that the Christian spirit keeps our conflict clean and crowns our vic- tory. Let us be Christian patriots—patriots of Edith Cavell's kind—malting her testimony our own experience. "This I would say, standing as I do in view of God and eternity: I realise that patriotism is not enough. I must have no hatred nor bitterness to anyone."

div.head: PRICE AND THE PRIZE.
div.p: THE PRICE AND THE PRIZE.
Rev. P. Meson And Cause Of Present
Chaos.

Preaching at the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church in the morning, the Rev. Percy meson took as his subject "The Cross, the Prize, and Price of a Just War," finding his text in Galatians vi. 14: "Far be it from me to glory save in the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." In the course of his remarks the reverend gentleman said that the present were days of amazement. Peace hides her head, her tender voice drowned by the deep baying of the dogs of war. Thoughtful men stand aghast at the latest product of civilisation—the world challenging Christianity—and asking if this is the result of 1,900 years of the rule of an impractical Nazarene; and failing to see tne obvious retort that it is just because men and nations have not submitted to His fule that we find ourselves in the present chaos., We are in the midst of days of perplexity, but they are also proud days—days of high deeds and lofty endeavour, days in which the nation was rising out of luxury to a nobler life. And yet though proud days they are quiet days. There was none of the tumult and shouting of the South African War. A deep seriousness prevailed; the glory and glitter of war only appalled and shocked. There was even a seri- ous gladness. In deep humility in the recesses of her heart our nation was saying: "Far be it from me to glory save in the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ."

div.head: Cross Will Triumph.
div.p: The Cross Will Triumph.

The Cross will not be made null and void in this war. True, the origin of the war was anti-Christian, but the Cross would in the end be the deciding factor. They had all seen the picture in the newspapers of a church, a veritable wreck, through bombardment by the enemy—the windows smashed, ornamentation ruined, the roof a mass of charred timber—and erect and unbroken over the wreckage was the Cross, untouched by all the fury. That was a symbol, The Cross of Christ, with all that it stands for, would remain when the wrath of men had spent itself, "towering o'er the wrecks of time." The Cross stands for the gaining of righteousness through sacrifice. So Christ 'suffered; so is God suffering! England now is suffering because of the stand she has taken for righteousness. She is acting on the principle of the Cross, seeking to gain right- eousness through sacrifice. The Cross is the price she has to pay. From the day when, as an Empire, 'we sprung together and said:. "In the name of all that is true, .righteousness must be maintained; the liberties of Europe must be guarded," suffering sharp and strong had been our lot. The All-Involving Struggle.

.We are having to pay the price. The whole nation, from the -highest to the lowest, is in- volved—the Cross, is in our hearts. But it is not only the. price we are paying. The Cross, is also the prize. It is a sign of high honour that we are deemed fit to bear it. We had grown depressed about ourselves. We said reli- gion was declining and that Christianity had failed. But when God calls us to stand kir what are the very principles of Christianity, in a flash the spirit of the Cross is manifested. Gladly we accepted the Cross. Patiently we are paying the price, and, 10, it is transformed to the prize—the sign that God is with us and that righteousness will conquer. We glory not in war; not even in victory; not in so many thousands of the enemy slain; but in the Cross of Christ. The same principle is revealed in the individual sacrifices made for our country at this time. The same principle is 'observed in the great spiritual warfare of good against evil. Take your stand for righteousness in any field. The Cross is the price you pay. It is Also the prize—that in which we can glory. It is a sign of God's call.and God's approval. A special prayer was offered for those who have 'gone to the Front from the Bevisey-road .Church, and the hymns "Break, Day of God," "0 God, our help in ages past," and ." Peace, perfect peace," were sung, as well as the National Anthem. •

div.head: IN THE END
div.p: IN THE END
Standpoint From Which Christian Must View Events.
Mr. R. Howson Sutton' gave the address at the Moore Wesleyan Methodist Church in the evening. The church has sent four recruits to the Forces of the Crown.

Mr. Sutton took as the subject of his sermon "The Importance of a Right Point of View," and in .the course of his remarks said that the events of the last fifteen months had presented many problems to the minds of the Christian and had proved a severe test of faith to many. War was an absolute negative of all that Chris- tianity_ stood for, and how could the oppres- sion of non-combatants and other numerous violations by •the enemy of international law be reconciled with the conception of divine love, justice and power? The Christian to-day must see events from God's point of view and then he would see them in true perspective, and he would have a vision which would en- able him to believe, even when the. days looked dark, that in the end "the earth shall be filled
Continued in Next Column.

div.head: WESLEYAN ANNIVERSARY
div.p: WESLEYAN ANNIVERSARY
Bold-street Wesleyans Keep Church's 65th Birthday.

div.head: SPECIAL SERVICES AND LECTURES.
div.p: SPECIAL SERVICES AND LECTURES.

Saturday, Sunday and Monday were red-letter days in the history of the Bold-street Wesleyan Church, for they saw the celebration of the 95th anniversary of the establishment of the church. On the first-named day the new min- ister of the church, the Rev. Percy meson, lectured to a large audience, on the second day services of a special and appropriate character were held, and on the third day a preacher well-known throughout the connexion gave a most interesting and thoughtful address on the subject which is in the minds of all at the present time—the war.

div.head: "LOVE, LIFE AND DEATH."
div.p: "LOVE, LIFE AND DEATH."

Pastor Lectures On A Great Painter. The Rev. Percy meson's lecture, given in the church schoolroom, was entitled "Love, Life and Death," and dealt with the paintings of the late G. F. Watts, R.A., particular attention being paid not so much to the technique of Watts's painting as to their inner meaning in relation to the man himself. Watts, said the Lecturer, was a tremendous worker; for assur- edly few men could cram more into a day than did he. He had ideas of his own and he held fast to them. He thought no creature was without powers and that all men should be creators. His thoughts were as grand as some Alpine cluster; they took as wide a sweep as some rolling plain. With it all he was gentle, kind and modest, and he once remarked to a friend: "God would never have made us so imperfect.if he had not intended to be kind to us." Though a deep thinker, he Wks a man of the utmost simplicity—happy in the common- place. He once said: "When I am gone, I suppose they will want to put some tomb over my remains. I hope it will be simple, the in- scription consisting of just five words: "An aspiration; not a regret." Watts refused hon- ours, though he did not despise them, and he strove to live up to the ideals of his pictures. He had a deep, fine, beautiful character. A number of beautiful lantern slides of the great painter's pictures were then thrown upon the screen, and the Lecturer proceeded, in most interesting fashion, to describe and comment upon them all, introducing many anecdotes con- cerning the artist and his work. In him, said Mr. meson, gentleness and strength were wedded, and he was in close touch with the spirit of his age, whilst, being the child of Welsh parents, he had more than the ordinary share of vivid imagination and poetical enthu- siasm. If he had been able to carry on his great desire he would have been not a painter, but a sculptor. There was no special age, no special religion, no special epoch clearly marked in the great mass of his works. His ideas were wide; his principles fundamental. "The ut- most for the highest" was the characteristic of the man. He spent his utmost to reach the highest he knew. The lecture was presided over by Mrs. Dodds, of Penketh, who expressed her pleasure at being able once again to meet so many Wes- leyan friends, and, at the close, was accorded, together with the Lecturer, an expression of thanks for her services.

div.head: SUCCESSFUL SUNDAY SERVICES.
div.p: SUCCESSFUL SUNDAY SERVICES.
Large Congregations And Good Music.

The Rev. Dr. J. T. Wardle Stafford, of New- castle-on-Tyne, who was the special preacher, as well as the lecturer on Monday night, found large congregations awaiting him, and hip earnest and eloquent discourses were greatly appreciated. Special interest attached to Dr. Stafford's visit by reason of the fact that he preached his sermon as a candidate for the ministry in Bold-street Church, no fewer than thirty-three years ago. The church choir ren- dered special music at all the Sunday services, giving Booth's anthem "Arm, soldiers of the Lord," in the morning, and Gaul's " Thine is the Kingdom" in the evening. Their singing was most effective. At the evening service Miss Hylda Cragg-James sang most charmingly Sul- livan's masterly setting to the well-known words "God shall wipe away all tears." Miss Cragg-James also sang at the afternoon service, which was of a musical character, and was presided over by Mr. John Taylor. Miss Cragg- James' solos on this occasien were Gounod's immortal "There is a green hill," Dvorak% "God is my Shepherd," and Sir Frederick Bridge's arrangement of "A joyous Easter song." Mr. Bradford Barton contributed in polished manner three violin solos—Dvorak's striking " Humoreske," Couperins' dainty "Pavane," and Pergolesi's pretty "Aria." Mr. W. H. Payton presided with his usual skill at the organ, playing Lemaigre's " Magnificat in F" and "Andante in F."

div.head: BY-WORD AMONG TIIE NATIONS.
div.p: THE BY-WORD AMONG TIIE NATIONS.
Germany's To-Be-Shattered Dream Of
World-Power.

On Monday evening Dr. Wardle Stafford lec- tured to a large and attentive audience on the subject of "The Decline and Fall of the Ger- man Empire." The soldiers in doe Allied Armies, he said, knew that 'their cause was righteous, and they were prepared to defend it with their last drop of blood. Why were we fighting Ger- many? It was as well to know and under- stand what we are fighting for. Belgium was the occasion, but was not the cause. Germany found the occasion in Belgium, but the cause was in herself. For forty years she had been preparing herself for this event; in fact, ever since the Franco-German War she had been getting ready to wage the most terrific on- slaught on record. She had, during the period which has elapsed since the war with France, deliberately formed her plans with the inten- tion of achieving world-empire. And to achieve such an end militarism was a sine qua non. If a ,nation was to, be a world conqueror she must be prepared to fight for it. He believed that whilst things are as they are in this world a standing army is a regrettable neces- sity. What was militarism? His dictionary made answer: "Militarism is an excess of the military spirit." And Germany stood for militarism; to-day in that country the mili- tary party ranked next to the royal family.

div.head: Most Arrant Snobs In The World.
div.p: The Most Arrant Snobs In The World.

The military party in Berlin were the most arrant snobs in the world. On one occasion some friends of his (the Lecturer's) were din- ing in a Berlin hotel, when some military men entered. After a few minutes one of 'the wait- ers came up to the •English diners and an- flounced: "The military gentlemen wish to oay that they do not intend to offer any objec- tion to your presence in the dining-room." That was a small incident, but it was typical of much. Geiman snobbery and German in;.

div.head: " GETHSEMANE OF GRIEF."
div.p: " GETHSEMANE OF GRIEF."
Rev. A. J. Morton On The Tearless
Morn Ahead.

At the Padgate. Wesleyan Church, in the evening, the Rev. A. J. Morton, in the course of an eloquent address, said that he did not wish to use the occasion for cursing the Kaiser for causing the nations to welter in blood. He could safely leave him to Heaven,' and. to "the thorns that in his bosom lodge to prick and sting him." Referring to the present sorrow through which the 'nation was passing, he wished 'to 'warn them against the subtle temp- tationS 'which caitie through grief and loss. Many .had felt' the' poignancy of these sinister whispers Which suggested that God did not care and that prayer was useless, and were thus tempted to doubt the goodness and mercy of Him who, was known as the Heavenly Father. But the experience and triumph of all great souls who had' done most for the world assured us that, in our Gethsemane of grief, the angels of succour and deliverance were at hand, and out of- the night of sorrow should come the tearless morn.

solence had become the menace of Europe. In this war we were fighting for Christianity. It was impossible to over-estimate the significance of the contest. Germany would in the end go under, but she must go completely under if the peace of Europe was to be secured. We were fighting for posterity and we could not afford to repeat• this experiment—this world-war— more than once in a thousand years. He be- lieved that England was ordained of God to humble Germany, in order that Jesus Christ might be exalted. German kultur was now a by-word among the nations of the earth. What had helped to kill Germany? False philosophy—the philosophy of men like Nietzsche—had helped her to her death. The ideal that Nietzsche set before himself was that of the Over-man or Super-man, and pity, sym- pathy, magnanimity and gentleness had no place in his programme. He proposed a revi- sion of the marriage laws, the education laws, and, in fact, all the other laws. Next in im- portance in the moulding of false doctrine came Trietschke, who was a thorough-going hater of England.

One Cause of Germany's Impending Downfall. The first cause of Germany's downfall waa an immoral system of philosophy and the second an oligarchal Government—a system of Government by a small and exclusive class who had the supreme powers of the State in their hands. But the world to-day was not to be governed by a small class of so-called cul- tured people, and he did not hesitate to say that the future of England would not be determined by her men of letters, but by her industrial and commercial classes, and by her intelligent working men. (Hear, hear.) Cul- ture had its place in a nation's development, but the future of England would be deter- mined by its men of honesty rather than by its men of culture. What was the secret of the success of British Government? Was it not the freedom of the people? They might not always realise their ideals, but they had got them steadily before them. The loyalty of the British Colonies was the admiration and envy of the world, and that loyalty had not been won by oligarchies and military despots; but by mutual trust and by the fact that the Motherland gave her Colonies the freedom of self-government, plus the protection of the British flag. Britain had trusted her Colonies, with the result that in the day of stress and strain her Colonies rallied round her with a spirit of loyalty which had never been sur- passed. (Applause.) This country trusted her Colonies, and in return they trusted her. Days of Slavery Gone.

The days of oligarchies, of slavery, had gone. The Socialist rising in Germany was to-day growing in volume, and if Germany had not been held up by external forces she would have been disintegrated by internal forces. The fact was that tyranny and despotism could not Hire where the gospel of Jesus Christ had warmed the air and brightened the sky. The spirit expressed in the words "God bless the squire and his rioh relations and help us poor people to keep our stations" had passed away in this country; it had gone for over. We did not wish the squire and his rich relations any harm, but we were not going to surrender our manhood or womanhood either for him or the aforesaid rich relations. (Hear, hear.) The moral to be drawn from the lesson of Germany was: "Trust the people, for ultimately their good sense would assert itself." The judgment of the majority was not always a perfect judg- ment, but, on the whole, it was a judgment to be relied upon. Parenthetically, the speaker made reference to the German sneer concerning our "contemptible little Army," and pointed out that however contemptible it might have been it had been good enough to keep the Kaiser's millions at bay. (Applause.) This war would be a failure if the law of treaties— the law which the Germans had so unblushingly set at defiance—was not again established on a secure and impregnable basis. If the law of treaties between nations was not held to be sacred, the day was not far distant when busi- ness treaties would also be violated. Derma:4y A Discredited Nation.

Germany is to-day a discredited nation. In- cidentally the Lecturer mentioned that his son happened to be a spectator of the bombard- ment of Scarborough, adding, amid laughter, that be had been particularly fortunate, hav- ing been present at one bombardment and two Zeppelin raids, with the result that he said now that he was quite acclimatised to them. What had been the result of the bombardments and Zeppelin raids? The result had been to stiffen the back of John Bull until now it was as' stiff as a poker. (Laughter and applause.) T.he whole world outside Germany and her allies had revolted against the barbarism of the raids, and they had given a stimulus to recruiting such as no platform oratory could ever have done. Germany's methods were the methods of the brute, and her end would be the end of the bully. Steadfastness on the part of the Allies would bring the war to an end satisfac- tory to the whole of the civilised world. Ger- many was a dead angel, and another of the things that had helped to kill her was destrui:- tive Biblical criticism, a thing which had played no small part in her disintegration. German philosophy had done much to destroy the faith as well as the morals of the German people. In things spiritual Germany might be said to have stolen our bread and given us a stone.
Germany and Our Faith.

The man who belonged to no organised reli- gious body, but said that he could worship God as well in the green fields as he did in a church, usually ended by not worshipping Him at all. He charged Germany with having done much to destroy Christian faith in this coun- try. In this war we were fighting not for Empire. but for home and for the Kingdom of Jesus Christ. (Applause.) Our Christianity was not all that it might be, but it was better than that thing called German Kultur. (Hear, hear.) War was a hateful thing, but there was one thing which would have been worse, and that was for this nation to have stood aside without protest whilst the military class of Germany marched with rapine and murder through the territory of her peaceful neigh- bours. (Hear, hear.) The Lecturer went on to make touching reference to the men who have given their lives for their country, and to those who have been mutilated in the war, remarking, apropos of the latter, that surely the country would care for them in the days to come and not allow her broken heroes to go short of those things which they could have won for themselves if they had not gone out to fight for other folk. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: GERMANY'S INEVITABLE FAITH.
div.p: GERMANY'S INEVITABLE FAITH.

The lecture was presided over by Alderman Bennett, who, in the course of a few -prefatory remarks, made sympathetic reference to the death of the Rev. Wilkins Rees, a former min- ister of the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit, and went on to refer to the war, observing that after fifteen months the enemy were still in possession of the best part of Belgium, as well as of part of France, and a good slice of Russia; in addition to appearing to have made headway in the Baltic. Still he was not despondent, but, on the other hand, regarded the downfall of the German Empire as abso- lutely inevitable. The reason why he did not think that Germany would maintain her great- ness was that she had lost her soul. (Hear,. hear.)
At the close the Rev. W. Thompson Derry expressed the thanks of the audience to the Chairman and the Lecturer.

div.head: DRINK MENACE: JOINT MESSAGE TO THE PEOPLE.
div.p: THE DRINK MENACE: JOINT MESSAGE TO THE PEOPLE.

Sir,—ln this solemn hour of national history we are constrained to make a united appeal to the Christian people of Britain to use their full influence to free our land from the curse of intemperttnce. By the sharp test of war, indulgence in Strong Drink stands revealed as the foe of moral discipline, and a grave and immediate danger to our country. It weakens our power to concentrate on the serious duties we are called to discharge. It stands between us and a wholehearted return as a nation to the God of our fathers. Face to face with more solemn issues than have ever before con- fronted our race, we are convinced that the time has come for us, by combined and vig- orous effort, to thrust this shame and menace from our midst. We ask, therefore, that the voice of Chris- tianity shall be raised everywhere in urgent protest against this evil; we appeal that the example of Christian people shall be in all respects consistent with the Christian claim for Temperance Reform; and that with good- will, and at all costs, the State shall be sup- ported in its present and future endeavours to remove the peril of intemperance. For these reasons we call for prayerful sup- port on behalf of the newly-formed Temperance Council of the Christian Churches of England and Wales. The Council is officially represen- tative of the Temperance organisations of eleven Christian denominations, and will speak and act with the authority which such a fed- eration represents. Its aim is to secure legis- lature and other Temperance reforms. It represents the union of many forces which have hitherto worked in independence of eagh other. From our hearts we thank God for this union, believing that with His Holy Spirit guiding His faithful people they shall know what things they ought to do, and have grace and power faitlifillly to fulfil the same. Joint Presidents:— RANDALL CANTUAR FRANCIS CARDINAL BOURNE. W. B. SELBIE, Mansfield College. • (For the Temperance Committees of the Free Churches.) W. BRAMWELL BOOTH, Salvation Army.

div.head: MUNITIONS AND _ DRINK
div.p: MUNITIONS AND _ DRINK
HESTRIMONS.

Sir,—lf I am not mistaken your correspondent "J. E. Simpson, of Liverpool" (a description very similar to "Mr. Jones, of Wales "), has on many occasions lately championed the drink trade in your columns. I don't refuse to argue the matter out with Mr. Simpson on that account, but I certainly shall not waste any time on a persistent apologist for the Trade. For the moment, however, it is sufficient for me to remind Mr. Simpson that the "logic of facts" is dead against him. His dogmatic statement "I can tell 'Citizen' that in our area the Control Board restrictions have only' resulted in irritating everybody without decreasing drunkenness to any extent, or helping the production of munitions," is a distinct perversion of facts, and further the figures given a few days ago of the convictions for drunkenness in the Controlled Areas before and since the control has been exercised, are eloquent in proof of the axiom—reduce the facili- ties for drinking and you reduce drunkenness. For Mr. Simpson's comfort I may tell him that there is every prospect of the operations of the Control Board being greatly extended very shortly, because the Board is so satisfied with the effects already produced by the restrictions imposed. I stand by my opinion (which is supported by personal experience), that the vast majority of our toilers are ex- emplary in both conduct and work, and I know that they are not harassed or cven incon- venienced by the Control Board's restrictions, but I do know that many of our steady work- men are seriously handicapped by the wastrels, who make "gods of their bellies," and to whom the country's danger ma.keo no appeal. Facts have been brought to my knowledge where one drunken workman has caused a dozen, and in some cases, a score of others to lose time and the firms concerned to lose considerable output. For the good of the State all must combine, and I confess I have little patience with men like your correspondent who, under the pre- tence of advocating non-interference with the working men's liberties and comforts, are merely doing all they can to maintain intact a Trade, the mischievous ramifications of whicn. are terrible beyond description. Your correspondent might profitably consider the Report of the Prison Commissioners, published last week, in which they state that the number of criminal convictions is the lowest an and they attribute as the second most important cause of this great reduction i n erime Ike. " Reduced hours for the sale of intoxicating liquors." Only on Saturday last I saw no less than six men—all elderly—in khaki, every one of them obviously partially intoxicated, and in that condition four of them went into another public-house—with what result I cannot tell; but I do know this that any man who helps to make a soldier drunk, whether the soldier is on duty or not, is guilty of a gross moral offence against England; and when it comes to this that eminent firms engaged in the making of munitions whose works are under military guard, have had actually to construct cells on their own premises in which to incarcerate drunken soldiers who come on duty drunk, or are made drunk while on duty, it is time to apply drastic restrictions on the sale of drink, even if the fat purses of brewers and publicans are depleted in consequence. Sir, the present conditions as to drinking facilities are the gravest menace to our success in this war; and it is imperative that all per- sonal interests which militate against the pub- lic well-being shall be, at any rate for the period of the war, extinguished. No doubt your correspondent and others of his " ilk " would prefer that there should be no chance of trying what effect general restrictions apply- ing alike to all parts of England would have. Why? Is it because they fear that once the experiment of a sober England was tried, there would be no going back after the war is over? CITIZEN.

The threatened strike of the Monmouth Work- house officials against the use of salt butter has been averted by the guardians reverting to - the supply of fresh butter.

div.head: INLAND BOOK RATE.
div.p: INLAND BOOK RATE.
This rate, merged in the Inland Letter Rate as from the 22nd June, 1897, up to the present time, save as, regard the halfpenny packet rate. is revived as a rate separate from the Letter Rate.

The articles and documents admissible at the rate are those at present shown on pages 10-13 of the Post Office Guide as admissible at the halfpenny packet rate, with the single exception of blotting books and pads and coloured papers attached to price lists and trade circulars. The rate will be as follows Not exceeding 2oz. in weight
Every additional 2oz. or fraction of 2oz. id. No packet will be transmissible at the Book Rate of postage which exceeds 51b. in weight, 2 feet in length, and 1 foot in width or depth.

div.head: INLAND NEWSI.APER RATE.
div.p: INLAND NEWSI.APER RATE.
Copies of 'publications registered for trans- mission at the Inland Newspaper Rate , are sub- ject to the following rate of postage:—
For every copy -not exceeding -6oz. in lk weight For every additional 60z. or fraction of _ 6oz.

If two or more copies are enclosed in a single packet, each copy is liable to the same postage as if it had been posted separately. But in no case will a packet of such copies Ell chargeable with a higher rate than that chargeable on a book packet of the same weight. No packet will be admissible at the newspaper rate of postage which exceeds 21b. in weight. In other respects the regulations set forth at page 14-15 of the Post Office Guide will remain unaltered. ,

div.head: INLAND SAMPLE RATE.
div.p: INLAND SAMPLE RATE.

This rate, which, like ,the Book Rate, was merged in the Inland Letter Rate as from the 22nd June, 1897, up to the present time, is also revived as a rate separate from the Leiter Rate. The rate is :---
Not expeeding 4oz. , , Between 4 and 6oz. lid. Between 6 and Boz.
No packet will be transmissible at this rate which exceeds Boz. in weight, 12 inches in length, 8 inches in width, or 4 inches in depth.

No article will be admissible at this rate un- less it be in fact a sample, itself without sale- able value, of goods for sale. Packets must be sent in wrappers marked " Sample Post," open at the ends, or in un- fastened envelopes, and must be made up in such a manner that the contents can be easily withdrawn for examination. "Seeds, tea, flour, drugs and such like articles, which cannot be sent in open wrappers or envelopes, may be sent in boxes or in bags of linen or other material fastened in such a way as to admit of easy examination.
The name, trade, and address of the dealer by whom, the packet -is sent must be in all cases printed or conSpicuonsly stamped on the out- side of the wrapper or on the label.

div.head: INLAND PARCEL RATE.
div.p: INLAND PARCEL RATE.
The rate of postage for Inland Parcels will be as follows:-- .
Not exceeding lib. 9 f If 2Ib. 3, AP 3Ib. Mb. IP 7Ib. IP 8Ib. 2/ 91b „ 101 b. 21, 111 b In every other respect the Inland Parcel Regulations remain unaltered.

div.head: ACTIVITY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: ACTIVITY AT WARRINGTON.
Reduced Staff Has Greatly 1 Increased
Duties.

The alterations were due to come into force on Monday, November let, but the authorities allowed the public a day's grace, the alterations not being made until Tuesday. .In an interview with an " Examiner " repre- sentative on Wednesday, Mr. 11. Chambers, the Warrington Postmaster, said that so far the public were using the Post Office in the same manner as before the alterations. There had been just as much posting, though, added Mr. Chambers, it would take a week or two before the attitude of the public could be definitely gauged: -

- The patriotism of the staff of the Warrington Post Office has left it depleted of many of its workers, and much delay was caused at the be- ginning of the week owing to the numerous in- quiries as to the alterations. Numbers of people wanted their letters weighing in order that they might be sure that the packages did not weigh more than the stipulated amount. This greatly occupied the time of the officials, thereby caus- ing the delay. Apart from this, Mr. Chambers informed our reporter, the changes came into force without a hitch. Many people, however, did not even know that there had been a clinge. More than one man has walked in with a tele- graphic message of 12 words and offered the usual sixpence in payment. When asked for the additional 3d., however, he has paid up with- out complaint.

div.head: SAMPLES BY POST.
div.p: SAMPLES BY POST.

There is one point which the users of the "Sample Post" should bear in mind, and that is, no written document should be enclosed with t' • sample, nor should anything be written on the sample, or the recipient of the sample will be charged with double the deficient Postage at letter rate.

div.head: TELEPHONE CHARGES.
div.p: TELEPHONE CHARGES.

The 'alteration in the charges for the use of- the telephone came into force on October, Ist; but so far as Warrington is concerned, the 'phone seems to be in use just as before. The increased charges affect the Warrington Office little, as the financial side of the system is dealt with from Liverpool. The new scale of charges is as follows :—Trunk telephone lines: 25 miles, 4d.; 50 miles, Bd.; 75 miles, is.; and 100 miles, is. 4d. For every additional 40 miles or raction of 40 miles, Bd. extra is charged. The fee for the use of. a call office for three minutes for a local call will be 2d. in the area outside London.

div.head: Bonnie Annie Laurie.
div.p: Bonnie Annie Laurie.

William Douglas, whose love ballad, "Annie Laurie," has become one of the famous lyrics of the world, wooed, but did not win Annie Laurie. The real Annie Laurie gave "her promise true" to Douglas, but wedded an- other, a wealthier suitor, Fergusson, of Craig- darroch. Douglas, who was ready to "lay me doon and, dee," went to the wars, and when he came back married also, and left a goodly Crop of heirs, The tender melody that has won the hearts of people the world over was set to the words many years after by Lady John Scott. Annie Laurie was born December 16th, 1682, at the home of her father, Stephen Laurie, at Maxwelton, Scotland, an old-fash- ioned stone mansion that had -once been the castle of the Earle of Glencairn.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 6, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 6, 1915.

maintain intact their religious and educational system. It was the pivot upon which social and domestic life had worked since the Reformation; it was the pivot that Would remain long after the present troubles were past. In the pat the annual sales of work had been very useful in producing sums of money, averaging about £3OO. In the present year they had to look forward to additional expenditure. The Parish Church was a fine, but expensive building, and required con- tinual repair, and about .2100 would be required for that purpose. Then their Missions, which were doing such fine work under the Revs. Vickers and Buckmaster. They were new centres of activity, spreading Light and affirmino. the Faith, and they must be kept going, with the result that another £5O was required to maintain them in state of efficiency. Then there were the Sunday ,schools, and for those an- other £5O must be found, and the Working Party required £4O, whilst general expenses ran to another £lO. That gave a total of £250, and all who helped to raise that sum would be ,giv- ing to one of the best purposes for which any moneyi coold be spent, viz., the maintenance of religion, its establishments and its faith. (Ap- plause.)
Mrs. Stewart-Smith then declared the sale open.

div.head: PAROCHIAL SALES OF WORK,
div.p: PAROCHIAL SALES OF WORK,
THE PARISH CHURCH.
Rector On Local Roman Catholic Effort.
A CALL TO CHURCHMEN.

The Fairfield Schools, off Manchester-road, present a gay appearance this week-end, for in them is being held the annual sale of work in aid of the funds of the Warrington Parish Church and the Mission Churches associated with it. The sale was formally opened on Thursday by Mrs. Dudley Stewart-Smith, the wife" of the Vice-Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, who accompanied her and shared in the hearty welcome accorded by those present
at the inaugural ceremony
CANON WILLIS AND PAROCHIAL WORK.
Important New Project in Contemplation:

The opening ceremony was presided over by the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis), who, in the course of his prefatory remarks, said he wanted to speak to them about a matter which he felt of great importance—a future object; one that would come bef9re them next year. The Bishop of Zanzibar had lately put to the Archbishop of Canterbury the question, "What does the Church of England stand for?" The answer to that question was that the Church of England stood for the Holy Catholic Church—for the Catholic faith and for Catholic worship. Else it ,stood for nothing at all. Just what the Arch- bishop felt about the Church of England, he .(the speaker) felt about the Warrington Parish Church, and about every other parish church. As all present knew, the. parish, at the head of which stood the Parish Church, was a very large one; in fact, nominally it contained some twenty thousand people. At the present moment they had four clergy to attend to the spiritual wants of that large parish. A Fifth Clergyman Coming.

However, he had just completed arrangements with another gentleman, who would come to Work with them next Lent. There would, of course, then be five clergy, bet the parish would still adhere to its four divisions—the four other clergy would take those divisions, and he (the Rector) would hold himself at liberty to go any- where in the parish. At the present time the parish expended something like £5OO a year on its clergy. Ile wanted £6OO a year for that pur- pose.- At the present time the congregation gave him nearly £lOO a year towards the clergy; he wanted them to give him £l5O. They had prac- tically promised that they would do that. He did not ask it for this year, but for next year, and the way in which they would give it might well be .2.50 at Easter, £5O at the harvest, and £5O from the parochial sale of work. He was sure that the money would be given willingly and gladly. The four districts which would be worked were the Howley district, the St. Cle- ment's district, the St. George's district, and the Church Institute district. The Rev. Stanton would have the Church Institute district, and they knew what the Rev. Vickers had done at St. Clement's and the Rev. Buckmaster at St. George's. Work in the Howley District.

The new clergyman would take the Howley district. Ile was sure they knew what there was to be done up in the Church Institute dis- trict. There Was very little provision for the church; in fact, at the present moment they had only the first beginnings of the institute. On the other hand the Nonconformists had opened a large chapel in the district, and he was. thankful. He would rather that the people had something than nothing, but they would not get the whole Catholic faith taught there. The Roman Catholics had just opened a new church in the district, and again he was, in a way, thankful for that. For he would rather that the people be taught too much than that they should, be taught nothing, because they' all wanted to know the truth, and if people found that the new church gave more than the truth —well, he hoped they would come back again to the truth. He had just seen a copy of a paper issued by the Romish Church, and relating to a special effort they were• going to make next week. Two Romish clerics were coming down to speak, and he had been looking at the paper which told of the addresses which were going to be given. He did not like some of the point; which they AN:ere going to put before the people. He would particularly mention one; viz.' the question of the real Presence in the Holy Eucharist. Every instructed Churchman be- lieved in the real Presence in the Holy Eucharist, but he did not like Roman Catholics using that phrase, because, if they were honest, what they were pledged to, by, the Council of Trent was Transubstantiation. The Disingenuous Catholic Church.

But they did not put that on their paper; he did not think they dared to! He called that sort of thing disingenuous and, frankly, he did not like it. Still he was glad that in the district he had referred to there should be some- thing in the way of religious effort rather than nothing. What they had said was that they were the Catholic Church, and that they had invited Catholic members to come accompanied by non-Catholic friends. What he (the Rector) wanted to do 'was to form another centre up there belonging to the Parish Church. which he contended stood for the Holy Catholic Church, the Catholic faith,;-and for .Catholic worship. They had just the beginnings of such a church in the shape of their institute, and he hoped that when the war was over they would be able to go on and have there a flourishing mission, just as they had in the St. Clement's and St. George's districts. For that purpose he wanted another clergyman, to come and work in the Howley district, so that the Rev. Mr. Stanton might give his whole efforts to the Church Institute.
VICE-CHANCELLOR STEWART-SMITH AND WAR-TIME GIVING.
Must Be No Drying Up Of English Charity.

Vice-Chancellor Dudley Stewart-Smith, speak- ing on behalf of his wife, said that their primary object in coming there that day was, to help the congregation in raising the sum of 5.:250, or such larger sum as they might be able to get together. It was not easy at that time to raise money. The nation stood in a crisis absolutely unparalleled in its history. Not only the services, but the fortunes of every patriotic man and woman must be placed at the disposal of the State if the nation was still to preserve its greatness and they were to preserve their freedom as a people. Almost every day fresh demands were made upon them, either by the Government in the form of direct taxation, or by charitable appeals to help the soldiers, to help the Red Cross hospitals, or to help our Allies driven over the sea and now dwelling among us. They had responded to those 'appeals and were continuing to respond to them, and it would be wrong to say that there had been, during the fifteen months the nation had been at war, any drying up of the channel of Eng- lish charity. But, in the time that was coming, they would find themselves )in more strait- 'cued circumstances.

div.head: Duty of Every. Patriot.
div.p: The Duty of Every. Patriot.

It was the duty of every patriotic man and woman to devote not only personal service to the State in the present juncture, but also to so administer such. fortunes as, had beeit,entrusted .to them that thonation would obtain the utmost benefit. The question to-day was' not 'what they could afford to give; it was what they in justice could afford to keep. Outside the neces- sary maintenance of one's family on a reduced scale, all, that was theirs should be devoted to the service of the nation in some form or other. They must give up the luxury of accumulation; they must, so far as they justly could, even reduce the provision they were making for the future of themselves and those who would come after them. But, At the same time, they must not forget the father exceptional endeavours, such as that which brought them together that afternoon. They must not forget that there were charitable purposes. In times of struggle and distress, the thoughts of men and women turned to the spiritual side of their nature; all that material joy could give them was reduced to its true proportion—Land it was very little, after all, that material things could affect or help them. In such trouble as the nation was passing through at ' present they naturally turned to religion aild to their church. The Teaching of the Church.

They found in the teaching which they got in their church that which braced the nerves of the strong, which helped to strengthen the weak, and was a consolation in all trouble and mis- fortune,: Consequently it was of firstimportance that, in spite of all the extra strain, they should

div.head: CHURCH AT HIGH WATER-MARK OF EFFICIENCY.
div.p: CHURCH AT HIGH WATER-MARK OF EFFICIENCY.

Councillor Craik, one of the churchwardens. proposed a vote of thanks to the Vice-Chancellor and Mrs. Stewart-Smith, and in doing so re- marked that the requirements of the parish were heavy, and that the church official's always in- sisted upon keeping up the large Parish Church to the high water-mark of efficiency. Mr. R. T. Harding seeondei the vote of thanks, mentioning that the yice-Clianceibr and Mrs. Stewart-Smith had given to the war one who had proved himself a brave son. (Applause.) The proposition having be carried with applause, the Vice-Chancellor expressed his thanks, and the business of buying and sell- ing was then proceeded with,

div.head: SECOND DAY'S OPENING.
div.p: SECOND DAY'S OPENING.
Canon And Unifying Effect Of War.
On the second day the sale—which will be continued to-day—was formally declared open by the Rev. Wilfrid Stanton, of Thelwall.
"NO NEED FOR A POPE."

In Introducing the opener to the meeting, Canon Willis traversed some of the ground covered by him in his speech of the previous day, and, reterring to the fact that a mkt, school would in the near future be opened in the neighbourhood of the Church institute, said he was sure the secular education that would be given in that school would be as good as possible, and that the religious education would be as good as it could be as far as it went, but there would be no Church teaching given there. They knew that that school would in all probability 1343 a great attraction to a large number of people, so that the popu- lation would grow in that direction. The only spiritual provision was a new chapel which had been opened there—he was not going to say anything against the chapel—and a Roman Catholic Church which had been opened not very far off. Referring to the. forth,!oming special effort to be put forth in connection with St. Benedict's Church he commented upon the Catholic claim that there was need for a. Pope, and asserted that there was no need whatever for a Pope—for a head of the Church on earth. Jesus Christ was the only Head of the Church, both on earth and above. The Canon went on to say that he believed that one. result .of the war would be to draw all parts of the Church closer together; nay, he was sure that one result would be that the Eastern Church and the Anglican branch of the Western Church would be brought closer and closer together. Roumania, Bulgaria, Sersria, ,Greece, and Rus- sia all belonged to the Patriarchate of-Constan- tinople, and one grieved to think that the Bul- garians had thrown in their lot with the Ger- mans, Austrians and Turks.

div.head: Coldness of Greece.
div.p: The Coldness of Greece.

One could see why! , It was because their King was related to the German Emperor, and it was because the Queen of Greece was also a relative of the Kaiser's that Greece was so cold in the matter. Just as the Anglican Church repudiated the Papacy, so did the Eastern Church, haying done so , from the be- ginning. The Rector ' then called upon the Rev. Wilfrid Stanton to open the sale, and, in doing so, said that the - Parish Church and Warrington in general were very much in- debted to the reverend gentleman, both for spiritual and material help. They were all very sorry that the Rev. Stanton was going to leave the neighbourhood, and hoped that he would often visit them in the future. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: KEEP CHURCH WORK GOING.
div.p: KEEP CHURCH WORK GOING.

The Rev. Wilfrid Stanton, who was cordially received, then declared the sale open, and referred to the wrench it would be to him to leave the neighbourhood, bUt added that circumstances made it imperative that he should seek another residence. War- rington and district, however, would always have a warm place in his heart. Continuing, he said that it seemed to him that in a time of anxiety and trial like the present they had, more than ever, to see to it that the ministra- tions ,of,, the Church, above all things, were kept in a high state of efficiency.' Indeed, they. had to see to it that the whole of the organisa- tions of the Church were preserved in a state of even greater efficiency than usual, for at a time like the present the people naturally turned more and more to religion for help and consolation. Again, for the sake of the men who were fighting their battles, and who, after the war, would have a more firm belief in the truths of religion and would require more than formerly, the ministrations of the Church, they would require to keep their parochial organi- sations in an effective state. (Hear, hear.) Councillor J. T. Locker proposed, and Mr. E. H. Coates seconded, a vote of thanks to the Rev. Stanton, which was accorded with acclamation. FIRST DAY'S PROCEEDS.
The takings on the first day were £lO6 Os. 10d., apart from Lady Greenall's usual dona- tion and £5 from the lady-opener.
THE ENTERTAINMENTS.

On the first day a miscellaneous entertain- ment was given by the Misses Collin, N. Davis and Reynolds, Messrs. D. Scarisbrick, G. Walker and T. Humphries. On the second day members of the Girls' Friendly Society took part in an operetta.

div.head: "KEEP THINGS GOING."
div.p: "KEEP THINGS GOING."
St. Peter's church Bazaar Held "As Usual."
SUCCESSFUL WAR-TIME EFFORT.

The sale of work held annually on behalf of St. Peter's Church, Warrington, this year took place on Monday and Tuesday. On the first day it was opened by Mrs. Ireland Blackburne, who was acting as deputy for Mrs. Charlton Parr. who had hoped to be able to open the sale, but who found herself unable to do so. • A QUESTION ALL ARE ASKING?
Commencing the proceedings, the Vicar (the Rev. B. Percival), expressed his sorrow at the absence of Mrs. Charlton Parr, but extended a cordial welcome to Mrs. Ireland Blackburne.

Last year, he said, they met under a war cloud, and he was sorry to say that they met under the same cloud that day, indeed, the cloud was, perhaps a little more extended and, perhaps also, a little deeper than it was last year. Often the question was asked "How long will the war last?" That was a question which could not be answered by anyone in the world. They had no idea where the war was going to spread; and they did not know when the great war machine would break down. They had "tried, as far as possible, fo keep things going at home. They all knew that spiritual forces were th, strongest, and if they were to be strong abroad they must have spiritual things right at home and encourage the hearts of the people in eve' possible way. "A Very Excellent Work."

Therefore in keeping their business going a their organisation intact as far as possible they were doing a very excellent work. Mr Percival went on to thank the ladies who hak charge of the stalls, saying that he was ver, grateful to those who helped, and to those who contributed year by year. Lady Greenall had sent her usual contribution. (Applause.) Re- ferring to the distribution of the money from last year's sale, the reverend gentleman, said that 265 was given to the Curates' Fund; £25 to the Lay Helpers' Fund; £l2 10s. to the Churchwardens' Fund, and Ell 15s. to other organisations of the parish. In deUaring the sale open, Mrs. Ireland Blackburne emphasised the fact that the people at home had to do their best to keep things going.

She was accorded a vote of thanks on the pro- position of Mr. T. Reddish, who said that the name of Blackburne was one that was always honoured and revered in Warrington. Mr. G. Greaves seconded, and the proposal. was carried with applause, Mrs. Ireland Black- burn° suitably acknowledging the compliment. The business of buying and selling was then proceeded with. The stallholdess were:—
Vicarage Stall.—Mrs. Percival, Mrs. Greaves. Mrs. Kay, Mrs. East, Mrs. Lang and Miss Lily P'..r(•:‘ al.
Sunday School Stall.—Mrs Smith, Miss Hughes and Miss Booth.
Rareshment Stall.—Mrs. Ling ley, Mrs. Clay- ton, Mrs. Grounds, Mrs. Reddish, Mrs. Atkin- son, Mrs. Webster, Mrs. Skelland, Miss Nellie Grounds and Miss Pemberton.

Sweet Stall.—Miss Dorothy Fletcher and Miss Dorothy Houghton. Flower Stall.—Miss Marton and the Misses Young. The competitions were in the care of Mrs. Padmore, and the Misses Hardy ,had charge of the 'dips."
