div.head: SECOND DAY'S OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: SECOND DAY'S OPENING CEREMONY.
Mrs. Peter Rylands's Welcome Visit.
On the second day the sale was opened by Mrs. Peter Ilylands, who was accorded a hearty reception by a goodly attendance of buyers and workers.

The Rev. B. Percival briefly expressed the pleasure it gave the parishioners of St. Peter's once more to welcome Mrs. Rylands in their midst, and announced that the proceeds of the sale the previous day amounted to £75 us. 3d.

div.head: DIFFICULT PARISH.
div.p: A DIFFICULT PARISH.

Mrs. Rylands, in declaring the sale open, said that it was always a great pleasure to her to be able to do anything to help St. Peter's Church, a church in which she was deeply interested. She often thought what dreadfully hard work it must be for the Vicar to "Carry on so many organisations in a parish like that, where there were no rich residents. The poorer people could not afford to do very much in the way of money contributions at the present time, their position being rendered more difficult owing to the war. She knew the difficult task it was .t. get, up a bazaar and that it meant much hard work, and therefore she had great admiration for those who had succeeded in bringing that bazaar to fruition. She trusted that the final result would bv such as would amply reward them for all the hard work they had put in.

div.head: THANKS TO THE LADY OPENER.
div.p: THANKS TO THE LADY OPENER.

The sale being formally declared open, Mr. T. S. Steel, the Vicar's warden, moved a vote of thanks to Mrs. Rylands for her ser- vices in opening the sale, and said that he thought the first day's takings constituted a parochial record. Mrs. Rylands had rightly said that the work of a parish like that was very difficult, ,and, in the present_troublous times, it had been rendered more difficult still rm account of the claims made upon parish- ioners to support various organisations in con- nection with the war. In the best of times. the means of the majority of the people of the parish were not very great, and the church had largely to depend for support on outsiders. 'Mr. Thomas Reddish, the people's warden, in seconding the expression of thanks to Mrs. Rylands, said that it seemed to him as though that lady's life was largely made up of doing kind things. It must be a labour of love to her to come down to perform such a task as she had performed that afternoon. The par- ishioners of St. Peter's might not be. rich in this world's goods, but they were rich in gratitude to those who did kind acts.
The vote of thanks having been carried with acclamation, Mrs. Rylands briefly returned thanks, stating that it had been a real pleasure for her to come there that afternoon.
The second day's proceedings realised £57 15s. 541., making a total for the two days' sale of £133 Gs. 81d.

div.head: ST. JAMES', LATCHFORD. Raising Funds For Electric Light In Church.
div.p: ST. JAMES', LATCHFORD. Raising Funds For Electric Light In Church.

A sale of work was held on Thursday at the St. James' School, Latchford, for the purpose of raising a sum of money sufficient to cover the expense of the installation of elec- tric light at St. _James' Church. The sale was opened by Archdeacon - Maitland-Wood, the Rev. H. Firth (vicar) presid- ing over the inaugural ceremony. Other clergy present were Canon Acheson (an honorary canon of Chester Cathedral), the Rev. H. V. Pigot, the Rev. James Collins (vicar of Stockton Heath), 'the Rev. H. H. Corsbie (formerly of St. .tames' Church), and the Rev. C. F. Waller.

Opening the proceedings, the Chairman gave a cordial welcome to Archdeacon Maitland-Wood, who, he said, was no stranger to the parish of St. James'. The Rev. H. Firth also welcomed to the sale Canon Acheson.

A CHURCH THAT DOES ITS OWN WORK. Declaring the sale open, Archdeacon Maitland- Wood expressed his great satisfaction at coming into a parish church where the congregation did its 'own work. He had been a colleague of the Rev. H. 'Firth's for about ten .years, and knew what thorough good work he could do. The object of the sale was an admirable onc,and it seemed that the congregation, Vicar and wardens were determined to have their church thoroughly lighted. There was nothing that the Church of England liked better than having plenty of light. In their Church there was nothing to hide; if anything, the Church erred on the side of publicity. Sometimes they were given to " washing their dirty linen abroad." Al; times that sort of thing was dangerous, but on the whole, it was better that they should have plentt of light, than that anything should be kept back. Proceeding, the speaker said that he had no patience with the people who decried sales of work and bazaars. He had seen much good work done by people who could not give much money. It. was a most desirable thing that the people of the parish should work together and raise money for the church. He had great satisfaction in declaring the sale open. (Applause.) Archdeacon Maitland-Wood was heartily thanked for his services by the large number of peoi)le present, on the motion of the Rev. H. V. Pigot. .

NATIONAL REGISTER.
Rural Council And Payment For Preparation

div.head: AND WHITEHALL'S
div.p: AND WHITEHALL'S
ANSWER.
Mr. W. Furness presided over the monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural District Coun- cil, which as held at the Council's Offices in Bfiwsey-street, on Wednesday afternoon.

div.head: WAR AGRICULTURAL COMMITTEE.
div.p: WAR AGRICULTURAL COMMITTEE.

The Clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton) reported that the, Clerk.to the County -council (Mr. Harcourt Clare) had sent to the Chairman of the Council an important communication with reference to the War Agricultural Committee, enclosing therewith a letter received from the Board of Agriculture stating that it would be necessary to form district committees with regard to the matter of increasing the food supply of the country, and asking whether the Council would give facilities for the holding of meetings of farmers in the Council buildings, assuming a request for such accommodation was received from the different local agricultural associa- tions. He (the clerk) conferred with the Chair- man and wrote, in reply to the letter received, that he was authorised to say that so far Gs practicable the Council would give the facilities asked for.
The Council approved of the Clerk's action.
PAY FOR REGISTER-PREPARERS?

Mr. Sutton further reported that he wrote to the Registrar-General with regard to the matter of payment for the maintenance of the National War, Register, and the Registrar-General hail replied that he fUlly-appreciated the manner in which the additional duties imposed on local officials had been performed, and recognised that voluntary effort only could not be relied upon. The Local Government Board, to bem the Registrar-General referred him hail rerlied to him that the question of an allowance in connection with the Maintenance of the register as under their consideration, and that he would later on, make a further stat3raent en the sub- ject. "This," Mr. Sutton added, "is a very important work, as many as twenty-five altera- tions being received every morning." The Chairman said that the registratian work was growing rapidly, and involved a great deal of work on the part of the officials, and it had suggested itself to him that ,it was hardly fair for the Rural District Council to have to take upon themselves the conducting of the register, because it was taking the Council's men away from the clerical work which was ordinarily required of them and putting them on to work for which they got no pay. It followed, as a matter of course, that the imposition of this extra work meant that the ordinary work' of -the Council must be in a measure neglected. He believed that he had taken the right course in asking Mr. E. J. Sutton (assistant clerk) to take upon himself the responsibility of keeping in touch with the registration work. The Council were under no obligation to pay him for his extra services, but the Government would, no doubt, make provision later on for granting certain allowances for dealing with the work which might arise from time to time. The work required a great amount of detailed atten- tion.
The Rev. A. Me, Mitchell said that the worl: was only just really beginning, and it might even lead to the establishment of a new depart- ment. _ _

div.head: CONCERNING COAL PRICES.
div.p: CONCERNING COAL PRICES.

The Clerk said that another letter had been received re the Board of Trade's suggestion that the Council should consider whether it would not be possible to make an arrangement with the coal merchants of the district for a limitation of the profits from the retail sale of household coal. Mr. G. Mather said that the charge for coal was less in the rural district than it was in the town of Warrington. Mr. Kerfoot (the sanitary inspector) said that he found that the price in the rural district was about normal, as compared with the price charged in Warrington, viz.: Is. 3d. to Is. 30. a cwt. The Chairman said he thought they were satisfied that as far as possible the local traders were doing justice to the public.

div.head: SOLDIER'S DEATH AT WINWICK.
div.p: SOLDIER'S DEATH AT WINWICK.

The Acting Medical Officer (Dr. R. B. Sephton) mentioned in the course of his report that during the past month only one of the soldier-patients in the Lord Derby Hospital at Winwick had died. TO REPRESENT THE COUNCIL.

The Chairman and the Surveyor (Mr. B. S. Newcombe) were appointed to represent the Council at a forthcoming conference to be held in Manchester with a view to co-ordinating voluntary efforts for the turning out of com- forts for our soldiers.

div.head: HELP FOR BELGIANS.
div.p: HELP FOR BELGIANS.

The same two gentlemen were appointed to get into touch with the National Committee for the Relief of Indigent Belgians in Belgium with a view to organising another "Flag Day" in aid of the fund for relieving distress in the war-swept country of King Albert, his Majesty's birthday, November 15th, being suggested as an appropriate date. Mr. G. Mather said that he considered the cause a very good one to work for. He thought the people of this country should do all they could for the Belgian people.

div.head: MR. ASQU ITH'S STOCK-
div.p: MR. ASQU ITH'S STOCK-
TAKING.

Hr. Asquith's review of the situation has once again cleared, the air and inspired the country with increased confidence and resolu- tion. It leaves no opening for hostile critics to accuse the Government of endeavouring to suppress any essential in order to cover up mistakes or evade responsibility. In regard to the Dardanelles operations, which have been the chief cause of any division of opinion either in the Cabinet or in the country, the Prime Minister frankly admitted a great dis- appointment, and accepted the fullest respon- sibility, both personally, and for the whole Cabinet. But he stoutly refused to adopt a penitential attitude—" a white sheet and a candle in each hand "-Land scornfully re- torted on " the small coterie of professional whimperers" whose Press "constantly feeds the enemy with falsehoods." In an eloquent peroration, at which Sir Edward Carson thought fit to sneer, Mr. Asquith declared:

"I am as confident as I was fifteen months ago that we are . going. to carry a righteous cause to a triumphant issue. And lam not going to shift the burden that has been laid upon me until ,I. am satisfied that I cannot bear it, or, that it can be borne better by others." •

For those who try to belittle the achieve-• ments already accomplished and the efforts already put forth by the Empire, Mr. Asquith had an overwheln;ting and circumstantial answer. There are already nearly, a million men engaged in active operations in France, apart from the large forces we have employed elsewhere. The pominions have sent large contingents. The number of recruit g is "enormous." The figures given for the transport work carried out by. the Navy are astonishing, and on all this sea traffic the losses have been under one-tenth per cent. German commerce has ceased to exist. The German navy, on which so much treasure and skill have been expended, is locked up; in futile and exasperated impotence Germany's "furtive submarines" have been mastered by our vigilant patrol of the seas. A bril- liant series of successes in Mesopotamia has brought our expeditionary force within meas- urable distance of Bagdad. The effect of these successes upon our prestige and influence in the East is highly important, though Ilia campaign to the general public may appear only as a slight episode in the great drama of the World War.

In regard tp the Dardanelles operations, Mr. Asquith stated what had been long a matter of conjecture: that is, that the naval attack was undertaken in the face of doubts and hesitations on , the part of Lord Fisher, who was, of course, the First Sea Lord at that time. But that 'enterprise was not under- taken without careful consultation between the Admiral on the spot and the War Staff of the Admiralty here. It was entirely approved by the. French Admiralty, and enthusiastically acclaimed 'by the Grand. Duke Nicholas, the GeneralissiMo of the Russian Army. at was impossible at the time to send out a military force in co-operation. The subsequent com- bined ,expedition to Gallipoli has also resulted in disappointment. But it has held up, and is holding now,, a force of. some 200,000 Turks. It probably prevented 'a serious Russian set- back in the Caucasus; it averted a great at- tack on Egypt, and extreme danger to the Mesopotamia • expedition. Nor can there ,be any, reasonable doubt that it delayed, for
months, the entry of Bulgaria into the alliance with the Central Powers.

div.head: SINGLE MEN FIRST.
div.p: SINGLE MEN FIRST.

Some friction has been caused by a misunder- standing as to the method in which single men and married men, respectively, who offer themwlves to their King ,will be called upon to join .the colours. The Prime Minister ex- plained the situation clearly as follows :

I am told by Lord Derby and others that there is some doubt among married men who are now being asked to enlist whether they may not be called upon to serve, having enlisted, or prom- ised to enlist, while younger and unmarried men are holding back and not doing their duty. Let them disabuse themselves of that idea. So far as I am concerned, I stould certainly say the obligation of the married man to enlist ought not to be enforced or binding upon him unless and until—l hope ,by voluntary effort and, if not, by some other means—the unmarried men are dealt with first.

That Means, and was intended to mean, that before the married Men are taken each "group" of unmarried men must have done its duty—and if it has not dope its duty, vol- untarily, "some other means ", will be adopted. It rests with the unmarried men to -see that the "some other means" have not to be applied. For our part, we have never doubted for one moment that the men will be forthcomin without compulsion—and as liber- ally in numbers aa freely in action. The local election agents are still appealing for men and women canvassers to .undertake the necessary recruiting duties. If the volun- teers for this work Niere as plentiful as they ought to be, they would have less than six men each to visit. That is not a very big task for a man who is clear of war duty to per- form for love of his country.

div.head: "OLD FOX."
div.p: THE "OLD FOX."

If an Englishman's house is his castle, as *e have always been taught, the articles IN*"1-1101 Mr. A. Moupfield is contributing to our columns ought to have interest for everybody, for they tell how. the home came to be what it is. The facts given concerning medimval houses. certainly will not set anyone sighing for the good old days, and the vision of chim- neyless houses will produce creepy feelings among womenfolk. But after a perusal hf the article in this issue we ,imagine that all our readers will want to pay a visit. to the "Old Fox" to study the mysteries of wattle, daub, and timber framing.

We imagine that all Warringtonians will approve of the decision to preserve the " Old Fox " by re-erecting it in one of the Parks. We have few examples left of timber-built houses, and none of them are so complete or so suitable for preservation as the old inn. Those who reflect only upon the cost need to be rentinded that it is no mere fad that prompts the suggestion. An old building, left open to the public, is. a. perpetual object les- son. of how our fathers _built and how they lived. It will be interesting to young folk who are learning history; and will be prized more and more in future days.

The Council have decided to preserve this valuable piece of ancient local architecture, but we believe they never passed on to .wags and means stage.- That iA li,difficult point just now; but we suggest thiat. some local lady or gentleman of means might provide the funds. It Would be doing a public service that would create lasting and valuable associations.

div.head: £8 FOR SOLDIER'S BELT.
div.p: £8 FOR SOLDIER'S BELT.
Fancy Price Realised At Second War
Auction.

So many gifts were Sent in at the last moment for inclusion in the war fund sale by auction conducted by Mr. Herbert Johnson last week, that on Wednesday: evening of this week he ,had, at the Parr Hall, to hold a supplementary sale for the purpose of clearing out .the large stock left on hand owing to want of time to sell it. Again there was a large attendance of buyers, and the sum of £B2 was realised, which, added —to the £95 realised .at the first sale, brought the total to be divided between the Red Cross ,Funds at .Raddon Court, Thelwall Heys and Oaklands Hospitals; the local Tobacco Fund for providing smokes for the wounded soldiers in the Warrington district, and the fund for the purchase ofcomforts for prisoners from the South Lancs. Regiment who were resi- dent in Warrington, up to nearly £lBO, a very satisfactory am9unt, and, one which the, funds concerned will find of great service. The sale lasted long, indeed 'eleven o'clock was about to strike before the last lot was offered. The most interesting lot put up took the form of a belt knitted, by a wounded soldier in the Raddon Court Hospital. He was one of the men saved .from a boat which went down in the Dardanelles. The belt fetched £8 us. 6d., Mr. J. H. Smethurst becoming the possessor after it had, been bought and 'sold twenty-six times.
APPEAL FROM THE TRENCHES.

div.head: Penketh Man Calls His Workmates To
div.p: Penketh Man Calls His Workmates To
Arms.
We have received the following letter, dated October 30th :

Sir,—l hope lamin no way causing' you any inconvenience in asking you to put these few lines in your valuable paper, which I have read for years, and which is weekly sent to me, 'Somewhere in Prance.' I joined the A.S.C. September 11th, 1914, having previously served in the local battalion, which has earned .such a glorious name for its prowess on the battlefield. "I send this appeal to the young men of Penketh to .help and .keep up the traditions of the South Lancashire Regiment; also to relieve them in the arduous work which they have endured for months. So, young men of Pen- keth, I appeal to you, as your friend and work- mate, to answer your country's urgent call, and to aid the gallant Serbs against the hordes which are sweeping down upon them. You have often earned the praise.of the public for your keen sportsmanship, but how much greater the praise when you voluntarily answer the call in such a noble cause. I know the village has responded well to ,Lord Derby's appeal, but still there are many more left, who are more suitable for military life than those who have recently joined. . If You Could Only See!

"If you could only see the ruin and devasta- tion--.-whole villages raised. to the ground—and understand the cold-blooded way Miss Cavel was murdered, I am sure you would acclaim in one Voice': aro arms!' and down with the kul- tured Huns, who have made France into a huge cenietery, and caused thousands of widows and orphans. So it lies with such men as you whether they repeat such outrages on the poor Serbians, who are crying, out for help, like a child to its mother, in their distress. Now is the time, men! No 'wait and see!' but join, at once and show the bull-dog breed of Penketth. By doing so you will save married men being torn from their wives and families. So he men and act as men in the defence 'of our noble Empire. ,C4Od save the Bing, and may his . armies ever be victorious..
"From your old workmate. BENNETT."

Prosperous Warrington. There .should have been a monthly sitting of, the Warrington Bankruptcy Court yester. day, but it was found unnecessary, no debtors having filed their, petitions---a fact which Speaks well for trade and commerce in the :town.

div.head: LATE MR. HARRY HEY.
div.p: THE LATE MR. HARRY HEY.
Quarter Of A Century In Messrs. Rylands's Works.

We regret to record the death of Mr. Harry Hey, of 1, Boundary-street, Warrington, which took place suddenly on Saturday morning last from heart failure. The deceased gentleman was making preparations for his departure to work, when he passed the remark that he was "not feeling very well." Before medical assist- ance could be procured he passed away. The late Mr. Hey, whose .age was 49; years, was highly esteemed by a host of friends. For over 26 years he was employed by Messrs. Rylands Bros., in whose works he was departmental manager over the .continuous wire-drawing de- partmen.t. His geniAlity and good fellowship endeared him to the hearts of his workmen, who

div.head: LATE MR. HE V.
div.p: THE LATE MR. HE V.

paid their last tribute to his memory by walk- ing in procession at the funeral. Fond of all classes of sport, he took a kindly interest in the doings of the Works Recreation Club, which interest earned- him the gratitude of more than one official. His religious attach- ment was the Parish Church. .

The interment took place at the Cemetery on Wednesday, in the presence of numerous mourners: Behind the cortege were managers and other members of the staff of Messrs. Rylands Bros., accompanied by the whole of the workmen in the deceased gentleman's de- partment. Before the interment Mr. B. Farrar, of the Wycliffe Congregational Church, conducted a brief service and paid an eloquent tribute to tM virtues of the deceased. The committal prayers were ,read by the ,Rev. C. F. Waller, curate of St. James'. Many handsome floral tributes were received, including those from the following: Mrs. M. J. Jones (mother) and children, Mr. and Mrs. Dakin (uncle and aunt), Miss Annie Taylor (daughter-in-law), Mr. and Mrs. J. Taylor (uncle and aunt), Mr. and Mrs. Blagbrough and family (Halifax), Mr. H. Ashton and friends, and Mr. and Mrs. A. E. Denham. The following depart- ments of Messrs. Rylands's works also sent tri- butes: Office staff, works staff, employes con- tinuous wire--drawing department, employes steel department, engineer department. The mem- bers of the Works Recreation Club also sent a wreath.

div.head: CHANGING COAST LINES.
div.p: CHANGING COAST LINES.
When Trent And Thames Were Rhine Tributaries.

Mr. G. A. Dunlop, of the Warriugt Dri Museum, giving an illustrated lecture to the Natural Science Society of Chester, at the Grosvenor Museum, Chester, on "Changes in the Wirral Coast," explained the map of Great Britain before the Glacial period, and showed that Britain in those far-off days rested on a part of land stretching from Scandinavia to France. The Rhine once flowed through the North Sea, emptying itself into the ocean above the Shetland isles, and had as tributaries all the great rivers of the East of England. Passing from the Ice ages to later Pleistocene times he dealt with the great changes in land and sea level that took place then, until the time when the coast line of Lancashire and Cheshire began to assume something like its present shape. Dealing with more recent .and historic times, the lecturer referred to the map of Ptolemy, the great Roman geographer, and the work of the late Thomas Glazebrook Rylands in connection with it. The Mersey Estuary.

Ptolemy's map raised the question ,of the Mersey eStuary, which the lecturer maintained did not exist hr Roman times. No mention is made of the Mersey estuary by. any Roman writer, not even Tacitus, although Roman soldiers were- constantly marching North and South to and from North Wales to stations in the North of England. The next map thrown .on the sdreen was that of ,John. SPeede in 1610, ,which 'shows the Mersey 'entering the sea via the Dee, along the route where the Ellesmere CanaL now is. !Mr. Dunlop went on to deal with the problems raised and the 'coastal chanw.,_s brought about since the Mersey found its new outlet through the Crosby Channel.

div.head: Coast Erosion.
div.p: Coast Erosion.

The questions of subsidences and coast erosion were next referred to, the coast line from Wallasey to Meols being examined in detail, showing that during • the last 400 years land measuring from two to four miles hud been robbed by the- sea. The changes at Leasowe Castle, the lighthouse, and the old weather- beaten house the " Warren " were shown from actual records taken.

The lecturer next gave a survey of the famous submerged forest at Dove Point, and gave an instructive account of the long occupation by man through long successive periods of English civilisation, as evidenced by some of the 8,000 objects of agriculture, tools, buildings, dress, ornaments and pottery found on the site. In the discussion which followed, the Chair- man (Mr. J. Bairstow), Mr. W. E. Brown, the Secretary of the Geological Section (Alderman Egerton Gilbert) and the Honorary General Secretary of the Society (Mr. G. P. Miln) took part. The proceedings closed with a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Dunlop for his very able and interesting lecture.

div.head: MASONIC INSTALLATION.

The New Master Of " Friendship "

The new W.M. invested his officers as fol- lows:--S.W., Bro. J. .Upson; J.W., Bro. C. Garton Stone; chaplain; Bro. the •Rev. 11. V. Pigot, P.P.G.Ch.; treasurer,: Bro. T. J. Lee, P.P.G.D.; secretary, Bro. ,11. H. Evans, P.M.; S.D., Bro.' Sydney Walihead; J.D., Bro. J. E. Birtles; D.C., Bro. W. Greenhouse, P.P.G.D.• organist, Bro. Frederick Webster; 1.G., Bro. .1. H.. Clarke; S.S., Bro. R. N. Silcock; J.S., Bro. IT. B. Monck; A.S., Bro. H. H. •Taylor; A.S., Bro. J. T. Cooper; tyler, Bro. G. S. Rice.

Election of Mayor.
The annual meeting of the Town Council for the election-of Mayor, -committees,. and the transaction of other routine business, will take Place 'at noon on Tuesday.

div.head: Medal for the Mayoress.
div.p: A Medal for the Mayoress.

The Mayoress has been presented with a bronze medal bY the Joint Committee of the Red Cross Society and the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, as a small token of their appre- ciation of her efforts in raising £6OO for the Warrington Motor Ambulance for the Front.

div.head: Coming Liberal Teas.
div.p: Coming Liberal Teas.

Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield will be present at a Women's Liberal War Sewing Class tea and concert to be held at the John Crosfield Memorial Hall for the Orford Ward on December 6th, and for the Town Hall and Bewsey Wards on December 7th.

div.head: Scarlet Fever Still Rife.
div.p: Scarlet Fever Still Rife.

During the week ended October 30th twenty- five scarlet fever cases were reported, showing that the epidemic which has troubled the town for months past is still with us. There were, on October 30th, no fewer than 106 scarlet fever cases in the Borough Hospital. Fewer Births: More Deaths.,

The Medical Officer of Health's weekly return shows that for the seven days ended October - 30th forty-two births were registered in the borough, twenty-two of "the -little strangers" being boys. The deaths during the same period numbered 22. In the corresponding week of last year there were 55 births and only 17 deaths.

div.head: Assessments Reduced.
div.p: Assessments Reduced.

A meeting of the Warrington Union Assess- ment Committee was held on Friday morning, Mr. W. Furness being in the chair. Several applications for reductions in rateable value were heard, and in each case a reduction was granted.
Brick-street Missitn Choir Sermons.

The choir .sermons in connection with the Brick-street Independent Methodist Mission will be preached to-morrow. by Mr. Boyd, of St. Helens. 'ln the afternoon the choir will render the, cantata "The King of Glory," and they will also give two special anthems at the even- ing service.

div.head: Branches of the Church.
div.p: The Branches of the Church.

The Rev. IL Bedford Pim will lecture at the Patten Hal}, Winmarleigh-street, on, Fridays, November 12th. and December 10th. His sub- ject will be "The Church of England in rela- tion to the other branches of the Church in Europe—Russia, France, Italy and Germany:" The lectures are arranged by the Warrington Church Sockety.
Golborne-street Baptists' Sale of Work.

On Thursday a sale of work was held in the Golborne-street Baptist Church, at which a goodly number .were present, the object of the sale being the realising of a substantial amount SO as to pay off the interest on the half-yearly mortgage.—ln declaring the sale of work open the Pastor (the Rev. H. Ogden) remarked on the difficulty of the position of the church and regretted that so many of its members resided a distance away.. He paid a glowing tribute to the men of the congregation who had joined the Forces, and said that the fact that so many had volunteered accounted for so few men being present.—The majority of the stock for disposal represented the remainder left over from the annual sale of work held a short time ago.

div.head: Death of a Warrington Grocer's Widow.
div.p: Death of a Warrington Grocer's Widow.

It is with deep regret we have to announce the death of Mrs. Sarah Jane Leigh, widow of the late Mr. Peter 'Leigh, who carried on business as a grocer, wine and spirit merchant, at 7, Horsemarket-street, since the year 1862 until the time of his death. The deceased lady had rather a serious illness Some years ago, but lately had been in much improved health. ;!le passed away very suddenly on Wednesday -morning at her residence, 9, Mount-street, at the age of 72 years. She was of a very retiring disposition. Generosity was a marked trait of Mrs. Leigh's character, and she did much good work in a quiet and unassuming manner. She leaves a family of three sons and two daughters to mourn their loss. ,The funeral will 'take place at noon to-day at the Warrington Ceme- tery.

div.head: Late Mr. James Broadhurst.
div.p: The Late Mr. James Broadhurst.

The funeral of the late 'Mr. James Broad- hurst, of 33, Oldham-street, Latchford, who died at the age of 55, took place at the War- rington Cemetery last Sunday. Wreaths were sent by: "With deepest sympathy from his loving wife and "ills son Peter," "Daughter Sarah and son-in-law and chil- ren," "Brother Will and Jane," " Sister Ann, and. family," "Sister Lizzie and 'family," "Sister Mary and children," Mr. and Mrs. Shepherd and family, Mr. and Mrs. Hough, Mrs. Thload- hurst and family, Mr. and Mrs. Lloyd, " His Friends at the Liberal Club, Members of the Warrington .Works' Amateur Bowling Associa- tion, • Mrs. Rigby, His fellow-workers at Flet- cher, Rusgell's, Mrs. A. Atherton, Mr. and Mrs. Kay &Golden Lion), His Friends at the Golden Lion, Mr. and Mrs. J. Atherton and family.

The late Mr. Broadhurst, who leaves a widow, And grown-up family, worked for Messrs. Flet- cher, Russell & Co. He was a well-known Warrington "bowler and a great - lover of spOrt in his younger days. He-was a member' of the Liberal 'Club.

div.head: Baptist Missionary Wepk.
div.p: Baptist Missionary Wepk.

Last Sunday the annual missionary services in connection with the Baptist movement were held throughout the churches in the district, the .missionary deputation this year including the Rev. E. C. Smyth, a veteran missionary from China, and one of the most acceptable deputations connected with this sphere of work. In the morning the Rev. Sixiyth preached at Hill Cliffe Baptist Church and in the evening at the Latchford Baptist Church, in Wash- lane. There was an afternoon service at the Golborne-street Church, and it was of special interest, the room being full of scholars and members of the Boys' Brigade, who attended in uniform. An interesting and educational lecture was given by the Rev. E. C. Smyth on "Child-life in China." The chairman was the Rev. H. Ogden,' pastor of the church, who took the evening service. An excellent solo was effectively rendered by Mr. Turton. Mis- sionary services have been continued through- out the week in the country districts, meetings being, held at Little Legh, Widnes and Acton Bridge. •

div.head: Latchford Cadet Corps.
div.p: The Latchford Cadet Corps.

A most enjoyable social was given by the above Corps on Thursday in the Cairo-street Schools. About 160 were present. The pro- gramme opened with a laughable sketch "The Master Spy," played by members of the Corps, who must be congratulated upon their excellent portrayal of the various characters. Madame Lily Fairhurst charmed the audience with her beautiful rendering of "An Englishman's Home" and "Two Eyes of Grey." Mr. J. W. Warburton gave in good style "There's a Land" and " Lighterman Jim." Sergeant F. IL 'MvCollam, a late officer of the Corps, gave a good rendering of "Asleep in the Deep" and ".When the Ebb Tide Flows." Humorous selections "The Village Bazaar" and "11.69 ExpresS," contributed by Mr. Gordon B. Starkey, who was well received, concluded a very successful programme. Mr. G. Starkey was the accompanist. Mr. J. B, Starkey. who presided, stated that 24 members of the Corps had answered the country's call. He regretted to sEty four had been killed in action, and five wounded. He was very proud to be connected with the Corps, who certainly gave a lead to the young mtin of the town. The Cadets looked very smart in their uniforms, and carried their duties .out admirably. Special thanks are ,due to the artistes, to the ladies, and to all who assisted in any way to make the social a success-. The proceeds are to be .devOted to the local Prisoners of War and the Corps Band Funds. . , .

div.head: Sir Gilbert Greenall's Irish Estate.
div.p: Sir Gilbert Greenall's Irish Estate.

Sir Gilbert Greenall has appointed Mr. Henry Renshaw as agent to his estate at Mount Coote, Kilmallock, co. Limerick. Mr; • Renshaw waF, formerly in charge of the University Farm at Cambridge, and more recently was agent to. the Histon estates of Messrs. Chivers an SGIIS-

div.head: Licences Transferred.
div.p: Licences Transferred.

• At the Licensing Transfer Sessions, held at the Borough Court on Monday, the following- transfers were granted: Lion Hotel, Bridge- street, from John Wells (deceased) to James Fulton-Smith; beer off-licence, 271, Thelwall- lane, from Mary Lythgoe to Joseph Fairclough Cucksey; 'beer and wines off-licence, 22, Coek- hedge-lane, from James Powell to Daniel Mahoney.

Choir Sunday At The Parish Church.- Sunday last was observed as Chi:dr Sunday at the P,arish Church, when there were goodly-sized: congregations both morning and evening. Smart's " Te Deum " was rendered .by the choir at the morning service, and at the evening ser- vice two numbers from Mendelssohnts "Elijah" were given, the aria "Hear ye, Israel," being. rendered by Master Neville Davies. and the ch.)ir singing the chorus "Be not afraid." The offer- tories were devoted to the choir fund.

Central Picture Palace: A Correction. In last Saturday's "Examiner" there appeared an advertisement stating that in consequence of the increased costs caused by the war various picture houses in Warrington had decided to raise their prices of admission. Mr. Griffin, manager of the Central Picture Palace, Sankey street, was given as one of the signatories to the agreement. This was an error, Mr. Griffin having decided to retain the prices she has hitherto charged.

div.head: School Children's Help.
div.p: School Children's Help.

The following sums of money have been sent from Fairfield Day School during the last twelve months: Foreign Missions, ct 3 10s. Bd.; War- rington Motor Ambulance, £3 Bs. Id.; Princess Mary's Christmas Fund, £9 35.; Y.M.C.A. huts, £8 168. 6d.; French Relief Fund, 12s. 4(1.; Red Cross and St. • John Ambulance, £5 16s. 3d.; total, £3l 6s. 10d. In addition, this school has adopted four prisoners of war in Germany, and despatches two boxes of food weekly at a value of 3s. each. We thank both children and par- ents for this practical expression of loyalty and sympathy.—" Parish Church Magazine."

div.head: All Souls' Day.
div.p: All Souls' Day.

TuesdAy was All Souls' Day, and. it was ob- served in the local Roman Catholic Churches in the usual manlier, with this addition that, in- cluded in the Masses were those said for "the repose of the souls" of all, both friend and foe, who have fallen in the war. The Rev. Father Basil Mawson, assisted by the Rev. Father T. A. Hind, deacon, and the Rev. Father Philip Will- son as sub-deacon, conducted a Requiem High Mass at St. Mary's, -Buttermarket-street. Assisted by Fathers Hind and Willson, Father Mawson gaie the absolution for the dead. The Gregorian Chant was sung by a male choir, Mr John tekersley being at the organ.

div.head: B.W.T.A.
div.p: B.W.T.A.

The monthly. meeting of the Warrington branch of, the British Women's Temperance Association was held in the Bold-street Wes- leyan Church Parlour on Wednesday evening. The President (Mrs. Owen) was in the chair,. and a very helpful temperance address was given by Mrs.. Lloyd Jones, of Latchford. The association have been holding a series of even- ings of cheer for the wives and mothers of the local soldiers and sailors on active service, and these gatherings having proved of much benefit, it has been decided to hold another on Decem- ber Ist, in the Working Men's Mission School- room, Bank Quay, at which refreshments wif be provided free of charge.

div.head: Brave Boy.
div.p: A Brave Boy.

Arthur Andrew, aged 13 years, of Algernon- street, Warrington, who some time ago pluckily saved the life of. a little -boy, was publicly re- warded and praised by the Mayor of Warring- ton (Alderman Peter Peacock), at the Borough Police Court on Monday morning. On August 29th, Andrews pulled a boy named Shaw, who resides at Mersey-street, out of a pond near the Twelve Arches, Arpley. Presenting him with a certificate and 15$. postal order, the Mayor said he had been asked to make Andrews this award for his gallant conduct, when another boy was in danger 01 losing his life. Andrews very pluckily went into the water and saved the lad. The certifi- cate was the highest award that the Bench could give him. The boy's father briefly thanked .the Mayor.

div.head: Shorthand Writers' Association.
div.p: Shorthand Writers' Association.

The members of the Warrington Shorthand Writers' -Association held their first annual meeting on Friday evening of last week. An interesting programme for the ensuing session has been arranged, making provision for abund- ant epeed, practice. Several evenings have been set apart for lectures, the first of which will be given by Mr. Madeley at the . Museum Lecture Room on Friday evening, November 26th, at 7.30. In addition to the valuable speed practice given, examinations by the National Shorthand Association are held quar- terly at reduced fees to members. Meetings are ,held every Friday evening at 7.30,- in the Win- marleigh Cafe. The qualification for member- ship is a speed of GO words per minute. The secretary is Mr. Metcalfe, of Marbury-street, Warrington.

div.head: Value of Sales of Work.
div.p: Value of Sales of Work.

"Sales of work are apt to be spoken of in rather contemptuous tones by unthinking per- sons,' writeF the Rev. IT.B.Firth, n 'St. Jane- Parn. Dlagazlne,""but-ve shoub., br, very ha.lly off without them. Within the last twelve years we .have made a. variety of expensive improve- ments to the church and school in this parish, and we have built a new Mission Church. Some £3,000 has been expended on these undertakings, which are manifestly good and useful, and the greatest help that we have received has come through the sales of work which have now be- come quite an institution with us. In a few weeks' time it is hoped that the church will benefit greatly by the introduction of electric light, and it is the sale of work that we are look- ing to to provide the funds; so please come and add ,your own. contribution towards its success."

A "Disgusting Habit." The Rev. H. B. Firth, in "St. James' Parish Magazine," says : "The solemn season of Advent begins on November 28th, and on the same Sunday opens our new Sunday school year. lam gravely con- cerned about Sunday school prospects. From one end of England to the other the same sad story is forthcoming—Sunday schools are not so well attended as they were. Parents are less careful about sending their children, the dis- gusting habit of rising very late on Sunday mornings—too late for school and church—is, very prevalent—children are allowed to 'go where they like,' and the result of all these and other causes is that Sunday schools do not flour- ish as much as they did. We are hoping for a revival in this matter, and we exhort all Church- people to help the clergy in this respect. We desire a large influx of new scholars, or of those who for various reasons have not been in oat- tendance at our schools lately, on Advent Sun- day, November 28th. Please do 'your best to make our desires become effective."

div.head: Devoted Sunday School Worker.
div.p: A Devoted Sunday School Worker.

The “Wesleyan Methodist Church Record," re- ferring to the celebration of Mr. R. Corbett's twenty-one years' honourable and faithful ser- vice in connection with the Bewsey-road Sunday school, says: "This service has not been limited by any means, but one cannot do full justice to ,him without recognising particularly his de- votedness to the school, in the capacity of super- intendent, for it is chiefly due to his guiding hand that the school holds such a high position in local Methodism. His tact and forbearance, coupled with his persistency, have ever been a marked feature in his efforts to win the young lire of our Sunday school for Christ, and which has both endeared him to the hearts of the scholars and teachers alike. It was only fitting that this gathering together should be taken advantage of by recognising in a small but tangible way such faithful service, and through the instrumentality of the senior scholars (past as well as present) and teachers, a finely uphol- stered easy chair and reading desk were pre- sented to him.". . .

div.head: "UNSTARRED."
div.p: THE "UNSTARRED."
F` Straight Question " Put To " The Eligibles " :
"ARE YOU GOING TO 'JOIN UP ' ? "

The " unstarred " men of Wo rrington are this week having "the straight question" put to them: "Are you going to take up arms for your country, and if not, why not?" In other words Lord Derby's recruiting scheme has been in progress, and voluntary workers have., been engaged in paying calls upon such men as are of military age, with, we learn, encouraging success. The task is a big one, and has not yet been. completed, so it is impossible to• tabulate results, but it is confidently expected that the many "heart-to-heart" talks between the would- be recruiters and the should-be recruited will be found to tell a gratifying tale at the office where, the doctor passes; the recruiting officer attests and the list of the nation's patriots is kept.
HOW. THE " OVER-AGED".HAVE HELPED
AND CAN HELP!

• Of course, the interviewing .has been ..done by men over military age, and by ladies, and. the 'districts which they have worked, and. are still working, were apportioned to •them by the Civilian. Recruiting Committee, through its two honorary organising secretaries, Mr. Ernest A. Sanders. and Mr. Herbert .Hayes. The com- mittee .has its headquarters at 3, Horsemarket- street, and as there is still plenty of ,work to do, volunteers for canvassing will be welcomei. By giving .assistance in this matter those who, by reason of age or sex, are debarred from render- ing more active service will be able later on to lay to their souls the flattering unction that, if they could not go to fight themselves, they did .at least all they •could to persuade those who can and should go.

. CHANCE FOR TALL AND SHORT ALIKE! , Tall men are being asked to joi n any of the ordinary branches of the - Army; short men— those between sft. and sft. 2in.—.are urged to hand in their .names for the Bantam, Battalion of the South Lancs. Regiment, now being raised ,at Orford Barracks—the "Little-and-good Twelfth " as they have been dubbed. And, by the .way, these soldier lads of .few inches and stout hearts look so neat and business-like on Parade that one sometimes wonders why-, in the past, it has always been considered necessary to have none but the very tall or the compara- tively tall for the Army. It is possible that the present one may .be the last opportunity that the short men-may have of " joining up " with their " pals " in an ex- clusively "bantam" battalion, and 'so it be- hoves them to hurry along to the recruiting station.

div.head: IF NOT THE ARMY PROPER, WHY NOT
div.p: IF NOT THE ARMY PROPER, WHY NOT
THE RESERVE?

Opportunity is given to men to join the new Army Reserve; but, welcome as'recruits for this branch of the Army are, they aFe doubly- welcome for the ordinary branches,---the branches that will put a recruit into training immediately and make a soldier of him, as quickly as possible, so that he may *go but into the war-zone and prove the worth of his man- hood and his patriotism. Men who join the new Army Reserve Will remain in their present civilian occupations until the classes Of men in which they are placed shall be called up. During the week, in addition to the practical work of putting the'" straight question," pub: lie appeals have been Made to the young men by means of recruiting meetings held in "a place where people oft do congregate "; viz., Market Gate.

div.head: "MEN. MUST NOW AWAKE!"
div.p: "MEN. MUST NOW AWAKE!"

The most recent of such meetings was held lastnight, and one of the first—one of the first, that is, in . connection with the present .great effort—took Place On Saturday evening, when a Crowd that almost blocked the thoroughfare assembled to 'hear Captain Mathams (who has charge of the recruiting work at the Drill Mall) and Mr. Chas. Plinston make their appeal .for "men. and still more men:"

The burden of the gallant captain's speech was that men must now awake to the fact that it they are fit for military work they must he up. and doing i, and not dallying any longer and leaving their share of the responsibility to be borne by somebody else. The men Of the coun- try had got to be made to realise to the utmost the fact that the situation is a grave one. "When the War began," continued the captain, "men said it would be over quickly, that the British •Navy would bottle up the German fleet, -and that Germany would be starve&

div.head: One Wonderful Thing.
div.p: One Wonderful Thing.

.`.`There is one thing in this war which is abso- lutely wonderful. People in the years to come Will read how Germany was able to sustain the ravages, of -war, to feed her people and to? send ttn army into any part of the theatre of war. When we thought they ought to be getting tired they drove the Russians back, and • when the Russians by heroic efforts stemmed the tide they , turned southwards, and they are rushing through Serbia to-day. We blocked them on the Western and Eastern fronts, ..but. the clues.- tion is, Are we able, at the beginning of wiliter; in an inaccessible country, to block them on their march to Constantinople?' •I don't want to be misunderstood; I don't want to say that the war is lost, or that it will be—far from it, for I firmly believe in • the destiny of the British people, and hold thlit they are, better qualified to rule than any other nation. I look into the dark places of the earth, savage Africa • and else- where, but whertwer I look I see that justice and liberty hold sway under the British flag. Because I see that I am proud that I am a Briton. It is because I believe all these things that I venture to suggest that unless we take decisive action now, and if we become careless and short of, energy, the Germans May succeed in their latest movement. They are a powerful and 'a determined people„ .and if they succeed, it will bea 'ease of Good-bye to liberty and justice, and to all the freedom we have :hitherto en- joyed !" .

div.head: DEEDS, NOT WORDS.
div.p: DEEDS, NOT WORDS.

Mr. Plinston, who was accorded -a good recep- tion, and who spoke first,. asked the men of Warrington not to let their -aUrniration for the voluntary system stop at 'speaking about it, but to show their 'appreciation for it by joining up under it, and thus 'doing away with the neces sity for any other and more drastic system. It was an Old saying that "What Lancashire thinks to-day England thinks to-morrow," and if Lan- cashire set.,the .example in this matter of 're- cruiting he believed that the rest_of the country would follow, and that the men would roll in in the numbers required,. "We , want," said . Mr. Plinston, by way of conclusion, "to be able to have, the proud boast. at the end..of this great war that we did our part- in it, .and helped .to win it, under the good old voluntary system, and not :under any system of compulsion" The speeches were frequently punctuated by applause.
WHAT WE ARE FIGHTING FOR. " Great, High and Noble Principles."

Another meeting was held at the same place on Monday evening, when Captain Mathams again spoke, reminding his audience of what the ." sons of , the Motherland" from the great Colonies across the seas had done, and asking those among his hearers of military age and fit- ness whether they were going to be behind their brothers and cousins on the. outposts of • the Empire in defending the very heart of that Empire and in keeping the old flag flying and the old country and its womenfolk inviolate? Mr. E. Wynne Jones also spoke, remarking that this country and her brave Allies, were fighting for the 'great, high and noble principles and with the object of, once and for all, break- ing down the power of an arrogant military caste and bringing about a newer and brighter *lay for the whole of the world.
FIVE HUNDRED CANVASSERS WANTED.

The Warrington @than Recruiting Com- mittee require the serVices of five hundred can- vassers, and make an appeal to the men and women of the town to 'come forward immedi- ately and enrol themselves as honorary workers for the next few .weeks. ,They also require the loan Of motor cars. ,The committee's head- qUarters are at 3, Horsemarket-street.
Soldiers To Help Police Court Mission.
' In aid of the local Police Court Mission a concert will be given in the Latchford Parish Room on Thursday evening next by the patients of the Raddon Court nospital.
WOUNDED. Private Wesley Kettle.
PRISONER. Private Henry Herbert James.
MISSING. Lance-Corporal Archibald E. Freeman. Private Gilbert Roughley. Private W. Coyne. Private J. D. Renshaw.
TOTAL CASUALTIES TO DATE.\ Killed, 91; wounded, 427; missing, 16; prisoners, 2; total, 536.
WOUNDED.
PRIVATE V. KETTLE.
Well-known Local Pigeon Fancier " in AVqed." _ _ _ • _
Mrs. Kettle, who resides at 44, Leonard- street, has been officially informed that her husband, Private Wesley Kettle, of the War-

rington Territorials, has been wounded. He is now in hospital at Aldershot, his injury con- sisting of a gunshot wound in the buttock. He recently wrote to his wife saying that he was progressing favourably. Six Relatives Serving.

Private Kettle, who is twenty-eight years of age, is a native of Colchester, but has lived in Warrington for the, past ten years. He was formerly employed, by Messrs. 'Pearson And Knowles, Ltd., and he has been in the Terri- torials about fourteen months. He is well known as a pigeon fancier; and has been asso- ciated with the Sankey Bridges Homing Society. Private Kettle has two brothers serving in the Army, both of whom are in the South Lan- cashire Regiment- One is stationed in England, While the other is serving at the Front. - Mrs. Kettle has four brothers in the Army—two of whom belong to the Territorials.
THE EX_AIVENER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 6, 1915. TERRITORIAL ROLL OF HONOUR.
PRIVATE 'WESLEY KETTLE. Wounded.

div.head: SEVERAL MEN MISSING SINCE THE GREAT
div.p: SEVERAL MEN MISSING SINCE THE GREAT
ADVANCE.

Last week we announced. the first Warring- ton Territorial taken prisoner by the Germans. This week ,another has to be added. Privatf, H. H. James, reported officially " missing," has written home tO say that he is in Germany. Private W. Coyne, 159, Longford-street, whose brother was killed in the charge on June 16th; is reported "missing." Private J. D.. Rensha*, who is reported missing, we ,have been unable to trace, as his address is entered in the official list as Renshaw-street—evidently an erroneous repetition of his own name. Private H. Webster, also reported missing, is dealt with in our Stockton Heath news.
MISSING.
LANCE-CORPORAL A. E. FREEMAN.
Not Seen Since " Terriers " Were Forced. To, Retire. Lance-Corporal Archibald Edward Freeman,

a married man, of 40, Selby-street, and one of the Warrington Territorials, is officially posted as missing. Mrs. Freeman was unofficially noti- fied of this fact about a month ago, when,, after the big advance, Lance-Corporal Bale, also of the Territorials, and a bomb-thrower with Lance-Corporal Freeman, wrote home: "Tell Mrs. Freeman that Archie is missing. When we were retiring he- did not come back. I think he is wounded, and has been made a prisoner. As soon as I find out I Will let her know." , Buried Alive With a Comrade.

Private .Alfred Wilson, of 6, Selby-street, also wrote the same week: "Lance-Corporal,Freeman was buried alive With me. I was in the first line over the trench and it was like hell." Mrs. Freeman received the official communi- cation on Saturday, and preceding it there came the, following letter :from. Private J. R.. Hogan, a stretcher-bearer: "Your husband was one of my comrades out at the Front, and a while ago he was selected to at as a bomb-thrower. I am sorry to say that he, did not return with the other bomb-throwers, and I think he was taken' prisoner. I .hope and trust that nothing else , has befallen him, as he was a fine soldier, and always willing to do anyone a good turn. lam sorry I was not with him this time, as we both pulled through without a scratch on June 16th. I hope that you will be able to bear up in this time of trial."
LANCE-CORPORAL A. E. FREEMAN. Missing.

div.head: Previously Wounded by Rifle Grenade.
div.p: Previously Wounded by Rifle Grenade.

*Aged 26, married, and the father of two chil- dren, Lance-Corporal Freeman was born at .Ris- ley, but was brought up at Grappenhall, attend- ing the school there.. Later the family went to live at Denbigh,. North Wales,. and it is only four years since he returned to Warrington, entering the employment Of the Pearson , and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd. He is brother to Mr. Q. F. Freeman, licensee of the Bull's Head Hotel, Wariington, . He joined the Terri- torials a little over a year ago, and has seen several months' fighting in France. On Sun- day, May 16th, in fact, he was wounded, being cut about the head by a German rifle grenade, fired into the trench. A few • days previous to that another brother—Thomas S. Freeman—gave his life for his country in the Dardanelles.

div.head: PRIVATE G. ROUGHLEY.
div.p: PRIVATE G. ROUGHLEY.
Birthday Parcel Distributed Among
Comrades.

On Saturday morning Mrs. Roughley, a widow, of •33, Golborne-street, received official news to the effect that her son, .Private Gilbert Roughley, of the Warrington Territorials, has either been •killed or has been taken prisoner. Mrs. Rough- ley was unofficially informed that he was miss- lug about a month ago, and, anxious to learn the facts, if possible, ..she wrote to the War Office: - The following letter was sent.: in reply: ."We have received a report, dated October 26th, from Sergt. -Manoguee, now in hospital abroad, whO says that on the 25th September, at the South Lancashires took three trenches, 'from which they were, eventually driven by the Ger- mans. • • •

div.head: One of the Bomb-Throwers.
div.p: One of the Bomb-Throwers.

"Your son was one of the bombers, there being three of them in the front line. The German 4, outflanked us, both left and right, and the order was given for us to retire as quickly as possible. Of the three bombers, two—Privates Gleaver and Rowles managed to escape. From this re- port it would appear that Private ROughley was either killed or taken prisoner. I sincerely hope that the latter is the case, and if so, his name ought to appear in one of the official lists of prisoners of war. If it is so, or ifltny othe'r in- s.9rmaticni is received, you will be informed as soon as possible." Message Postman Brought Back. •

On October Bth Mrs. Roughley sent her son a special letter and a parcel, in view of his forth- coming twenty-second birthday. The letter was returned, marked, "Cannot be traced," while word was sent back that the contents of the parcel had been distributed among other sol- diers. Another relative also sent a postcard, and this likewise was returned. Private Roughley, who is a member of II Com- pany, attended as a boy the Heathside School. He is a married man—having entered the matri- monial bonds whilst recently home ,on furlough. He has been in the Territorials about three years, and Was formerly employed as a fireman r on the London and North-Western Railway. He : could sing a good comic Song, and used often to , impersonate Harry Lauder and George Formby. With the aid of his voice and his mimicry he frequently amused his comrades, both in camp aLi at the Front.
A nother son of Mrs. Roughley's is serving i the Royal Navy.
DOG CAUSES ACCIDENT.

div.head: How Mr. C. Jackson Holmes Sustained
div.p: How Mr. C. Jackson Holmes Sustained
Broken Leg.

, On Sunday morning, at about 9.30, Mr. u. Jackson Holmes was walking in his garden when a large dog came behind him at full speed .and, running into him, knocked him ,down; the fall causing a fracture of the right leg above the ankle., Thanks to the kind, assistance of neigh- bours-, Mr. Jackson Holmes was got into., the house and surgical assistance was soon obtained, the injured limb being successfully ,set. So far excellent' .progress has . been made by: the patient, hut so far .he finds it impossible to reply to all the letters ot.sympathy which he has received, though he hopes to do so later on.

div.head: PRISONER OF WAR.
div.p: PRISONER OF WAR.
PRIVATE 11. H. 'JAMES.
XX rites Mine From Germany For Food
And Money.
Mrs. H. James, who formerly lived with her sister, Mrs. Woods, at 38, Battersby-lane, but

who now resides at 15, Derby-row,. Vulcan, near. Earlestown, received on Saturday an official in- timation from the War Office to the effect that her husband, Private Henry Herbert James of the Warrington Territorials, was missing. Pre- vious to receiving that news, however, James got a letter from her husband saying that lie s 1 as a prisoner of war in Germany, and ask- ing for food and money to be sent to him 11,, stated that his health was good. •
Four Years in " Terriers."

Private James, who is 29 yeays of age, was formerly employed at the Vulcan Foundry. He has been in the Tewritorials about four years, and has been at the 'Front some nine months. He had .only returned there about three weeks, after having a four days' leave, when he was captured. Private James is a keen disciple of Izaak Walton.

div.head: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
div.p: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
Miss Marie Houghton At White- cross Hospital.
On Saturday evening Miss Marie Houghton and Mr. C. Lambert gave the first of a series of concerts which' they are arranging for the wounded soldiers at the Whitecross Military

Hospital on alternate Saturdays during the winter months. The Brooklyn Concert Party have kindly offered to fill the intervening dates. As was to be expected, an excellent programme was provided. Warrington audiences are to be congratulated on having a local artiste in their midst so talented as Madame Albani's pupil. Miss Houghton was in excellent voice, and gave a great variety of songs, which were highly appreciated and loudly applauded. Miss Houghton was assisted by Miss Doris Read
(whose pianoforte solos and accompaniments were a feature of the evening). Mesdames F. Short and Waddington, and Messrs. Pearce and Hannan as vocalists. Mr. C. Lambert con-

tributed recitations and humorous songs. Most of the items were deservedly encored, and a word of praise must be given to Mr. Pearce for his vigorous and dramatic rendering of the ." Toreador" song from "Carmen." He gave several other songs with great taste, and was heartily encored. In the three songs she gave, Mrs. Short was very well received. Mrs. Waddington obtained very hearty recalls for her songs, and Mr. J. Hannan joined Mr. Pearce in a duet, and gave several songs himself. Mr. C. Lambert secured a double encore for his humorous character songs, which concluded the programme.

div.head: OPERA ARTISTES AT RADDON COURT.
div.p: OPERA ARTISTES AT RADDON COURT.

Several of the principals engaged at the Royal Court Theatre have this week visited Raddon Court Hospital and sung to the patients. who greatly appreciated the kindness of the Singers and the musical treat they provided.

div.head: T. ATKINS, ACTOR-AUTIIO4I.
div.p: T. ATKINS, ACTOR-AUTIIO4I.
Wounded Warriors Give Enjoyable
Entertainment.
The versatility of the English soldier was Lemonstrated at the :larish Rooms, Latchford, n Saturday afternoon, when :a number of. in-

mates of tlie Raddon Court•HoSpital produced a military drama entitled "A Spy Somewhere." This little drama had been. written by the soldiers, and was admirably produced by them. In foui scenes, it gave some idea of "life out at the Front." The dramatis person a 3 were:—

Colonel Whorlow; Trooper Whewlow; Wireless Operator, Corporal Molyneux; Assistant Oper- ator, Private Sheehan; Corporal of the Guard, Corporal New;. The Guard, Corp-oral Mapston; and Staff Orderly, Bugler Monrad. In addition to the playlet, the programme con, tamed other "good things," the chief of which was .provided by the soldiers. The "New Zealanders" were very popular in their little sketches, especially in "Five Minutes of Mystery," when they were assisted by Private Johnson. It is 'interesting to note that the New Zealanders * (Private. Sheehan and Bugler Nonrad) are two members of a New Zealand contingent which has played an important part in the Gallipoli Peninsular. Mrs. Garnett recited! “The Hell Gates of Soissons " in emotiOnar manner. This poem was written by a French soldier after the battle of the Aisne, and it describes the courage of a. party of Foal Engineers. • Mrs. Garnett received consideralle applause. ' With their vocal items the soldiers were just as successful: Corporal Buckley with his two 'songs "When the -Angelus 'is Ringing" and "Good-bye, Virginia" . was very popular. "Entente Cordiale," song by Sergeant-Major Northeote, was pleasing item, and a verse had to be repeated by the -singer in response to the applause. His other song "She's Proud and She's Beautiful" was just as successful. Songs were also sung by private Hoyes "Wrong Side Up "), Private King (" Boarding in the Gloaming "), Pri'date ilde (" Michigan " end "Meet. me tonliirf "Drelimland "), COrpbral Mapston, (a song;..written by himself). Songs wore also sung by Miss Shz, w and Mrs. William- son.

div.head: WALKING-STICKS.
div.p: WALKING-STICKS.
Mr. Stewart Royston's Effort For Our
Heroes.

Mr. W. *§tewart Royston; of Sunnyside, Pad- dington, who appears to be always devising :some scheme to bring comfort to someone, is making an endeavour through the pages of "Great Thoughts" to be "a soldier at holm,

by helping those he is unable to' join. The conductor of• the Pansy League in "Great Thoughts," in a recent issue, *wrote:— : I am indebted to Mr. Stewart Royston for a letter just'received in which he pleads for this tisTew- Fund'. He says:— "At. the present time walking sticks are in great demanc). For 'ei-9ry one cif..lre.i there are ten urgently needed! Some of the Fol diers' wounds are so .bed that during their recovery they; can only walk with the help of two sticks —as was witnessed recently when • His Majesty the King pinned ,on the breast of one hero a well .merited V.C. .

"We who can number among our dear ones a wounded hero need be heartily thankful for the doctors and nurses and orderlies, who are slav- ing night and day, with an,entire disregard for self, in the service of our fellow men.

"Not only will the success of • the walking stick fund be a tribute to our brae wounded soldiers and sailors, but will help to express our feelings of thankfulness for the. noble manner they. Were. tended and cared for by the British Red .Cross_ nurses and doctors! ;

. . "Every single shilling given to the und will cover the expense of providing one. walking stick for a brave man, and each donation will be acknow- ledged in "Great Thoughts." If my countless unknown correspondents will now give. a help- ing hand to this appeal they will have earned the lasting and heartfelt gratitude of thousand, of our wounded who have come to help us in this most stupendous task of our mighty Empire." This 'is a really urgent matter and' T sincerely hope all you who read this page will send in your shillings at.o.nce. Ile gives twice who gives quickly. Postal orders ,may be addressed 'o "Great Thoughts 'f Pansy League: 37, T':...mphl House, Tallis-street, E.C.

div.head: FOR THE RED CROSS.
div.p: FOR THE RED CROSS.
Successful Concert In Aid Of Haddon Court.

A thoroughly enjoyable and deservedly sip cessful concert in aid of the funds of the British Red Cross Society's Hospital at Raddon Court, was held in the Patten Hall, Winmarlei gll- - on Thursday evening, the sum of £l5 being cleared for the object in hand. The major portion of the items in the • programme were supplied by Mrs. W. B. Roberts's orchestra, who were in fine form, and who, among other at- tractive items, played a " Fau6t " seleetion, "The Marriage Market," "The Lost Chord" (in which Mr. Robert Smith took the solo Part), and "Boys in Khaki." Mr. Herbert Geary delighted with to brilliantly eigecuted yiolin solos, and Mrs. Haviour also Won the enthusi- astic plaudits of the audience for her polished performance on the same instrument. Mr. J. Babbitt was successful with his breezy "Song of Britain," and with his "Motherland," and Miss Gertrude Henshall recited, with much effect Kate Douglas . Wiggin's delightful trifle, "The Rehearsal." • Mrs. 1.1 J. Mee sang sweetly "Love is meant to make *Us glad;" and "Keep your toys, 'addle boy." • The Misses Queenie Voisey and Mary Roberts danced daintily, and Mr. R. Dickinson caused great merriment with two •comic songs—" The Old Trombone" and "Oh, that Gorgonzola Cheese." Mr. F. Jubb contributed two fine piccalo .solos. •

div.head: ANOTHER POUND DAY.
div.p: ANOTHER POUND DAY.

Another Pound Day will be held at the Raddon Court Red Cross liospital on Friday next, when the special needs to be borne in mind will be tea, groceries, •vegetablee, rigar- ettee, notepaper, timber for shelves, and towels.
of friends, as Witness. the following letter from a Bradford lady, who visited Rifleman Heesom when lying in hospital wounded. It was writ- ten to his mother and is dated November 2nd, 1915 :

"I am taking the pleasure of writing yo it a few lines • just .to inquire how. your 'dear son, Arthur, is getting along. I wrote him a long letter a few weeks ago, but -have not had a reply *yet. I am anxious about him and won- dering if he is quite well and saW I do not *ant to. lose sight of .him,. as we have taken a great- interest in him. How is your .other son who joined the Army at the same time as Arthur? I hope he is quite well, because I am looking forward for a time to come when I shall have the pleasure of seeing you all . _ .
-The son mentioned in ;he above letter suc- cumbed to wounds .received during the big advance.

notification from the Infantry Record Office, Shrewsbury :—" I regret to have to inform you that a report has this day been received here to the effect that No. 16272, Private Martin Hughes, 7th South Lancs. Regiment, was admitted into the Ist War Hospital, Rubery„ Birmingham, having been gassed on October 23rd. Any further information received into. this office as to his condition or progress will be at once notified to you." Private Hughes, who is forty-five years of age, and who spent his birthday in the trenches, enlisted on January 4th, and was sent to France on August sth. He has a son and a son-in-law serving in the ,2/4th South Lancs. Regiment— now in training in Kent—and a nephew 'serving in France. In peace times he is employed by the Firth Mattress Co., Howley.
INVALIDED.
COLONEL PILKINGTON.
Lieutenant-Colonel Charles Pilkington, 6th Manchester Regiment, one of the heads of the colliery firm of Richard Evans and Co., of Hay- dock, has been invalided home from the Dar- danelles.
"OUR DAY."
Daresbury. Division Raises Nearly £350.

A meeting of the Warrington township of the Daresbury Division of the British Red Cross Society, was held at the 'Town Hall, yesterday morning, under the presidency of the Mayor. The other townships of the Daresbury Division, in which Warrington is included, were also represented. Mr. A. T. Hallaway, hon. treasurer for War- rington,. presented a report, from which it appeared that the works' collections realised the net amount of £59 15s. 4d., the school collections £37 3s. 11d., and the concert at the Parr Hall C 65 13s. 10d., or a total net result of £162 13s. Id.

The report was approved and adopted. Mrs. Mocatta, the Warrington township leader, proposed a vote of thanks to his Worship• the Mayor for presiding at the meetings, to the committee and officers, and also .to the public and the Press for their assistance in the effort. which had resulted in such' a handsome sum being handed over. In seconding the vote, Miss Sylvia Broadbert said that the amounts sent in by tjie different townships were as follows:—Stoekton Heath, £53 10s4 Latchford. £3l 10s.; Grappenhall, £22; Daresbury, £4; Whitley, £2l 18s. 3d ; Stretton. £5l. _ _ _ _ _
The total amount raised by the division would be £349 ss. sd. • _

There were. however, still other amounts cut.- standing. and those people possessing them were requested to send them, to Mrs. Mo.7.atta,..Stan.. ley-place. The Mayor, in his reply, congratulated Mrs. yoeatta on the result of her first effort in War- rington as township leader ' The money is entirely devotedlo the wounded at the Front.

div.head: PRISONERS OF WAR.
div.p: PRISONERS OF WAR.
Caledonian Association Whist
Drive For The Funds.

A whist drive and dance, inaugurated for the purpose of raising funds for the Prisoners of War Local Fund, was successfully carried through on Thursday evening by. the members. and friends of the above Association. Whist was played till 10.30, Mrs. W. Murray distribut- ing tile prizes to the following :—Ladies: 1. Miss Cotterill ; 2, Miss Ward; 3, Miss Lowe. Gentle- men: 1, Miss Fairclough (playing as gentle- man); 2, Mr. Fairclough ; 3, Mr. -Shaw. ,Dancing- followed, and was interspersed with songs by Madame Sanders, Mr. F. Robertson and Mr. G. Marshall. Mr. J. L. Davenport and Mr. W..- Murray acted as M.C.'s. The, Ladies' Com..i mittee, with Mrs. Bowman as convener; catered • well for the company present. A vote c f•thanks to the pianist (Mr. Louis Hales) was proposed by Mr. Bowman and carried. The singing of "Auld lang syne " in Scotch style brought a very enjoyable evening to a close.

div.head: FUND STILL PROGRESSING.
div.p: FUND STILL PROGRESSING.

The prisoners of War Fund is still progress- ing, though the demands upon it are not getting less. It is very pleasing to all r•onnected with the fund to notice that even children are using their talent and their time to help this worthy cause. The following letter from three little Bewsey girls speaks for itself:— "November 3rd, 1915,—Dear Sir,—The enclosed sum of money, being the proceeds of a. bazaar, amounting to 125., we wish to be given to the British War Prisoners in Germany. for Christmas parcel fund.—We remain, yours truly, Rose Chetter, Emily Barber, Cissie Gibson." • Every morning brings ,numerous acknow- ledgments from men who are interned in Ger- many, all of whom recognise with gratitude the efforts made to alleviate their sufferings. We would refer our readers once again to the boxes It Market Gate; where constant changes of acknowledgments are taking place, and there readers can see the actual cards from these men.

div.p: "Slackers."
