Rccruiting ccting.—A meeting in Connection with the canvassing of recruits is to be held on Monday ev.zning next at eight, in the Grammar School, when it is hoped a goodly number will put in an appearance who will be willing to assist in this patriotic duty. Particulars appear in an adveetisement on another page.

Death of Mr. Frank Warburton.—The inhabit- ants of the district will regret to hear of the death of one of their prominent tradesmen, Mr. Frank Warburton, of the Cross, which sad event has taken place rather suddenly. For the past week the deceased gentleman had been lying seriously ill with an attack of pneumonia. He was widely known and .respected by a large circle of friends in the village, and, although he did not take an active part in the affairs of his native village, where he had resided 41 his life, yet he had at heart the welfare of the citizens. The late Mr. Frank Warburton was engaged in business as a grocer, and the news of his decease has come somewhat as a shock to the inhabit- ants.

Sudden Death.—We regret to announce the death of Mr. Thomas Fogg, of Moston-street, Newfields, which took place on Tuesday. He was employed at Messrs. William Robertson and Co.'s works at Latchford, and was returning from his duties there, when he suddenly col- lapsed about twenty yards from his home and died immediately without regaining conscious- ness. Deceased was well-known and widely respected in the district, and for some years was secretary to the local football club. He was forty-one years of age, and.he reaYes:a widow and six children.
The funeral took place yesterday at Lymm Parish Church, in the presence of a large circle of friends. Numerous floral/ tributes were received.

Death Of Mr. James Rowles.—We regret to announce the death of Mr. James Rowles, son of Mr. and Mrs. John Rowles, of Booth's Hill, Lymm, who passed away on Tuesday. The de- ceased gentleman, who was only 29 years of age, had been suffering for some considerable time, and his death was•due to phthisis. He was a member of the Lymm Association Football Club, and was esteemed by a large circle ef friends. He worshipped at Lymm Parish Church, and was employed as a packer in a large Manchester print works. The interment took place yesterday at the Lymm Parish Church, the officiating clergyman administering the last rites being the Rev. S. Evans, of Oughtrington. Numerous floral tributes to the memory of deceased were received.

War Workers' Concentration.—At the ex- pressed wish of the Government, work for our soldiers and sailors is to be organised in a less promiscuous way than was the case last winter, and special efforts are to be concentrated on the needs • of the wounded and sick under the auspices of the Red Cross Society. An exten- sion is therefore desired, says the Lymm Parish Magazine, in our weekly gatherings of mothers. an extension to include those who have not been accustomed to attend these meetings. The Rectory mothers, by the kind permission of Mr. and Mrs. Green, have transferred their place of meeting to the ad Masonic Rooms, opposite the Church; this will give far more accommo- dation. and we hope before long to find the room full each Thursday afternoon; will all mothers who-live at this end of the parish take this as a cordial invitation to be present?

Death Of Mr. A. Frost.—We regret to an- nounce the death of Mr. Arthur Frost, of Canal Bank, Statham, which took place on Thursday. The, deceased gentleman some three years ago sustained an accident whilst in the execution of his duties at the works of the Partington Steel and Iron Company, where he was employed, from which he never really recovered. He had been ailing for some considerable time past, suffering from bronchitis, and complications set in a month ago which has hastened his death. The deceased attended the Primitive Methodist Church. and was of a retiring disposition. although widely respected and esteemed by a large circle of friends. He was 56 years cf age and leaves a widow to mourn his loss. The interment takes place on Monday next at three p.m., at the Lymm Parish Church.

Adopted Prisoners Of War.—No difficulty, says the Lymm Parish Magazine, was ex- perienced in getting six of the 740 prisoners of the Cheshire Regiment in Germany adopted by Lymm people. Mrs. Tatton, of Wythenshawe, in a letter to the Rector, expresses- her satis- faction that among the adopters are the Trades- men's Association, the staff and porters at the railway station, and Miss Cadman and her friends. The men adopted will receive a parcel of food or clothing, or both, every fortnight. Arrangements have been made by the Prisoners of War Help Committee with the American Express Co. for the transportation of packages exceeding 111 b. in weight; those less than 111 b. are sent free of charge through the Help Com- mittee, 5 and 7, Southampton-street, Strand. Miss lanes, who has kindly consented to act as secretary for Lymm, will be pleased to give any information and parcels of clothing, &c., sent to her will be forwarded along with the other con- signments.

Private Percy Clare's Letter From The Trenches.—Private Percy Clare, cousin of Sapper Joseph Clare, whose photograph we re- produce on this page, has written home to his mother, who resides at Booth's Hill, Lymm, the following letter, which is dated 30th ultimo : "I am keeping in the best of health, thank God. Cousin Joe was slightly wounded last night and has now gone away. Don't upset your- self, and tell my aunt he is quite all right. and in the ' pink ' when I left him at the dressing station. It happened when we were going up the trenches last night. We had several wounded and two or three killed, poor boys. Joe was first caught on his top lip. It cut it a little and made his face swell, and with a bit of luck you may have him at home before long. Dear mother, don't get downhearted, all will come right in the end, for God is good. We are going to a picture show to-night in motor wagons, it is just fine to pass a night away. Remember me to all at Daniel's." Private Clare is attached to the same regiment as his cousin.

To-day's Mancauvres.—The Cheshire Volun- teer Regiment will hold manceuvres in the.dis- trict of Millington at 3.30 p.m. to-day. They will take the form of a sham fight, in which the Lymm, Oughtrington, Rostherne and about forty mounted will defend Millington, and the Altrincham company will engage as the attack- ing force. The attacking party numbering to the ratio of three to one. The Lymm Platoon will fall-in at 2.30 p.m., under the command of Captain G. R. Williamson and Sergt. S. D. Moston, respectively. They will be transported in motors to Mill- ington, where they will meet the remainder of the defending party at 3.15. The defenders will be distinguished by wearing their brassards on the right arm, the attackers by brassards on the left arm.

"A Fearful Day."—Mr. Frederick Lockyer, of the Star Hotel, Statham, Lymm, has this week received the following interesting letter from Corporal J. H. Booth, at present serving with the 2nd Welsh Regiment at the Front. It is .dated the 27th ultimo :—" I am pleased to say that at present lam going on fine. The weather -out here is awful, nothing but rain and cold. I must tell you that we had a fearful day in the trenches on the —, for the enemy put about 30 to 40 shells into us and knocked all the trench in. We lost a lot of men, buried alive and killed by pieces of shells flying about. They also shelled our reserve trenches with gas shells, and I can tell you it played havoc with our eyes. I suppose my brother Jim till be relating his experiences when he gets out of hospital and reaches home."

div.head: PRIVATE HARRY BROOKES.
div.p: PRIVATE HARRY BROOKES.
Congratulated Upon Obtaining Russian Decoration.

At an executive meeting in connection with the local Tradesmen's Association, held a short time ago, it was decided that the hon. secretary, Mr. W. E. Hillier, the Crose, should forward the following letter to Private H. Brookes, who is at present serving his King and country : "At an executive meeting held on the 30th September, it was proposed, seconded and car- ried unanimously, that a letter of congratula- tion be sent you, conveying the sentiments of the Association. It gives me great pleasure, as hon. secretary of the`Association, having known you all your life, to say the Association considers your decoration by ouaßussian Allies, for your brave acts and manly disposition are a credit to your officers, an honour' to your regi- ment and an example and honour to your native village, who are proud of you. May you be spared to -continue in the work, and to add further to, your laurels." At the annual meeting of the Tradesmen's Association the' following letter was read from Private H. Brookes, which has been received by Mr. W. E. Hillier, the hon. secretary. Dear Sir,—Just a few lines in which I desire to express my sincere thanks in answer to the letter of congratulations which I received from the members of the Lymm Tradesmen's Associa- tion through you, its hon. sec. It has been very kind and thoughtful of many; people, both from my native village and elsewhere, who have sent me kind and encouraging words since I received my decoration. Although, as you see in our daily papers, endless numbers of .names of men who have received various honours for gallantry on the field, there are, in my opinion, numbers of others who equally deserve rewarding for that which they sacrifice for the welfare of their helpless comrades. When the battle is raging, in excitement these things face you, wherever you go, and therefore it is up to us as English- men to do our best at such times. We must not think of the honour we may receive for it, but we must and do take such work to be part of our duty. We must go forward, even in the heat of the fight, as this is no place for shirkers. The price is great, but we must purchase that which England will be proud of in generations to come. Some day, when the fight has been fought and won, and the victory is ours, I hope to return, together with my Lymm comrades, to that joyous welcome which I know awaits all of us. I beg to close, wishing you and the members every good luck and success.—l remain, sincerely yours, H. BROOKEL"

div.head: OUR WAR-TIME TRAIN SERVICE.
div.p: OUR WAR-TIME TRAIN SERVICE.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."
Sir,—Rumours are rife in Lymm regarding cer- tain alterations to be made to the already wretched train service.

It is said that the 7.26 a.m. from Lymm to Manchester is to be abolished, and that the 8.12 a.m. also from Lymm to Manchester is to be put some twenty minutes earlier. May I enter a very strong protest against such an absurd proposition?

The 8.12 a.m. is the busiest and most used train of the day to Manchester, and is the busi- ness train beyond all others. Any interference with its already poor run- ning will cause intense resentment, which will make itself felt in the days to come on the traffic side.

The 5.40 p.m. from Manchester to Lymm is also reported to be under sentence. Surely, it cannot be the fact that the railway company intend to tamper with the trains which are the only really useful ones to the majority of contractors?—Yours truly, TRAFFIC MANAGER.

div.head: RECRUITING COMMITTEE.
div.p: RECRUITING COMMITTEE.
Meeting 01 Local Helpers To Be Held.
The local recruiting committee on Thursday sent the following circular letter to those people whose names had been handed in ag likely to assist in connection with the present Government canvass :

"Your name has been suggested to the com- mittee as being willing to assist in the canvass in connection with Lord Derby's scheme, and we venture to hope that you will place your valuable services at the disposal of your King and country. With this object in view, we earnestly request you to attend a meeting to be held at the Lymm Grammar School on Monday evening next, November Bth, at eight, and to bring any friend who is willing to assist in the work."
The Grammar School is considered jv the committee to be conveniently situated for hold in the meeting.

div.head: WAR AND RELIGION.
div.p: WAR AND RELIGION.
Apathy In Safety; Earnestness In Danger.

The Rector. in this month's Parish Magazine, expresses the opinion that the coming winter months will afford a special opportunity for ex- tending Church work, especially among those with relatives at the Front.

"Here." he says, "are two extracts from letters from the Front to show how our men have learned to view such things, and what they expect from their friends at home. In ,re the writer says: 'The chaplain toli us at service yesterday always to remember those wcrds, 'Cover my defenceless head with the snadow ef Thy wing '—very good wools to have in one's mind when going into battle. This war is bringing us face to face with the realities of life with all its uncertainties, and it is a e nnmon occurence to see men at silent prayer, and these prayers have their effect, because I have ex- perienced it. I do hope the people of Lymm will change with us now, and not be like what many of us were before the war, and that they won't wait till they are in danger. We had delightful little service in a barn just behind the firing line, so near that we dared not sing the hymns, but just whispered them, for if the Germans had heard they would have shelled us.'
Service With Rifle In Hand.

"The other extract gives an account of a Holy Communion service. We had the privilege of attending service and receiving the Holy Com- munion last Sunday; all attended who could laf spared, for we dared not weaken the line, even for that short time. We are obliged to attend in fighting order, ready for action, if called upon. Does it not seem strange that whilst enjoying such a service to have our rifles in our hands. and loaded with equipment and ammunition? We go as many as we can to hear the good words, though in doing so we risk our lives, and yet our churches at home are so neglected, where there‘is no danger and a copfortable seat. I sometimes think we are cowards, because when we were safe at home we were apt to forget God and now we are in danger we appeal to Him for His tender mercy.'
"These oitracts speak for themselves, and need no comment."

Musketry.—The Central Association of the Volunteer Training Corps have organised a knock-out shooting competition to take place some time this month. Teams of eight ,from various platoons and companies will compete, the range being 25 yards,, with a 2in., one inch invisible target. In the preliminary round Lymm Platoon has been drawn against the Cyclists' Section of the Somerset Volunteer Training Corps.

div.p: :;"14FORtr
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 6, 1915.
CAPTAIN E. IL LOVELL.
Baptist Minister 'Son 11l In France.

Captain Edward Richardson Lovell, of The Manse, Lymm, son of the minister 'attached to the Baptist Church, Higher-lane, has written home to his parents stating that he is at pre- sent an inpatient gf the 20th General Hospital, Etaples, suffering from a bad attack of influenza Captain Lovell joined his 'Majesty's forces soon after the outbreak of war, and became medical officer to the Wiltshire Regiment, after qualify- ing at the Middlesex Hospital, London. He was drafted to the Front in June, and had not up to the present had a furlough. Prior, to hostilities Captain Lovell was study- ing with a view to becoming a medical prac- titioner, and already holds many diplomas, in-

div.head: CAPT. EDWARD R. LOVELL
div.p: CAPT. EDWARD R. LOVELL

chiding that of the Royal College of Surgeons. whilst he is a Licentiate of the Royal College of Physicians. Captain Lovell's age is 24 years, and he is widely known and esteemed in the village, taking more than ordinary interest in the affairs of the district.

div.head: An Old Local Cricketer.
div.p: An Old Local Cricketer.
Fond of all branches of sport, he played cricket on numerous occasions for the village club.
Two Narrow Squeaks.

In a graphic letter to his sister, dated some little time ago, he states that whilst at the Front he has had some stirring times, one in particular being very exciting. It seems that Captain Lovell had retired to rest for the. !light in a part of an old falmliouse used temporarily as a hospital for the wounded. Shortly after to his ears came the screech of shells fired from the German guns some distance away. Although within the zone of fire, Captain Lovell managed to snatch a few hours' sleep, tired with the exertions of the day. At daybreak he went out- side to see what damage had been done around the district, and at the entrance to the door noticed lying only a few yards away, a gigantic German shell which had failed to explode. "1 was a narrow shave" he writes. On another occasion he recounted his adven- tures with a party of his colleagues, whilst motoring along a country road. They were turning a bend in the road when shots w.)r,‘ fired at them by a body of Germans some di,3- tance away. Bullets penetrated th, back of the car, fortunately without hitting al.y of the occupants, and Captain Lovell arid his colleagues were able to get back safely to the British lines.

div.head: SAPPER JOSEPH CLARE.
div.p: SAPPER JOSEPH CLARE.
Wounded, But Tells His Mother To "Cheer Up."

Mrs. M. E. Clare, of Booth's Hill, Lymm, has received news from her son, Sapper Joseph Clare, that he is wounded. In a letter home dated the 30th ultimo, he states:—" It will upset you a little to know that I am now in hospital wounded, but don't worry for it is not serious. I was hit with a piece of trench mortar, which went straight through my mouth and lodged in my cheek; but I have now had it taken out and am keeping it as a sou- venir. There were anout twelve of our chaps buried by the debris, so I was lucky to escape with such a slight wound. I cannot send you my address at present as I do not know where I shall be mbved to, these next few days, but cheer up. I am going on well. I left Percy (his cousin) a bit downhearted. He was with me until I left him at the dressing station." Sapper J. Clare, who is in the 3rd Section Royal Engineers, is 23 years of age, and was in the " Terriers " for four years prior to the out- break of war. He was in the employ of the L. and N.-W. Railway Co. where, by his geniality and comradeship he is greatly esteemed and admired. Fond of all outdoor games, he is a noted Altrincham Association football player. He attended the Primitive Methodist Church. and as a boy was educated at the Lymm schools. Sapper Clare has two brothers serving King and country, one being on munition work.. the other
SAPPER JOSEPH CLARE. Wounded.

Company-Sergt.-Major H. Clare, at present with the 1/sth Cheshire Regiment "somewhere in France." The latter served through the late Boer campaign and came through without a scratch. The subject of our. photograph was drafted to the Front in February.

div.head: TRADESMEN'S ASSOCIATION.
div.p: TRADESMEN'S ASSOCIATION.
Election Of Officers For Ensuing
Year.

The annual general meeting in connection with the above was held on Tuesday at Hirst's Pavilion, when a full gathering of representa- tives were present. In the course of the meet- ing Mr. Rogerson, one of the vice-presidents, commented upon the excellent organisation of the procession at the 1915 Citizens' Sunday, and considered the Hon. Secretary (Mr. W. E. Hillier) was to be eonkratulated upon his M. 0.- ship. The question of the adoption of Private Wm. Massey was also proposed by Mr. Rogerson and seconded by Mr. H. S. Saville, that the cost in connection with same should come out of the Association funds. The next item dealt with was the hon. treasurer's statement, in which Mr. A. B. Richardson stated that there were 57 members, of which 52 had been fully paid up. The statement met with approval, and was per- fectly satisfactory, there being a balance in hand of, £5 4s. 3d., which was carried forward.

It was decided on the proposition of Mr. W. Allman, seconded by Mr. H. S. Saville, that the present hon. treasurer be again asked to officiate in that capacity, Mr. Richardson suit- ably replying, thanked the Association for again placing their confidence in him, and said he came into the room that night intending to ask to be relieved of the office, but after such glowing tributes had not the heart to do so. Mr. H. S. Saville proposed and Mr. J. Warhem seconded that Mr. D. Daniels be again invited to occupy the chair, and both gentlemen paid eulogistic .testimony to his efficiency which called for applause. Mr. Daniels. in accepfing, offered his thanks id apPreciation of the honour bestowwl him, closing his remarks with the well -under- stood sentenee "If you will stick to me I v ill stick to you, then we shall all stick tosreth3r." The Vice-presidents were elected en bloc;

Tn connection with the Executive Council. Messrs. F. W. %vice, E. N. Owen and .T. W. Gibbon's term of office expiring, two new names were put forward, viz., Mr. F. Morris and Mr. N. Booth, these two gentlemen being enlisted, as well as Mr. F. W. Druce.

On the proposition of Mr. D. Danielg, the president. seconded by Mr. H. S. Saville. and qunnorted by Mr: J. Rogerson, Mr, W. E. ilillir was asked to remain in office as hon. secretary. Mr. Hillier, in reply, eaid he weuld ,10 his best t 6 serve the Associatior.. isf whidt he was so proud.

div.head: Report.
div.p: The Report.

In his report, Mr. Hillier commented that the "Business as usual" policy was being carried on with a quiet and resigned disposition, pecu- liar to business men faced with great odds. At the last meeting the members showed the trend of their thoughts when they decided to "adopt" one of Lymm's brave boys, Private, Wm. Massey, of the Cheshire Regiment, who is now a pris- oner in Germany. Their adopted charge, through their generosity was receiving comfort in the edibles. Citizen Sunday, under their auspices, stood firm as an annual event. Mr. Hillier also referred to various public positions held by members of the Association, the British Red Cross Society, the Volunteer Regiment, and the Special Constables. He also thanked the Medical Officer and the District Council for their vigorous efforts to successfully cope with the recent outbreak of diphtheria. Shopping at Christmas.

In connection with the forthcoming Christmas holidays, it was decided that the Wednesday preceding Christmas Day tradesmen should re- main open until 7 p.m., shops to remain closed the whole of Christmas Day and the following Monday also; the same to apply to the :New Year.
The meeting terminated with the decision that the annual dinner in connection with the Asso- ciation do not take place this year.

A PRAYER FOR OUR SOLDIERS'.
0 Lord. our God, in whom we trust. Shield Thou the lads that leave our homes, To fight for country and for right, Till lasting peace in fulness comes.
In fierce temptation be their friend, Their refuge in the hour of need, And when for home and friends they, sigh, Thy comfort give, Thy succour speed.
Under Thy shadow let them dwell, Till every 'fearful storm sweeps past; And may they ever serve Thee well, As long as strength and life shall last.
In pain and trial make them brave, , Help them to suffer and be strong, And bold aloft, for all to see, The light and truth which scatter wrong.
And if upon the field they fall, Thy arms, 0 Lord, around them twine, And give them in that trying hour, • The soothing thought that they are Thine
Into Thy tender, loving care, 0 Lord, we give the lads we love, And if on earth we meet no more, Gather us round Thy Throne above. Written by' the Rev. E. Lovell, Lymm Baptist Church.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

For Waifs And Strays.—Preaching at Christ Church on Sunday, the Rev H. A. Wadman, organising secretary of the Waifs :earl Strays Society—which, among other places s7ipports St, George's Home, in Salisbury-street, War- rington—said that the work of his Society wai more important than ever at the present moment, as it had to care for many children whose mothers were dead and whose athem were in the fighting ranks. Over eight humire.l of: the boys befriended by the Society were known to be serviwg. either in the Army or the Navy, included in the total being two boys from the Warrington home, who were aboard H.M.S. Lion. -

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

Missionary Association.—The monthly meeting of St. Thomas' Missionary Association was held on Monday evening in the Parish Room. The Rev: James Collins (vicar) was in the chair, and there was a good attendance of mem- bers. An address was given by the Rev. E. W. Clarke, whose subject was "China." He spoke of the customs of the Chinese and on the work of the missions. He was accorded a vote of thanks on the motion of Mfr. Morriss, seconded by Mr. W. R. Smith.

Thirty-three-day Vigil In Trenches.—Mr. J. Leach, 75, Walton-road, Stockton Heath, has received the following letter from a friend who is serving "somewhere in France" with his regiment, the sth Cheshires :—" We have been relieved now after thirty-three days, during which time the weather was very bad. We are not sorry to be out of tb,e trenches for a change, I can tell you. We are at present in a ruined village just behind the firing line. • About forty are being sent on leave out of the battalion each week: so I may get a chance to come over before Christmas. The end of the war seems as far off as ever from what we can see of it."

War Versus Drink.—The Rev. Dudley E. Sturt, organising secretary of the Chur..2.h of England Temperance Society, paid a visit to St. Thomas' Band of Hope on Thursday evening, when he gave a very interesting address on "War versus Drink." His lecture was illus- trated by a number of war slides. There was a good audience. At the close, of the lecture,. on the motion of Mr. Whiteman and Mr: Stan- nard, a very hearty vote of thanks was.aceordeo to the speaker, to,. the Vicar, and to Mr. C. Hallows, who was at the lantern. In vply, Rev. Dudley E. Sturt congratulated the vicar and workers on their efficient ati.l up-to-date Band of Hope.

Wesley Guild.—The members of the Stockton Heath Wesley Guild held a musical evening at the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Thursday. Songs were sung by Mrs. Williams, MisS: Ethel Houghton, Miss M. Webb and Miss. Lawton Miss Turner .gave a pianoforte solo, and Miss E. Whitfield and Miss E. Houghton played a duet. Mr. A. Webb rendered two cornet solos and Mr.. G. Whitfield contributed a humorous reading. Selections were played on a gramo- phone lent by Mr. Williams, Mr. H. Dithfield being •in charge. Miss Turner and Miss . Lily Webb were the. accompanists. ilhe Rev. P. meson, who was in the chair, gave a short address. Refreshments were provided by the Social Committee. •

I ntercession Service.—A special intereession service was held on Sunday evening at the Wesleyan Church, in accordance with a resolu- tion of the Wesleyan Conference. The servire was conducted by the Rev. Percy meson, the form of service proyided from headquarters being used. During the service the names of the young men connected with the church who had responded to the call of their country were reasi out, and special, prayers were offered for their safe return. The choir, under the conductor- ship of Mr. F. E. Penketh, rendered the chorus "And the Glory of the Lord" (Handel), Mr. Peter Harrison presiding at the organ. The col- lections for the day were on behalf of the War Emergency Fund to support the ministers who had gone on active service, and also those who were acting as chaplains in the Army.

" Falstaff The Sensualist."—At the men's Sunday morning meeting, held at the Adult School, a short lecture was given by Mr. Wm. Landon, who gave a most interesting review of "Falstaff, the sensualist," as pictured by Shakespeare in three of his plays. It was shown how—in spite of the questionable character of Falstaff—Shakespeare had cast a glamour of romance and guileless humour over him which atoned for much of his extravagance and made him as attractive to many others as he seemed to be to the author himself. Numerous quota- tions were given which illustrated the brilliance of wit put into Sir John's mouth, and his won- derful _facility for getting out of tight corners. The Bible lesson, which was taken from the life of Jeremiah, was ably opened by the President, Mr. W. J. Rowland.

Adult School Sale Of Work.—The sale of work held last week was brought to a very suc- cessful conclusion on Saturday evening by a social meeting of a miscellaneous character. Songs were contributed by Mr. Kay—who sang in good style—Miss Sherburn, Miss f.anglf.y, Mrs. H. Sherburn and Mr. W. Hankey. Lanca- shire and other recitals were given by Mr. W. Hankey, Miss Dawson and the Chairman. After supper the stalls were cleared, when it was found that over £32 had been raised, which is more than sufficient to provide the desired instrument. The remainder of the money will be spent in increasing the comfort and homeli- ness of the school.
A whist drive was held on Thursday evening, when a good number of players were present. The prizes were won by Miss M. Norbury and Mr. Harold Mann.

div.head: NOT KILLED!
div.p: NOT KILLED!
Good News For A Stockton Heath Wife.
Last week we announced that the War Office had officially reported that Private Ernest
PRIVATE E. lIARPER. Reported Killed; now reported Prisoner.

harper, of 25, Derby-road, Stockton Heath, had been killed in action on September 25th. As a matter of fact he was wounded in the hand and leg and fell into the hands of the Germans. He was taken to a camp in Julich (Rhineland). Mrs. Harper, his wife, received a postcard and a letter from him on Wednesday. In the letter he writes:—" Just a few lines to let you know I am getting better. I cannot say much, as we must be as brief as possible." On the postcard, he says :--" My leg is improving, but my hand is very backward. It is hard work writing." This news, of course; has been received with great joy by Private Harper's wife and three children, his mother, who lives at 38, Walton- road, his other relations and many friends at Stockton Heath. A.brc,ther of his is serving in France with /the 4th South Lancs. Regiment.

div.head: PRIVATE W. H. DANIELS.
div.p: PRIVATE W. H. DANIELS.
Wounded In Dardanelles When Being Carried To Hospital.

News has been received by Mrs. W. H. Daniels, of Higher-lane, that her husband, Private Daniels, was wounded in the Dar- danelles, on October 14th. The information reached his wife through a letter from General F. L. Pew, commanding the Welsh Division, wherein he states that Private Daniels was being conveyed to hospital suffering from dysentery, when he was wounded by a stray bullet in the thumb. Private Daniels is an old soldier, and on the outbreak of war offered his services to the sth Battalion Cheshire Regiment. Shortly afterwards he was transferred to the Divisional Headquarters as the General's groom. Prior to the war he had 17 years' ser- vice to his credit in the old Volunteers, reach- ing the rank of Transport-Sergeant. He lias employed in the gas works under the Lymm Urban District Council, and is well-known and respected in the village. _ - -
Educated at the -Oughtrington Schools, he worshipped at the same church.

div.head: PRIVATE 11. WEBSTER.
div.p: PRIVATE 11. WEBSTER.
Parents Officially Informed That He
Is Missing.

Mr. and Mrs. Wm. Webster. of 20, Mitchell- street, have received an official intimation that their son, Private Henry Webster, of the 4th South Lancashire Regiment, is missing. The news, together with a photograph of Private Webster, was published in our issue of a fort- night ago, but though authentic, was unofficial.

GRAPPENHALL.
CHESHIRE VOLUNTEER REGIMENT.
Grappenhall Detachment.
Orders for week commencing Sunday, 7th November :

Tuesday, 9th November.—Squad Drill and Musketry Instruction, 7.45 p.m. sharp. Saturday, 13th November.—Company Drill and Parade, 3.30 p.m. sharp. Members are expected to fall in five minutes before the times shown. Orderlies for duty :—Sub-Section Commander W. Trantem, Private W. D. Jeans. By Order, F. A. FROST, Platoon Commander, O.C.

div.head: ROLL OF HONOUR.
div.p: ROLL OF HONOUR.

Seeing that an Army of more than three million men has been recruited from Great Britain and Ireland, it is obvious that all the towns and villages, great or small, must have contiibuted a good number of their men- folk, but it would be difficult to find a place that has proportionately given more of its man- hood than Stockton Heath. Though compara- tively small, its population being only dbatit 5,000, it has sent over 400 men into the various branches of His Majesty's forces.

div.p: CHESHIRE VOLUNTEER REGIMENT

Monday. ' Lecture in Church Institute at 7.45—" Out- posts and Definition of Objects."
Tuesday. Shooting at the Range of Messrs. Fletcher, Russell & Co., Ltd. (by permission), from 6.30 to 8.30.
Friday, Drill at Headquarters. "Fall-in" 7.45 sharp.

div.head: DATED 3rd NOVEMBER.
div.p: DATED 3rd NOVEMBER.
1. Official Notice.

OFFICIAL HANDBOOK.—From the date of its pub- lication every Volunteer will be bound by the Regulations contained in the Central Associa- tion's Official Handbook, and it will be assumed that every Volunteer is familiar with its terms Reference to the Regulations will be by para- graph, and number therein quoted in any order issuing from the Central Association. The publication can be obtained from the Headquarters of the Central Association at Judges' Quadrangle, Royal Courts of Justice, Strand, W.C., or from Messrs. W. H. Smith and Son, or Messrs. Wyman and Sons, booksellers.

3. Appointments. No. 4 DOUBLE COMPANY.—TO be Musketry Instructor, with rank as Section Commander— A. SHEPHERD. To be Physical Drill Instructor, with rank as Section Commander—A. MorrnAm. By Order, F. WARBURTON, Officer Commanding.

div.head: THELWALL.
div.p: THELWALL.
TIIE VILLAGE FAIINI.
County Court Case Concerning Farmhouse.

Mr. IL J. Westbrook made application at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, on be- half of Captain John St. Vigor Fox, of Lincoln. to recover the possession of a farm now occupied by Mr. J. Warburton, of Thelwall. Mr. War- burton was not represented in Court. Mr. Westbrook said that the farm was part of the Village Farm, Thelwall. The whole farm was originally let to the defendant and to the defendant's father, jointly, at a total annual rental of £123. On the death of the father in October, 1913, and at the request of the father's executors, Messrs. John White and Co. (Captain Fox's agents) gave formal notice to Mr. J. War- burton to quit. The farm was subsequently relet to Mr. Peter Warburton, as from Febru- ary, 1915. The defendant had allowed the new 'tenant to take possession of the land and the farm buildings, but would not give up the possession of the dwelling-house. The new tenant was about to be married, and naturally wanted possession of the house. Judgment was given for possession within ten days, with leave to issue execution under the Courts Emergency Powers Act.

div.head: WOOLSTON.
div.p: WOOLSTON.

New Assistant Overseer.—Mr. G. Stubbs was, at a recent meeting of the Parish council, elected assistant overseer in succession to Mr. James Daintith, who has resigned after twenty- nine years' service.

div.head: STRETTON.
div.p: STRETTON.

The Late Mr. Thos. Henry Lyon.—To the memory of the late Mr. Thos. Henry Lyon a massive cross carved from Annan stone has been erected in the churchyard, Thursday of last week marking the anniversary of his death. In addition to erecting the memorial cross, Mrs. Lyon has, as a tribute to her late husband, made a substantial gift to the Church Army in order to enable them to increase their fleet of ambulance cars for work on the field of battle. The collections at Sunday's services in the Parish Church were devoted to the working ex- penses of the car, the tetal raised being £l4 58., whilst a further sum of £1 3s. 6d. was collected in the week-day school for the same object. The memorial gravestone is the work of Mr. Walter Clay, of Warrington.
Advised the Limit.
A tramp applied for help at a house in the country. The mistress made it a rule never to turn any away empty-handed.

"Here's sixpence for you, my man," she said. "I'm not giving it to you for charity's sake, but merely because it pleases me." "Thankee," said the man, "but couldn't you make it a shilling and enjoy yourself thor- oughly, mum?"

div.head: WARBURTON.
div.p: WARBURTON.
The Poor Rates.—The magisterial Bench sit- ting at Altrincham on Monday sanctioned, for the parish of Warburton, a poor rate amount- ing to is. in the £ on land and 2s. in the £ on buildings.
RUNCORN GUARDIANS.

div.head: In Favour Of M.P.'s Giving Up
div.p: In Favour Of M.P.'s Giving Up
Salaries.
A meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at the Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday morning, Mr. J. S. Jones being in the chair,
A HINT TO M.P.'s.

The Lewisham Board of Guardians forwarded the following resolution: "This Board earnestly hopes that during the continuance of the pre- sent war, in view of the severe strain on national resources, the members of the House of Commons will set a notable example in economy and self-denial to the nation by Pe'" forming their duties gratuitously, and that thus° ,who are members of the Cabinet will accept sub- stantial reductions in their salaries; that the Government be urged to economise in all Government departments, and that copies ef this resolution be sent to the Prime Minister, Major Sir E. lA. Coates, and all Boards of Guardians throughout England and Wales." It was unanimously decided to support the resolution, one of the Guardians observing, amid laughter, that there was no alteration in the remuneration of the Guardians.

SICK POOR TO BE SENT TO WARRINGTON The House Committee recommended the send- ing of two patients to Manchester in order that operations might be performed on them. Mr. Morris pointed out that one of the patients was 68 years of age. Some time ago a resolution was passed by the Guardians and arrangements were made for Warrington In- firmary to take cases from the House. He wondered if Dr. Selby had weighed the matter carefully. The patients could be sent to War- rington with comfort.
It was pointed out that the doctor's recom- mendation must be followed tut owing to the urgency of the cases. and the minutes of the House Committee were adopted.
COST OF PAUPER LUNATICS. The rate of maintenance for pauper lunatic 4 in the Upton Asylum for the quarter ending December 31st was reported to have been fixed at 10s. 21d. per head per week.
TEMPORARY OFFICERS.
Mr. J. 11. Hudson and Mrs. Hudson wrote accepting the positions of temporary master and assistant nurse respectively.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.
District Recruiting Tribunal Appointed.
A meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held on Tuesday, Mr. Harrison pre- siding.
TO REPRESENT THE COUNCIL.
Messrs. A. Lister Kaye, Wm. Mclntyre and G. Pilling were asked to attend a Local Govern- ment Board Inquiry which. is to .be held at War- rington on Wednesday, November 10th.

div.head: MEN WHO CAN BE SPARED FOR THE WAR.
div.p: MEN WHO CAN BE SPARED FOR THE WAR.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board advocating the urgency of Recruiting Tribunals. The Local Government Board, the letter said, would do everything in its power to assist the local recruiting authority, by its in- fluence and encouragement, and in other ways. There were at present a large number of men who could be spared from their occupations. Some of the men who had been " starred " (de- barred from enlistment) would probably be found on investigation to be available. At the same time there were a number of men who could not be spared, and who had been " un- starred." With regard to both these classes questions might arise which should be decided by a local tribunal.. Further instructions would be issued on this matter. The Local Govern- ment Board proposed that a local tribunal should be formed for the district, and sug- gested that it should consist of not more than five men, who should be of impartial judgment. Owing to the size of the diStrict, it was de- cided by the Council that seven members should be appointed as a tribunal. These were Messrs. Linaker, Harrison, Wright, Jones, Pilling, Woodward and Britch.

PADGATE COTTAGE HOMES.

div.head: Satisfactory Record Of Past
div.p: Satisfactory Record Of Past
Year's Work.
APPRECIATIVE Gl_ A RDIANS.

The report on the Vadgate Cottage Homes for the year ended September 30th, 1915, was sub- mitted to the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday, on behalf of Mrs. Lawrence, the superintendent. The report was as follows : " During the twelve months 55 children have been admitted and 113 discharged. Out of the number discharged 63 are Roman Catholics, who have been .transferred to Roman Catholic Homes. .The numbef of inmates on October Ist, 1914, was 182, and-on September 30th, 1915, 124. Four children have been placed in situations during the year and all are doing well. The work in the schoolroom has gained a satisfac- tory report from His Majesty's Inspector .of Schools. The industrial training has been. favourably reported upon also. Good crops have been grown on the farm and the kitchen garden has been successfully cultivated. The general domestic training of the girls in needlework and housewifery has -gone on as before. Details of industrial occupations are as follows :—Shoemaker's shop-187 pairs of boots made and 1,100 repairs executed; tailor's slitif?-243 garments made, _825 _gstrinents re- paired; needlework-78 new frocks, 28 coats, 490 underclothes, pinafores, &c., and 6,900 other garments have been made, and all the neces- sary mending done. The general health of the children has been excellent, but there was an outbreak of measles in the Spring." The report concluded with details of repairs to the Homes and the expression of the thanks of Mrs. Lawrence to the •Cottage Homes Com- mittee. .

div.head: Commendation For The Matron.
div.p: Commendation For The Matron.
Miss C. Broadbent said that the year's work at the Homes had been very satisfactory and she moved that a letter of appreciation be sent to Mrs. Lawrance.

_ This was. seconded by the Rev. A. M. Mitchell. Mr. J. Billinga asked if it was not desirable to have a revision of the staff at the Homes? From a recent report as to the number of in- mates and the staff it would appear that there was need for revision. He hoped that the good work would continue.

Mr. A. J. -Jolley, who was in the chair, said that in Spite of very trying circumstances Mrs. Lawrance had discharged her duty with great credit :to herself, and in a manner that ought to be satisfactory to both the Guardians and the public. ,Miss Broadbent observed that if Mr. Billinge was present at some of the meetings of the Cottage Homes Committee he would think that the Homes were over-staffed. Mr. Jolley added that the Homes were still in si transitory stage and it was most unfair to make criticism- whilst they were crossing the stream. The proposition was carried.

div.head: GREAT TIMES.
div.p: THE GREAT TIMES.

The great times are before us—they beckon with bright hands, They lead us from Grief's valleys to the im- mortal lands; They sing to us in summer, and in the lone- some snow, They whisper of the daisies, and lead where violets grow!

The great times are before us—how beautiful they seem! They glimmer in the shadows like the sweet face of a dream; They ripple in the rivers that sing their way along, The Starlight of the darkness—the sunlight of a song!

The great times. are before us—we'll live to meet them all,. And on our every pathway the light of 'heaven will fall; With never any sorrow—no sighing and no tears, The .great times are before us—the bright im- mortal years!

MY DEAR CHILDREN,-

It would seem that most of you are fonder of birds than of animals, for my request for an essay on "My Favourite Bird" has pro- duced a splendid crop of essays—much larger than the previous week's response. In fact, at the moment of writing they are coming in by every post, and quite a lot of attempts have been pushed through my letter box by nephews and nieces. This is as it 'should be, and not only will the news that you are doing so well gladden the heart of our old friend, the khaki- clad Uncle Ned, but it will also encourage me to go on encouraging you by offering more of our lovely -hook prizes. Those who have won one know how lovely they are! Don't you?. For next neek's competition let me have essays on your favourite foreign country—and why.
UNCLE JACK.

teachers of botany in high-class schools and colleges. Others have specialised to meet par- ticular requirements of the florist, and there is a very large foreign trade, both in dried flowers and fresh blooms, which could be sup= plied at home. For instance, Germany used to send over large quantities of lilies of the valley for Christmas. These imports have now ceased and there is every reason to believe that the cultivation of this particular bloom will prove a profitable industry to women who would take it up seriously. Moderation In Food And Drink.

It has been said that, barring accidents, a man or a woman can live as long as may be desired. Those who wish to live long, and to enjoy an active and healthy old age, must, according to Dr: Alexander Bowie, eat moder- ately in youth and manhood and drink of alcoholic beverages most sparingly. The doc- tor is an expert on these subjects, which he has made a life study; he therefore speaks with authority. Ile has .devoted a • great-deal of time to the lives of those who in the past, and the present, have lived to an advanced old age. The majority he finds were vege- tarians, or, rather, they abstained from meat; they were also water drinkers. Some meat eaters became centenarians, as did also some who partook of various alcoholic drinks, but in nearly each case those men and women who retained their faculties to the end and reached a ripe old age, more or less abstained from meat and alcoholic drinks throughout 'their lives. • Excess in everything, in exercise, ath- letics and pleasures of all kinds, undoubtedly tend to premature decay and death: Two Economical Dresses.

Women of to-clef lead strenuous lives, and with not a few dress takes a secondary place. Something simple, easily put on and taken off, is sought, and the want is, of course, supplied. Hence the success of the one-piece pinafore frock, which is both becoming and pretty, and is intended to be worn over dainty afternoon dresses during working hours. It is at its best when made of thick washing linen, and of a thin alpaca, both of which may be had in the most charming colours. It buttons impartially in front or at the back, and is decorated at the neck and sleeves with touches of embroi- dery. Another sensible idea is the britelle bodice, in one with the skirt that can be worn over different blouses. In velveteen this ar- rangement is most satisfactory. •A very pretty corsage, designed for a dress of this description, is almest tight-fitting, fastens in front with

three large buttons, and has`plain little sleeves matching the skirt, and reaching half-way to the elbow. The neck is cut low, a long sleeve blouse, with a wide collar, filling the opening. Velveteen, in addition to many ether good points, blends remarkably well with transparent or light fabrics.

The Vogue of the Short Coat. • The long fur-lined velvet coat, trimmed with a flounce of skunk at the hem, and collars and cuffs of the same fur, is decidedly a garment for the elderly, and where the lining is detach- able, the wrap is available for day and evening wear. Although long coats will be almost universally worn, the velvet sacque that just reaches the hips has a future before it. Some models of this type are longer at the back (whore they stand out somewhat) than the front. Velvet coats of etery description are trimmed with fur, and some have outstanding pocket flaps to match the collars and cuffs. The buttons also are frequently of the same pelt. Very jaunty little coats of Russian colr. cr of earacul, fit quite tightly at the waist, but flare out below in a full basque that might perhaps be better described as a frill. Freakish they are undoubtedly, but on the right woman are not without fascination. The bolero mantle, or spencer, is a most comfortable garment, suited to the slight figure only. Below the waist it falls in graceful folds that appear to be dis- tended by a bustle, which the prpphets f‘sel t will be universally worn a few months hence.

The Marquise Hat. Metalic cords and trimmings are extensively used for millinery. They are neat and trim, and when used to bind the edges of velvet toques, form the only decoration. Gold and oxidised galons are much in favour also, and are finished with a bow, or a metal ornament. Sometimes three rows of galen are placed round the crown of a postilion het. The newest headgear is most comfortable, since it sets firmly and secitrely on the head, showing a part of the coiffure. Gauged vervet is again used for winter hats, or rather for either the crown or the brim, the gauging being rarely used for both. Pom-poms or single flowers form the sole trimming, very little being required in the way of adornment. Among the most becoming shapes must be • placed the marquise, which is picturesque and dignified, and therefore it may be chosen by the matron. There are various modifications of this hat., but all are very simply trimmed, for the days of costly aigrettes and Paradise plumes are over and gone, perhaps never to return.

div.head: CHAT and GOSSIP.
div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.

Nothing German. Every woman in these isles has it in her power to avenge the cruel martyrdom of their heroic countrywoman, Nurse Cavell. Quickly as passing events fade from the public mind, her death will be kept in remembrance at any rate by women. As soon as peace is proclaimed Germany will enter upon another campaign. She will fight to regain her lost place in the commercial world. That her methods will be unscrupulous and slim goes without saying, but she can be defeated by the women of the British Empire, if they one and all resolutely refuse to wear, eat or buy anything made in Germany, or by Germans, and hold no inter- course, social or otherwise, .with any man or woman of German nationality. Germany will be as completely defeated in her industrial campargn as it is to be hoped she will be in the war she so unrighteously forced upon Europe, and has carried on so mercilessly and so ruthlessly.

Buy British Sweets. Women and girls spend vast sums annually on sweets, more especially on chocolates. It may astonish many purchasers of these tooth- some morsels .to hear that tons of German chocolates find their way, even now, into our shops, where they are sold as French. The only safeguard, therefore, against this imposi- tion is to buy sweets made and labelled by British firms. These goods are generally superior in quality and purity to any foreign productions, and no dearer in price. Women all the world over are more patriotic than men, and they can accomplish much by combining together throughout the British Empire to defeat the enemy in his commercial war. Women and Horticulture.

Any industry connected with flowers appeals naturally to women, and many have in recent years adopted horticulture as a career. It was in 1891 that Swanley Horticultural College first opened its doors to women, and not long afterwards it was given over to them, the men being housed in new buildings. There are HOW over ten thousand women engaged in the various branches of horticulture, many being

div.head: HOME NOTES.
div.p: HOME NOTES.
Profitable Recipes And Useful Suggestions.
Rolled Breast of Mutton.

Take a breast of mutton, lay it on a board and remove the bones. Trim it neatly and remove some of the fat; Cover the side from which the bones have seen removed with slices of.ham, and then with a layer of veal stuffing flavoured with grated lemon. Quarter some pickled walnuts, and place them here and there on the forcemeat. Now roll the meat neatly and tightly, sewing the flap over. Bind it round with tape, and roast it. The meat should' be wrapped in. caul Or greased paper for the first hour it is in the roaster, and after- wards basted in the ordinary way. 'Place the mutton on a hot dish, remove the tape, and make a little good, rich brown gravy. Strain it well and Stir into it a tablespoonful of red- currant jelly, and pour it over and round the meat. Then take two tablespoonfuls of lightly- browned crumbs, a teasponful of mixed herbs, a quarter of a teaspoonful of pepper, and half a teaspoonful of salt, and mix thoroughly. .Sprinkle this over the Meat and serve.

Raisin Dumplings. Ingredients: 4oz. of self-raising flour; 4oz. of suet, finely chopped; skim milk; 4oz. of raisins; 1 tablespoonful of sugar; 4oz. of breadcrumbs. Thoroughly mix the flour with the other dry ingredients, then add sufficient skim milk, a little at a time (water in which condensed milk has been dissolved is a good substitute) to make a fairly stiff paste. Shape in little balls, and steam for about two hours and a half.

Raisin and Treacle Pudding. . Ingredients: 3oz. of shredded suet; .3oz. of flour; 4 tablespoonfuls of golden syrup; 3oz. of stoned and chopped raisins; gill of hot milk. Mix the 'syrup with the milk, and stir this very slowly into the dry ingredients, which You have thoroughly blended, in a deep basin. Pour the mixture into a well-greased pudding basin, tic a floured cloth over it, and steam for about three hours. Raisin Delight.

Ingredients: 31oz. of brown sugar; 1 gill of water; .2 teaspoonfuls of lemon juice; Vb. of raisins; Ipt. of apple pulp; pinch of salt. Stone the raisins, and chop them up finely. Bring them to the boil in a gill of water with a pinch of salt and simmer for half an hour; stir in the lemon juice and apple pulp, and simmer until the mixture thickens. Serve -in the centre of a mound of rice or with baked tapi- oca pudding. •

Casserole Cookery. The sooner the casserole utensil becomes a part of every kitchen outfit the better, for it makes in every way for economy—economy of food, time and labour—for materials often too tough for ordinary cooking may by this means be served in a nutritious and tender condition. When casserole cookery is once understood many
inexpensive viands will be put to use with very palatable results. •

- The initial cost of these utensils is very low, the simple clay casseroles which can now be bought in so many different shapes and sizes being admirably adapted to the purpose. A medium size in these, holding sufficient for four or five people, costs about 10d. They have much to recommend them from the point of view of cleanliness, being easily cleaned, and retaining no taste whatever from previous cooking. They are also economical as far as fuel is concerned. their heat-retaining power being so- great that they will simmer for hours over a gentle heat without burning the food. Perhaps the crown- ing advantage of .casserole cooking in families where, from various causes, meals are apt to be irregular, is that whatever is being treated in this way may be kept waiting for a consider- able time without deterioration. Food can always be left in a casserole with perfect safety. Fried Bananas. -
Remove the skins from the bananas, brush with egg, coat with breadcrumbs, and fry in smoking hot fat. To serve as a sweet, sprinkle with' sugar, and serve jam sauce or lemon sauce.

The Savageries of Fashion. The savageries of fashion were illustratod afresh by the visit of a bird lover to a colony of egrets, after havoc had been wrought by a party of plume hunters. The bird bunter made his visit during the height of the brefd- ing season. On his arrival at the colony he found the painful evidences of the recent raid in some 50 carcasses of adult birds floating in the water. These 50 birds had been ruthlessly shot while brooding their young. The young were left remorselessly to die a lingering death from hunger. Many had already succumbed. Others from time to time fell from the nests to share the same fate, while others again died from exhaustion as they sat in the nests. Per- haps the most pitiable sight of all was to watch those that still had sufficient strength to move and cry, attempting vainly to attract the attention of old birds flying heedlessly by with food in their beaks.

div.head: PARROTS FIRST FAVOURITE.
div.p: PARROTS FIRST FAVOURITE.

Many of the competitors selected the parrot as their favourite bird, and only one or two favoured the sweetest-voiced of all the feathered songsters—the skylark. One of my nieces, Lilian llimswortit, of 15, Fitzherbert-street, chose the dove, which "is very much attached to her mate" and laments sorely his loss. The dove, she recalls, is men- tioned several times in the Bible, and in the olden days "the poorer class of people used to offer two doves as a sacrifice, because they could not afford anything better." "It is," adds Lilian—who came very near to winning the prize—" because of its gentleness and purity that I admire it so."

•Dolly Shiplfy, of 109, Cartwright-street, favours the ". cuckoo; Florrie Barrow—(the naughty printer-fellow last week printed her name Burrows, and Florrie is righteously in- dignant about it)—" plumps" for the robin; Ada Connor is one of the parrot-lovers—and tells an interesting story of how a parrot once gave the alarm that burglars were in the house. Horace ,Himsworth is one of the few who votes for the skylark—'.' because its singing is very beautiful, and because there is no nicer singing- bird "• Gladys Taylor, 25, Fitzherbert-street, loves ;he robin because it comes to us in the winter months and sings to us, though the snow be on the ground; Louie Minshull, 29, Wakefield- street, dotes on the canary " because it is such a harmless and faithful little bird," and " be- cause it has such a lovely colour "; Florrie Stanway, 18, Edgeworth street, prefers the linnet to all other warblers, and Maude Higham, 35, Gladstone-street, is another parrot-lover, who writes a nice letter.

A host of other nephews and nieces have favoured me with their views, and I am sorry that I cannot give every one of them a prize., but that autocratic individual who wields the blue pencil and means "no " when he says " no," vetoes any proposal of the kind. And rightly so, don't you think, for if prizes were too easily won they would hardly be worth the having, would they? I hope that those who have not been successful this time will " try, try, try again" until they do manage to get an award.

Meat-Eating and Appendicitii. Appendicitis is chiefly a disease of youth. It is met with more frequently among males be- tween the ages of ten and tkirty years. The later in life the less liability one has of con- tracting appendicitis. It commonly occurs in those who are apparently in good health and strikes them down very quickly. What was commonly called a few years ago "inflammation of the bowel" is now known to have been appen- dicitis. It often follows constipation and catarrh of the bowels or colitis. Investigation of late years into. the causes of appendicitis have led many surgeons to believe that one chief cause is the diet of the people. The comparative immu- nity from appendicitis of the races who subsist upon a purely vegetable diet is worthy of con- sideration. This fact alone implies that the frequency ~of the dittltse ifm some communities has to do no doubt' with meat-eating.—C.. llayton, BA., M.D. Various Worriers.

The writer, who has for many years been meeting thousands Of Subjects of worry of differ- ent sorts, has been led to divide the subjects of worry into three classes : 1. Those who worry because. of the existence of real and natural causes of anxiety, such as great business respon- sibilities, with threatened financial disaster, the Prospect of the failure of cherished plans, &c. 2. Those who worry about trifles or even purely imaginary troubles, as the result of a general vital depression and mental disturbance due to toxemia, such as frequently accompanies eases of chronic constipation, especially when' associ- ated with incompetency of the ileoceeal valve; leading to the backing up of putrefaction material from the colon into the small intes- tine, and the rapid absorption of toxic sub- stances. 3. Persons' who, having formed the habit of worry through either one of the above- mentioned causes, continue to worry notwith- standing the fact that the original exciting cause has been removed. When we consider the pos- sible remedies for worry, it must be recognised at once that all cases cannot be treated alike. Diversion is one of the most potent remedies for worry. Concentration of the attention upon some wholesome subject is of utmost importance as a means of combating worry, whether due to present physical or mental causes, or merely 'a residual habit. Constant occupation of some sort is essential as an aid to diversion. Manual work is best. Gardening, boating, bird study, nature study of any sort which takes one into the open, and such manual arts as basketry, weaving, pottery, "-mother craft," sloyd and carpentry; are highly useful occupations for a worrying invalid.—Dr. Kellogg, in "Good Health."

div.head: EXTRA TIME PUT IN ON LESSONS.
div.p: EXTRA TIME PUT IN ON LESSONS.

A boy in :Kansas has a habit of putting an extra ten minutes on the preparation of every lesson. When he has completed the translation of his French or Latin for the next day, he goes over it again. The brief review, after the temp- tation has come to 'consider the task ended and to throw the book aside, is what fixes the trans- lation in his mind. It is the same with the history lesson and the problem in geometry and "the " theme " in English. The extra ten minutes fixes the boy's mental grip on what he has learned and set about tomaster. it has raised his classroom work from mediocrity to distine tion in contrast with the work of other boys, many of whom are naturally quicker in their studies than he is. The boy who is satisfied merely to "- get done " will not bother to give this extra. ten minutes to his lesson; conse- quently, in later years, his main efforts will be expended on " getting by," and he will find the 'great things of life not only unattained but un- attainuble. An effort, a little extra time, -a little extra care, a little oxtra Ahought—those are the keys that unlock the doors of success and happirt se.

div.head: DAWN.
div.p: THE DAWN.
In Memory Of The Glorious Fourth South Lancashires.
BY HAROLD MAYBURY
(Author of " A Russian's Impressions ").

The little French town of, lies secluded and sheltered from the breezes oi the Atlantic Ocean, far from the roar oi cannon and destroyers of human life, passing' its days in quietude of autumnal season, broken only occasionally by the news of a success of their countrymen, the sons of " La Belle France." To the north of the sleep 3 town the high cliffs tower majestically, like sentinels keeping watch, upon whose sides cattle seek their food from God, and Naturc sheds her leaves of golden brown along thc rugged paths, where white-washed cottages glisten in thq glorious rays of a fast-setting sun, now low on the horizon. The afternoon is nigh. gone, yet upon the breeze, wafted to the ears of these peasant folk of Brittany, comes the tramp of marching feet and sound of song. Hound the bend in the road the-. khaki-clad forms go marching by, to the familiar strains .of a patriotic British son, and then to the salutations and messages oi good fortune from these humble folk, soon disappear in the distance and are lost to view. A thousand or more there are, men bronzed with the life under God's sky, hardy, well- knit and in the fullness of youth, upon which the fading light of departing day lingers caressingly, seemingly smiling at the bug line of upright brown figures. The countryside is stilled in silence except for the sound of a trickling rivulet, plashing and dancing under an old granite bridge, over which the soldiers pass. It is a British regiment on its way to the firing line, their voices filled with laugh- ter, the -cares of a to-morrow unclouded with the thoughts of coming strife, or of a blood- red Death unseen as yet to eye and mind. It is a few hours before the Dawn.

The little French town has been forgotten, the month have passed, and the old line of khaki has been broken oftimes, to be replaced with fresh faces from this beloved country of ours. The miles that separate have given place from quietude and rest to horrors of war unspeakable. No longer does one see the cottages, clean and inhabited, but desolated and d'umbling. The earth trembles with the roar of cannon and screech of shells carrying Death in their train, and the land is. barren, as if a dread ffand had laid itself o'er all. Trees lie shattered, their boughs blown by shells a distance away. Intersecting this stricken land are rows of trenches, in which men lie huddled, seeking shelter behind the banked-up earth. Some are still, their proud faces upturned towards their Maker, lives cut off in the fullness of youth, half-told tales of an earthly career given for honour, justice, King and country. • Unceasingly the noise goes on, and with it each moment there de- parts another soul, unstained, to a Higher Power. The air is close and heavy, speaking of coming storm. Clouds of smoke, battered corpses, implements of warfare, shining steel stained with blood, and figures stiff and stark. A distance away the remains of a Catholic church breaks the evenness of the plain, around which there is to be seen rough crosses of wood, telling of fallen heroes. The little mounds of earth are barren except at the head. They are not even green, but only a dull brown, drab and commonplace, yet be- neath—who shall say? Of floral tributes there • are none, the graves untended by women's care, yet they live in memory, if only by the comrades who made them. The

roar increases, Nature blends with the handi- work of man, and across the sky through the haze of smoke and dust, there flits a grey dark bank of clouds, heralding the approach of storm and night. It is the hour before the Dawn.

lowly side by side, soldiers of sacrifice and honour, mourned by the nation, lives given for the cause of justice and liberty. To them the eventide has closed, the sands of time run out. To them has been given the wit- nessing of a glorious dawn, the dawn of a brighter world. Only does there remain the memory and the sad hearts across the seas, yet throughout the ages their names will _ _ . . .

- - stand revered and untarnished in the future generations of the world. The crimson blood has flowed. It has not flowed in vain. The sun sinks in the west, but full one knows it will surely rise again to cast its light upon the sacred spot where Britain's sons have fallen. It is The Dawn.

div.head: EVERLASTING FAME.
div.p: EVERLASTING FAME.

The night and storm have passed, and in 6he eastern sky long shafts of light proclaim he advent of another day. It is September 25th, 1915, a day memorable and eventful, withal a time of glory when honours shall become emblazoned once more on banners and in the records of history. All around on this cold grey dawn moving figures are astir, their ayes sparkling with excitement, feverish .with the lust of battle. The mist of early morn is not yet dispersed, when suddenly great blasts of sound, a hundred times louder than thun- der, rend the air. The earth trembles as with a mighty volcanic eruption, and to the hearers it seems likened to the craek of doom. Hoarse cries of command ring out, and with the utterances there comes tumbling out of the trenches, advancing under cover of the smoke, the glorious and inspiring lines of khaki, bayonets fixed, charging along the plain to spots a distance away, where lies the hidden enemy. On and on they move, irresistible and invincible the men from the unbreakable Fourth, side by side with the Scottish Borderers and other famous regiments, patriots of a common cause, seeking to annihilate the transgressors of peace and folders of civilisa- tion. Now they are a few yards from their goal. Spurts of flame, flashes of steel, meet the eye, masses of earth flung skyward, as well .as round objects' thrown unerringly into the German lines. Cries of the wounded, moans of the dying, laughter and song and appeals for mercy from the foe, all mingling in the first hours of this memorable day. Near by a piper of bagpipes cheering the in- domitable Scots on to fresh deeds of valour and glory. Over the parapets they go, slash- ing right and left at the enemy. Nothing could withstand them. Here it was that one saw what Britain's sons were made of. Men fell thick and fastt yet what of it Is it not war, and for the glory of England ? For a few hours it goes on, the .unbroken line ever moving forward, making straight for the vil- lage of . The battle has been won. Step by step through the narrow streets the foe are driven, giving no quarter and asking none, making the rout complete. Soon the soldiers seek respite from the achievements of the day, fatigued with the work they have performed. Labours are o'er and with them there comes the lull of battle as night casts her velvety folds over the scene. A pale wan moon rises, casting ghostly shadows in nar- row streets and byways of this small village. As the night grows on the laughter of the soldiers dies down slowly like a child being lulkid to sleep. September 25th has been added to history, the day of days by those who lived through it. There are those who answered not the roll-call when the victory had been won, heroes one and all. There in a stricken land they, lie at peace, exalted and

div.head: FOOD SHORTAGE IN GERMANY.
div.p: FOOD SHORTAGE IN GERMANY.

'The German authorities have now commanded that in Berlin and the province of Brandenburg, the retail prices of best butter shall not ex- ceed 2s. 10d. per lb. (2 marks 80 pf.). Persons infringing the order are to be liable to a penalty of about £l5O. Milk cards have now been introduced in Ber- lin, in addition to the bread cards which were general throughout Germany,. and the potato cards, which were being used in a few of the large towns. The milk cares are intended chiefly for the benefit of children, invalids and others who are confined entirely, or almost en- tirely, to a milk diet. The possessor of one of these is legally empowered to make arrange- ments with a retail dairy for as much milk es the card entitles him to obtain, and on the Friday of any one week he has to notify the dairy of the quantity of milk he may require from Monday of the following week. Also cream is not to be sold unless it is for butter making purposes, milk must not be used in the manufacture of chocolate and sweet- meats, and the sale of whipped cream is "absolutely forbidden." No milk must be used for feeding calves or pigs over six weeks old, nor skim milk for bread-making. Milk is no longer to be employed in the making of colours or casein, and no milk powder or cream powder is to be sold.
Fats of all kinds seem to be very scarce in Germany at present.
It is reasonably safe to treasure your suspi- cions of a man who writes to you on the stationery of a hotel at which he is not a guest. What It Is.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
An Adventurous Career.

• The mere mention of Constantinople in the title of Thursday's lecture at Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church, brought to my mind some curious facts in the later history of an old acquaintance of mine—a Scotsman named Petrie. He was motor 'bus manager in a district in which I lived for a while, and so reorganised the service as to turn an un- successful into a paying concern: He was granted increased remuneration, but was dissatisfied with the advance, and entered into an agreement to take charge of a similar system in Constantinople at double the rate of pay. A while before, the outbreak of war, he saw reason to clear out of the rotten Turkish Empire, but when he had got settled in South Africa he began to wonder if he had not jumped out of the frying pan into the fire. However, the turmoil there seems to be about over, whereas Constantinople is at pre- sent one of the least desirable places for a Britisher. My friend, whose plucky wife has accompanied him throughout, is now doing well in Johannesburg.

Official Dinners. The announcement of the High Sheriff's dis- continuance of the official dinners to the Grand Jury (whether the Jury might not also be "discontinued" is a moot point), reminded- me of some of the Corporation banquets at which I Have been present from time to time. In one Lancashire town in which I worked some years, two successive Mayors, being wealthy men, entertained quite lavishly. Eventually this hospitality came to be scandalously abused, and I ventured in my paper to protest against a system that had resulted in such a train of evils. What time members of the Council and officials drank to excess, waiters and bandsmen carried off champagne and cigars wholesale, and I went so far as to invite the kindly-intentioned host to abolish tlw institution' entirely. That was on the eve of one of these annual affairs, and on the occasion itself, during an interval in the speech-making, the Mayor came round to my table, and was good enough to ask if I had any objection to his taking public notice of my criticism. Of course—to employ the Parlia- mentary phrase—the answer was in the negative. Nevertheless, his Worship thowrit better of it; all the same, as the sequel proved, that was the last of the series of wasteful orgies, and certain deserving charities bene- fited by the change.

A Rich Hibernicism. Last week's incidental allusion to Dr. Thorp as temporary medical offic rir at Lymm reminded me of an Iri4i doctor of that name who die.l only a few days ago. He hold the like office in a borough in which I formerly resided. He had spent the greater part of his professional life there, and when I went to the place, occupied a fine house standing in its own grounds. He dearly loved a bit of gossip, and would at any time draw up by the roadside for a chat with a likely newsmonger.- Once he halted thus by .a low-lying old building which had pre- viously served him as surgery and dwelling. " Let's see, 'doctor," said the one whom he had accoFted, "didn't you used to live here ?" ' I did," was the reply; "and if I'd been living there now I'd have been a dead man long since!" Catching a Tartar.

He was an impulsive, plucky old fellow. Once, when driving along the highway to a country appointment, he came upon a liurly tramp brutally beating his wretchel ; an springing out of his carriage, he promptly administered to the cowardly ruffian such a thrashing that the astonished bully roared for mercy, and was fain to, promise never again to lay a finger on tho- poor woman. On another occasion, when on a similar journey, the doctor slipped and broke his leg. He forthwith set the fracture after a fashion; and bound the injured limb with a wisp of straw. Then he proceeded to attend to some pressing and important business, so that some time elapsed before his injury had proper treatment. However, he suffered perman- ently on that account, being lame for the rest of his days.

The (Mantahni's Phrase) Bow-wows. I note that juvenile competitors for the " Children's Corner" prize for the best essay on "My Favourite Animal," mostly give first place to the dog. I may have been peculiarly unfortunate in my experience, but it long ago impelled me to the conclusion that dogs are far too numerous. One small essayist tells us that " black retriever dogs have proved 'great lovers of little children." It may be so, but when I was a child I was severely bitten by a dog, and it happened to be a .black retriever. lam not going to trouble readers with the narration of other painful adventures of this kind, especially as I have reason to suspect that most of them would be ready with the retort that if the sight of my " phiz " rouses, a dog to anger and resentment, clearly I am no lover ot animals. That is not so at all; any such estimate of my character would do me grave injustice; at the same time, I seem o have been singularly unlucky with dogs, and nothing is likely to shake my conviction that there are too many dogs—and cats, too, for that matter. " Where He Want."

A variant of the last week's story under this, heading I have myself for many ears been in the habit of telling. When, as a young reporter, I attended the Halifax Police Court, there was in practice there a solicitor named Leeming, who died between 30 and 40 years ago. Once he appeared for the complainant in a case, and in the course of the examina- tion-in-chief asked his client, " And what followed that?" "Well, sir," was the reply, "he told me to go to the devil." "Then what did you do?" was the next question;' and the unexpected and startling answer was, ",Well, of course, I came to you at once!"
