div.head: VV. G.
div.p: VV. G.
"Punch's" Tribute To "Brave
Days That Are Gone."
This week's " Punch " has the following on the death of Dr. W. G. Grace:—

So W. G. is now more! Cricket itself has suffered the cruellest 'wounds since August of last year, and now the Father of it is laid low. And his place will never be filled again. There could not be another W. G.; there can be, if the Fates allow the game to recover, great cricketers; but there can never be another so immeasurably the greatest—never another not only to play cricket as Grace did, but to be cricket as Grace was.

Cricket and W. G. were indeed one. Popular superstition and the reporters had it that he was a physician, and it is true that, when a wicket-keeper smashed his thumb or a bumping ball flew into a batsman's face, first aid would be administered in the grateful shade of the " Doctor's " beard; but it was impossible really to think seriously of his medical activi- ties, or indeed of any of his activities off the field. Between September and May one thought of him as hibernating in a cave, returning to life with renewed vigour with the opening of the season, his beard a little more imposing, his proportions a little more gigantic; so that each year the bat in his hand, as he walked to the wicket with that curious rolling tumbling gait, seemed a more trifling implement. With the mind's vision one sees him in many postures. At the wicket: waiting, striking and running; and again bowling, in his large round action, coming in from leg, with a man on the leg boundary a little finer than square, to catch the youngsters who lunged at the widish ball (his "bread-anti-butter trick" W. G. called it). One sees him thus and thus, and oven retiring to the pavilion, either triumphantly—with not, of course, a sufficient but an adequate score to his credit—or with head bent pondering how it was he let that happen and forewarning himself against it next time. But to these reminiscent eyes the most familiar and characteristic atti- tude of all is W. G. among his men at the fall of a wicket, when they would cluster round to discuss the event and, no matter how tall they were, W. G.'s beard and shoulders wool; top the lot. Brave days for ever gone! Of late r..ars, since his retirement, the Old Man, he was best know,i among his fellow ainatews. was an oceas:owil figure at lord's. More than a figure, a landmark, for he grow vaster steadily, more massive, more monu- mental. What must it have been like to have that Atlas back and those shoulders in front of one in the theatre! At the big matches lie would be seen on one of the lower seats of the pavilion with a friend on either side, watching and commenting. But the part of oracle sat very lightly upon him; he was ever a man of action rather than of words; shrewd and sagacious enough, but without rhetoric. That his mind worked with Ulysses-like acuteness every other captain had reason to know; his tactics were superb. But he donned and doffed them with his flannels. In ordinary life he was content to be an ordinary man. Although sixty-seven, he did not exactly look old; he merely looked older than he had been, or that any such performer should be permitted to be. There should be a dispensation for such masters, by which W. G with his bat, and John Roberts with his cue, and Cinquevalli with his juggling implements would be rendered immune from Anno Domini. Almost to the end he kept himself fit, either with local matches, where latterly he gave away more runs in the field than he hit up, not being able to "get down" to the ball, or with golf or beagling. But the great beard grew Steadily more grizzled and the ponderous footfall more weighty. Indeed towards the last he might almost have been a work by Mestrovics, so colossal and cosmic were his lines.
Peaee to his ashes! We shall never look upon his like again. The days of Grace are ended.

div.head: SIIE " MOTHERED " GLADSTONE.
div.p: SIIE " MOTHERED " GLADSTONE.

I once witnessed, says an English writer, the "mothering" of her illustrious and aged hus- band by Mrs. Gladstone. On leaving the re- porters' gallery (of the House of Commons) late one night that Gladstone as Prime Min- ister had made a fine speech in support of his Home Rule Bill in 1893, I saw Mrs. Gladstone waiting with a brougham in palace yard. She was thinly clad in evening dress, with a light shawl over her grey hair. Presently her hus- band emerged from the Ministers' entrance to the House of Commons, with a puckered, wearied look on his mobile face. She at once ran forward and kissed him proudly on the cheek. Then catching' with both hands the lapels of his heavy overcoat, which was hang- ing open, as if to button it up, she cried out in a removing voice, "Oh, William, without your muffler !" and diving her hand into one of his pockets produced the wrap and wound it ten- derly round his throat. She then hurried him into the brougham, following after, and shut- ting the door. herself. It was like the tender solicitude of a mother for a precious only son in whom all her hopes, and alarms are centred.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.-
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.-
continued.

valuable contribution. Referring to the building which formerly stood at the corner of Brick-street and Cockhedge, he naturally expresses regret that Warrington's oldest house, and one of the oldest in the North of England, should have been demolished. In precisely similar circumstances in Halifax when I was there, a Mr. John Lister had the doomed old timbered structure carefully re- moved, every stone, &c., being marked, and rebuilt in his own grounds. Some interested reader may remember that, several weeks ago, I told how in a journey I had fallen in with the members of an Antiquarian Society who wore setting out on a ramble, how I was constrained to aecompany them, and bow we came upon an old long-case or grandfather clock by a Warrington maker of long ago. The Mr. Lister above mentioned is still President of that Society, and was present on that occasion. Although we had not met, during all those intervening years, he recog- nised me immediately, and so I joined the party and had an enjoyable and profitable time. The " House-part."

Our eminent and most competent local authority observes that " even yet among old country folk the kitchen is called the house. " Not only so; to my certain know- ledge the cotton operatives and other cot- tagers in various Lancashire towns invariably so .term it to this day. One who is unaware of this characteristic, or has not become thoroughly accustomed to it, is apt to be puzzled by the expression. An enthusiastic housewife, describing the interior of a new acquisition of the kind, may be heard exclaim- ing " It's a right clever house." A new arrival at the moment might well take this to be a general summing-up, but that would be a mistake, the reference being to the :itehen exclusively.

Other Examples. Since I came from the West Riding into Lancashire a quarter of a century ago, I have had to revise my vocabulary—and in some cases during the process were encountered certain ancient and deeply-rooted prejudices that proved too tough for disturbance. Thus, what in Yorkshire, and elsewhere so far as I know, is the worm becomes a snail when one passes over the East Lancashire border. 1 have many excellent friends thereabout who do not know, and never have known, the worm by any other name, and—well, even a WOllll will turn. Again, in Yorkshire and in other parts of the country, a teacake is—why, a teacake, of course, and, equally of course, a muffin is just a muffin; butin Lanca- shire the former is known as a muffin, the other being a pikelet. A native of this county told me of a- person of his acquaintance who thought nothing of eating " three dorfins o' monfins"at a sitting—that was, as understood in the-sister county, three baking or "oven" tins of teacakes, each containing four, or twelve in all.

THE "OLD FOX."
Another Chapter On The Ways Of Old. Time

div.head: Builders.
div.p: Builders.
THE ORIGIN OF CHIMNEYS.
BY ARTHUR M

It would be impossible to write a chronol- ogical history of chimneys. Their inventor is unknown to us, and we can therefore—richly as he deserves it—pay him no homage. it would be venturesome to oven guess at the century in which they first appeared, for they were originally of flimsy niaterials—of lath or 14 attle—and very few traces of the earliebt examples lin re survived.
Yet it is possible from fragments which remain to describe their evolution.

We must picture the ancient homestead with its centre fire of smouldering peat or wood, from which the smoke made its uncertain way through a 'hole in the roof. The first inven- tion that was designed to abate the smoke nuisance took the form of a lightly made flue which guided tile snioke to the roof. At its base this flue would be supported on timbers and would spread in the form of a canopy over the fire. Such references as survive in literature (we have only known of one actual flue) it would appear that they were often made of basket-work, daubed with clay, or, perl•aps, of wood.

div.head: CHIMNEY LiwriNEß.
div.p: THE CHIMNEY LiwriNEß.

From a light framework the fireplace easily developed. into a more substantial structure. Strong timbers were framed together to form a large square space, and a chimmey formed upon them which reached to the roof. Three sides of the timber square were filled in wattle work, and the result was that of a house within the house, called in later days the chimney corner. The fire burned on the floor in the centre. Seats tould be placed on each side; hams and flitches could be hung on a beam to gather soot and flavour, and those who sat in this warm shelter on looking up had a mixed vision of sparks, Dacon, soot and stars.

Such a fire chamber existed in the old house t Cockhedge, to which reference was made in our last article. It consisted of a heavy framing of oak filled in on three sides, and the chimney rose from tho cross beams to the roof. That tho chimney was of later date than the building seemed evident from the tet that the roof-tree had been cut through to admit of the chimney, the ends being left without support, except that which was given by the rafters. Though not so old as the building, the fire- place was one of the best examples of an early chimney corner, and could it have been pre- served, would have been of immense interest to antiquarians. .

div.head: SUPPOSED " HIDING HOLES."
div.p: SUPPOSED " HIDING HOLES."

These large fire spaces continued in English homes for a long time. In Elizabethan days when two-storied houses were built, they pre- served the central fire-place, even though its canopy-like chimney com- pletely spoiled the room above. Those who have examined old houses must often have noticed how the bedrooms were spoiled. The fire was placed not at the side or end, but in the middle of the ground floor. Hence the huge chimney space, often six feet square passed up through the middle of the room Adve. These large square spaces in the bedrooms often remain long after their original meaning has been forgotten. A modern flue may be built and a doorway cut into the " room in the chimney." It only remains for the amateur antiquarian to describe it as a " priest's hiding hole,".or an imaginative p6rson to weave a romance' and the innocent chimney becomes a hiding place of Cromwell or Charles 11.

When the a Old Fox " is rebuilt its fire- place must be left in its original open form, and it will be found, we think, almost mactly like the one in the famous old house at Strat- ford, in which Shakespeare spent hi g early years. _ _

- The chimney as we know it to-day, formed as a cavity in a wall, was hardly suited to the low-eaved timber house. But in the case pf stone-built castles it was found possible to place flues against tho walls. Leland, the traveller, expressed surprise on finding smoke tunnels in Bolton Castle.

"One thinge I muche notyd in the haulle of Bolton bow chimneys were conveyed by tun- nells made on the syds of the wauls, betwyxt the lights of the haull; and by this means, and by no covers, is the smoke of the harthe wonder strangely convayed." This was written in 1538, and marks The period when flues began to be fastened agn.ngt a wall. But this was only in a 'castle where walls would allow it. Aubrey, writing ninety- years later, said: " Antiently before the Reformation, ordinary men's houses had no chimneys, but fleus like louver holes; some of them were in being when I was a boy." The canopy to receive the smoke was some- times called a reredosse. There is an inter- esting bit of evidence to show tlat in early times the reredosso and chimney was made of wood, for in some bylaws of the City of Lon- don, dated A.D. 1419, it is laid down that no chimney should henceforward be of wood, but should be made of stone, tiles or plaster, "on payne of being pulled down." This was a precaution against fire in a city of wooden huts. THE EVOLUTION OF THE HOUSE.

The cruck-built house of the 12th century, evolved into the three-storied Elizabethan home by slow and easy stages. The tie beam described in our last article offered oppor- tunity for an extra floor, which was found a convenient sleeping Once, and a second floor became in course of time a per- manent feature. The large chim- ney often made it next to useless, but it offered a snug and warm, if not spacious, apartment. The idea of timber framework raised high enough to allow of two low stories, and surmounted by a tie-beam roof marks the next distinct.stage in domestic architecture. That our ancestors were slow to adopt this type of blinding must be confessed. The Romans built with walls and tie-beam roofs, and the model must have been known in England, but the hulk-shaped house per- sisted to the fifteenth century. Our fathers were conservative in their methods of house building, though not more so than other branches of the Teutonic tribe.

In the use of timber, also,, they were, con- servative. If they used stone it was because timber could not easily be obtained. The timber house meets us at the dawn of history. It persisted until the seventeenth century. We describe old housmas half-tintbered; but this is a misnomer. They are entirely tim- bered.. The wood framework is the house. All the rest.is filling in. Se entirely was building associated with timber, that the old 'English word for build was " timbran."

div.head: BUILDING METHODS IN 1575 A.D.
div.p: BUILDING METHODS IN 1575 A.D.

The manner of the setting itp of a timbered building has some little .inberest, and our readers may appreciate some sidelights which come from a builder's account of the year 1575. This date comes' so very near to the date of the " Uld Fox " that the items may almost be taken as applying. This is boil- the builder enters some of his costs.

Item Paled for goyttinge basinge stone ij [two shillings.] Item Paled to my Lord for viij trees ten s the tree Item Paled to Mr. West for vij trees and he gave my wiffe one tree besydes xvjs [sixteen shillings.] A glance at the "Old Fox" will reveal the

div.head: OUNFIELD.
div.p: OUNFIELD.

" basinge " stone—the base upon which the timber framework was placed. Fifteen trees for £4 16s. does not appear costly, but the purchasing power of the shil- ling was greater in those days. The old custom of giving an extra tree "for luck" was observed by Mr. West, but "My Lord" —probably the lord of the manor—was not so generous.

div.head: "REARING."
div.p: THE "REARING."

The timber framework was prepared and put together on the ground, and then reared in large sections. This explains the next item " For meat and drink that day the house was reared," £2 Gs. Bd. Remembering the rate of wages at that time this is a big item, ;did suggests that a large number of men were temporarily employed. It certainly would require many bands at the ropes to rear the heavy pieces of oaken framework, and the " rearing" would be a great event, and would be made to the accompaniment of a plentiful flow of ale.

In the building trade the putting on of the last part of the roof is still described as the " rearing," and within recent times was the occasion of gratuities and beer, though prob- ably no modern workman has any idea of what the term means. In Yorkshire and Derby- shire they still describe a timbered house as a " reared house," to distinguish it from a stone or " built " house.

There is an Act of the Realm dating from Henry the Eighth's time, which recites that some evil persons had been guilty of the seeret burnynge of frames of tymber pre- pared and made redy to be sett up, and edified for houses." This was placed on the Statute Book as a felony. Having reared the carcass—such was the old term—the builder must cover it and fill in the walls. The items for roofing are : First paied to John Rouksley for gayting mo xxxc slate stones xxxs [thirty shillings.) Item Paled to my Lord for the delp yre of the said stono
The house was evidently not to be thatched, but covered with slate-atones. There is a further item : Payd in part of a recconing for mossing of and slating my howse

div.head: WATTLE WORK.
div.p: WATTLE WORK.

The process of filling in tho framework to form the walls was that popularly, known as "wattle and daub." Some very good examples are to be seen in the gables of the "Fox," and an observation of them will con- vey a much better idea of ancient building methods than any description we can offer. The oldest plan was to weave twigs and, brushwood across staves of wood and thus fill in the spaces between the large timbers. This was daubed over with a mixture of mud, clay and cow dung. Some of the spaces of the " Fox " will be found to be filled in with plaited hazel twigs, and this, we think, is the oldest work. The old house at Cockhedge had hazel.twigs with clay and cowdung. After twigs and brushwood came laths, which were fitted into grooves made in the timber. It will be noted that some panels of the gable of the "Fox " are filled with strong laths. These belong to ,a later period, and have replaced hazel twigs.. The putting on of the daub was called parging or sparging, which may come from the Latin " spargere," to " sprinkle." Builders will not need to be told that parging is still a builders' word, but it is now only used to describe the daubing of the inside of fines.
Another item in the old bill of costs is very significant. To Dewk the glasyor for xvi foots of glasse for my windows viijs height shillings.]

A single cottage window of to-day would contain more, than sixteen " foots " of glass, so that the windows must havo been exceed- ingly small. This will give opportunity to say a word dpon the subject of domestic windows.

div.head: EARLY WINDOWS.
div.p: EARLY WINDOWS.

The word window carries with it the clue to its former and original meaning. It is " wind-eye," that is, an eyelet to let in air. It was for ventilation, and incidentally let in a small amount of light. In a study of win- dows it may be laid down as a guiding prin- ciple that the smaller the window the order the house. Of course large windows may have been inserted at later periods, but the student of architecture learns to distinguish these. In the case of the " Fox " it is to he doubted whether the projecting window of the second floor forms part of the original design for a large window of that type seems to be- long to a later date than the period of timber framework.

Probably the very earliest kind of " wind- eye" was a loop-hole such as may be observed in old barns and church towers. These were narrow slits which would let in air or let out smoke. They could be left open in summer and easily stuffed up in winter. They were sometimes covered with linen dipped in oil, and perhaps, as in Iceland and Greenland, our ancestors found a transparent covering in the caul of a new-born calf.

div.head: WHEN GLASS WAS PRECIOUS.
div.p: WHEN GLASS WAS PRECIOUS.

It must not be assumed from this that glass was unknown. Glass was in use in Britain in Roman times, and was never quite abandoned, but until the 16th century it was too•costly for use in humble dwellings. The churches had it, and so had the palaces, but it was beyond the means of poor men. This alone was sufficient to keep domestic windows very small. Before the time of Henry VIII. glazed windows were very rare, and after his reign the dearness of glass tended to keep windows of an insignificant size. In the sixteenth century glass became cheaper. It will be noticed that in 1575 our builder paid for it at the rate of sixpence per foot, a large sum in those days, and earlier in the ciSntury it was more costly still. The lowering of the price had a good effect. It led to large windows and consequently more Ihealthful homes. The rich builders began to I revel in glass, and of the famous Hardwick Hall, in Derbyshire, it was said :- 1 " Hardwick Hall, More glass than wall," which came near to literal truth .

Late in the century the fashion arose of carrying windows from end to end of the building, of which we have a good example in. the " Barley Mow." With the windows came something else—the discovery that Elizabethan houses were dirty. Then came internal decoration and house-pride. For a long period the glazed portions of the windows were made in the form of loose ease- ments, which could be easily removed from the frames. In early days, when glass was raluable, these casements were regarded as personal estate, and were separately be- queathed by the owner just as were pictures or works of art. They were regarded as some- thing apart from the house, and did.not pass to the heir as part of the freehold. But the sixteenth century and the cheapening of glass brought changes.
IT Our readers' patience is not exhausted we will devote vet another chapter to the ways of ancient builders and the buildings they pro- duced,

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.

DAIRY SHORTHORN ASSOCIATION. Sir Gilbert Greenall, presiding at the tenth annual meeting of the members of the above Society, moved the adoption of the report. Tha membership, he said, showed an increase in the year of seventeen. This was satisfactory, but he would appeal to members to bring the claims of the Association before their friends who are interested in Dairy Shorthorns, and endeavour to increase the membership during the coming year. The fifty-guinea challenge cup for the best group of Dairy Shorthorns, offered at the Royal Show, had now been won outright. Sir Gilbert subsequently presided at the meeting of the Council of the Association.

div.head: WHEAT AFTER WHEAT.
div.p: WHEAT AFTER WHEAT.

. In response to the appeal of the Government, farmers are sowing as much wheat as possible, and in order to find room for it without crowd- ing out other crops, many of them are growing two wheat crops in succession. In ordinary cir- cumstances it is considered bad farming to grow two consecutive white straw crops, but there is not the least reason why it should not be done when high prices justify a departure from the usual system. As is well-known, wheat has been grown on the same land for 72 years at Rothamsted, and yet the average crop is above the average for the whole country, whilst wheat was grown continuously for 50 years by Mr. Prout 'at Sawbridgeworth, and with commercial success. Dr. Russell, Director of Rothamsted, urges the importance of a suit- able spring., top-dressing for a second. crop of wheat. The land is not likely to be in such good tilth as it would be after a crop of roots, and the dressing should correct this as far as possible. He recommends soot' as being helpful in this respect, and, failing that, sulphate of ammonia. These are nitrogenous manures, but phosphates also are needed. Dr. Russell advises the following dressings: For light soil, 1 to 2cwt. nitrate of soda, 2cwt. superphosphate, 2cwt. common salt. For heavy soil, 14 to 3cwt. nitrate of soda, or, if had tilth is feared, sul- phate of ammonia, or 30 bushels of soot, and lewt. superphosphate. The salt is recom- mended in place of potash. The dressings should be applied early, say in February or March, with the exception of the-nitrate of soda, which should be applied alone in early April.

div.head: POTATOES FOR PIGS.
div.p: POTATOES FOR PIGS.

The past season has produced a good deal of disease in the potato crop. Diseased tubers, says "Farm and Home," unless in a state of decomposition, will do no harm to pigs. Good sound potatoes are too valuable for pig food, for the small ones and those attacked by disease may be utilised for the pig pen. Potatoes should never be given uncooked. When first got out of the ground it does not matter so much, but in the skin of the potato more especially, arid more or less through the whole tuber, is a poisonous ,substance called solaine. The older the skin gets, the more there. is of it, particu- larly if at all green. Cooking disperses nearly all, if not all, of this; a great deal is taken up by the water, and on this account water in which potatoes have been boiled should always he thrown away. Steaming is preferable to boil- ing, as there is then no chance of a careless person giving the water to the pigs. Potatoes, like turnips, may be boiled down, and kept for a long time, iind when a large quantity is affected by. disease this is the only way of utilising them. When steamed, break them up, and put in a large wooden tub—a treacle hogs- head is good—and, when the tub is nearly filled up, saturate the mass with kitchen slop, taking care there is always an inch or so of liquid on tile top, and the *potatoes will keep for many weeks. When, however, potatoes are sound, no plan of feeding is more economical than giving them freshly cooked each day.

div.head: INEFFICIENT FARMER.
div.p: THE INEFFICIENT FARMER.

The statement on home grown food published by the committee of the Farmers' Club includes a significant reference to the proper utilisation of the land. It says, "It is almost the duty of landlords and agents to see that those who can- not farm their lands properly should make room for those who can. At any rate, bad farmers should be warned of the 'risk they run." This remark raises a question as delicate as it is difficult. Like most other problems, that of the inefficient husbandman is easily solved in theory, but to deal with it in reality is a very different matter. In the first place, there is the question of providing a tribunal competent to decide as to when land is farmed to advantage or the reverse. If there were anything approach- ing uniformity in physical, climatic and other governing conditions, the application of estab- lished standards might be feasible; as it is this point almost defies equitable settlement. Cir- cumstances vary so widely, and often without causes intelligible on discernible grounds, that no group of adjudicators would care to under- take the responsibility of determining the efficiency or inefficiency of a farmer. In a general way the wider the knowledge and ex- perience he possesses, the less inclined a valuer Would be to lay claim to the requisite attain- ments. There are in most districts instances that will present no serious difficulty, since there are the records of the holdings under pre- vious tenants by which to measure the perform- ances of the present occupiers, but this can apply only to the most glaring cases of neglected opportunities, which are steadily decreasing. Perhaps the most formidable aspect of the problem is that affecting personal or political considerations. No one knows better than the landowner or his agent when a farmer falls short of the level of efficiency fairly expected of him. He is familiar with the capabilities of each holding, possesses data of what former tenants have achieved, and of the condition of the land when it came into the hands of the present occupier, and, making proper allowance for seasonal and other unstable conditions, he can arrive at a fair estimate of the manner in which results harmonise with reasonable ex- pectations. Neither the owner nor his agent, however, would be accepted as the sole arbi- trator on a question to which he was one of the principal parties.

- The landlord is in an exceedingly difficult posi- tion when he finds that he has been unfortunatA in his choice of a tenant. It is all very well to speak or write of displacing "bad farmers" by others of greater capabilities, but there are few among the great landowners of the country who have not had some experience of what results from an effort of the kind. They have had abundant proof that their estimate of what constitutes defective management is not accept- able to khose who, with or without ulterior motive, espouse the cause of the victims of their alleged oppression.—" Field."

div.head: TURKEYS AND GEESE.
div.p: TURKEYS AND GEESE.

November is a very important month in the life of a turkey, for towards the middle of the month the fattening process should commence. It must be remembered that it is the large birds that find the readier sale at Christmas. One can afford to feed turkeys generously, as they realise such excellent prices, and during the last six weeks of their lives they should be given all that they wilr eat. Ground oats form an excellent food, as nothing produces flesh of quite such excellent flavour or colour. Mixed with skim milk, and during the later stages with a litle fat, it forms the most suitable food that one can suppler. Middlings, barley nnal, and maize meal (the latter iu small quantities only) may be used, which has the effect of re- ducing the cost somewhat, but usually at the expense of quality and co!olr. Jia( kwlr3at at mid-day and in the afternoon is the best grain for fattening turkeys, peon ikd that it can be procured cheaply.. The Christmas Goose.

It is necessary to exercke rare in feeding geese, since they are huge rat.7.rs, while the value of the finished article is not sufficient to warrant expensive foods. A few years ago. when they were • worth more money, it was another matter; nowadays, when 7d. to SW. per lb. is as much as they are likely to make, it is necessary to economise as much as possible in every way, among which feeding is perhaps of greatest importance. Foods to avoid, although often used, are maize meal and pea and bean meals; the first because it produces fat rather than flesh, and the other because they form such very hard meat. Personally, I prefer to feed Upon meals only, although some breeders give grain in the afternoons. If it is thoroughly soaked it is quite all right, but, in a hard state it is indigestible, and does not produce flesh. quickly. A good ration for fattening geese con- sists of equal parts middlings, barley meal, bran and brewers' grains. Boiled potatoes, mashed and dried off with meals, are also useful. There

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
Cycling In France In War-Time
Conditions,
THE ECONOMY OF THE CYCLE.
(Queries and correspondence should be addressed to the Editor. Replies cannot be sent by post, and all queries will be answered in our columns.)

Ninety-nine out of every hundred people are endeavouring at the present time by any and every means to reduce their expenditure. £5,000,000 a day, we are told, is ,being spent upon the war, and the people of this country have got to find this stupendous sum of money somehow or other. Only a few days ago Mr. Montagu gave us the pleasant information that .half a man's income should be devoted to the State. And this at a time when a large pro- portion of the population is making far smaller incomes than ever before. With the ever-in- creasing price of food and other necessities—a pound has now a purchasing power of about 15s. as compared with two years ago—the ques- tion of how to economise is a problem that is almost impossible of solution. But somehow or other we must economise. This is where the cycle scores so enormously. Its initial cost is low; its running costs are almost nil.

div.head: RIDING TO OFFICE.
div.p: RIDING TO OFFICE.

It is cheaper as well as healthier to live in the country than in the town. But s there is always the drawback of travelling in a crowded train or a still more crowded tram, to say nothing of the added expense of a season ticket. It is just here that the cycle comes to our aid. It provides an admirable method of travelling; it saves the cost of a seasop ticket; and it gives added health. The ride to the office in the morning fits one for the day's work; the return journey enables one to dismiss all worrying though& of business. I know, because I have done it now for nearly four years. There are only two disadvantages in cycling to business, both of which can be easily overcome. There is the possibility of bad weather conditions, which can be provided against by wearing suitable clothing. Secondly, traffic-laden streets are a menace until one is accustomed to city riding. Familiarity brings a steady nerve and a quick eye, and these will help the cyclist to avoid accidents. Moreover, always remember to keep with the stream. Don't hurry or try to ,squeeze through the traffic.

div.head: CYCLING IN FRANCE.
div.p: CYCLING IN FRANCE.

The able cycling writer in the "Sunday Chronicle," who hides his identity under the name of " Ixion," has recently been spending some time in France. Ills remarks on the Position of cycling there are extremely interest- ing. "Cycling," he writes, "is confined now to girls and boys under military age and young fellows home recovering from their wounds or on duties which keep them out of the Army. I did not see half a dozen middle-aged men or women on bicycles. Cycling is confined to those who want to 'scorch,' or to appear as if they did. And there is much more about than I expected. You will not see ,such a procession out of the big cities on Sundays as you will see in England, but the stream is far bigger than ninny might think. The French don't be- lieve in the dogma of dulness. So far as limita- tions will allow, they are as keen upon pleasures as any on this side of the Channel, even within the sound of the guns. And remember that these guns are on their own soil. They know the value of recuperation.

div.head: FRENCH MACHINES.
div.p: THE FRENCH MACHINES.

"Although there are not nearly so many cyclists about as on this side, there are more than one might expect when it is borne in mind that practically every man of military age is serving with the colours. The French bicycle would not suit British riders. Frames are very low built, so low that mounting direct into the saddle is easy: Short heads are universal, but half the length of that on an English bicycle. Saddles are narrow, and must cut the riders

over any distance. Moreover, they are usually of the cheapest variety, and look as if the quantity of leather had been cut down to reduce the price. The brakes are all of the old- fashioned horseshoe pattern. I did not see a single instance of the neat rim brakes as known here. Every machine has a handlebar project- ing well beyond the stem; indeed, the entire effort appears to be to stimulate a racing appearance. Mudguards and rims are mostly of wood, with here and there steel. In many cases mudguards are discarded altogether. I even saw girls riding without them. I mar- velled what the mothers would have to say about the skirts. Almost every machine is be- decked with beautiful enamel in every imagin- able colour. Neither Frenchmen or French- women seem to like the plain black of British custom, although there is so much mourning about the streets that one can understand the aversion."
STARTING FROM REST.

There is always a tendency to get into top gear too rapidly when starting a motor cycle from rest. To do this often is very harm- ful to the engine, and no rider should be guilty of such a thing. The low gear is fitted for a definite purpose; to make practically no use of it will cause a severe strain to be put on the machine. This is bound to show itself in time. A number of riders change gear as soon as the machine begins to move, and then, after run- ning a few more yards, they slip into top. The noise made when travelling on low gear may not be pleasant, but it is worth while to put up with a little noise until forty or fifty yards have been traversed and a good speed attained before changing gear. No real advantage accrues by affecting the change too soon. To test this. make a series of trials over a given distance on the same road, changing at various points. Watch the speedometer meanwhile and note the result. The exact moment will 'quickly be found.

div.head: INIQUITOUS "TUPPENCE."
div.p: THE INIQUITOUS "TUPPENCE."

It is quite bad enough to have to pay an in- crease of 3d. per gallon on petrol, without hav- ing to pay an extra twopence to go into the pockets of the already wealthy petrol concerns. We may not like the extra threepenny tax, but motorists as a body are a patriotic lot, and they realise that somehow or other money must be found for the war. I have not heard a single complaint about the 3d. tax. But about the extra 2d. which is being charged I have heard remarks made that I dare not put into print, much as I should like to. There is no excuse whatever for this increase in price. It is merely a ruse to swell the already large profio made by the petrol companies. Second quality spirit now costs 2s. a gallon instead of the is. 7d. we have been accustomed to pay for so long. Why the manufacturers should have chosen the present moment for burdening motorists to an almost unendurable point is a thing I cannot understand. I have already written to my Member of Parliament about it, and I hope all my readers without exception, will do likewise.

div.head: MOTOR CAR IMPORTS AND EXPORTS.
div.p: MOTOR CAR IMPORTS AND EXPORTS.

It is certainly very surprising that the imports of motor cars, chassis and parts into this country during the first nine months of the present year show a slight increase only upon the corresponding figure of last year, and a still smaller increase, over those of the year 1943. The figures are 1915, £5,998,677; 1914, £5,476,971; 1913, £5,675,342. The chief increase was in com- plete ears, of which there were 12,501, valued at £2,421,458 this year, as compared with 6,510, valued at £1,523,128 last year, and 5,291, value.d at £1,341,155 in 1913. The number of chss,sis imported shows a considerable decrease, nalne'Yn' from 6,110, valued at £1,438,230 in 1913, to 5,93'3' valued at £1,400,980 in 1914, and 2,935, valued at £857,450, for the present year. The exports. as might be expected, show a marked diminution, the total value of cars, chassis and parts haying declined from £2,041,147 for the first nine months of 1913, to £1,878,865 in 1914, and £930,976 this year. This, of course, is due to the fact that nearly all our manufacturers have been putting all their energies into the making of munitions. Of the foreign and Colonial cars, chassis and parts imported and re-exported, the returns show a slight increase, viz., £682,904 for the nine months of the present year, as compared with £681,432 last year, and £602,067 the year before. This increase, however, arises entirely from tyres and tubes not imported with com- plete cars, the figures for these articles being £437,070 this year, as compared with £162,935 last year, and £lBO,OBO the year before.

IN THE COURTS.
A PUBLIC PEST.

Fine for an Offence That Deserved The "Cat." - At the -Borough -Police Court on Monday,, Samuel Hammon, railway shedman, 46, For- ster-street, Warrington, pleaded guilty to a charge of indecent conduct with intention to insult a female. The facts were outlined by the Chief Con- stable, who said that on Sunday 'afterneon a young lady was going home after being at work t in an office, and when walking down apassage to the rear of Bank Quay Station the defendanr 'indecently behaved himself. The girl ran away and the defendant followed her. She gave in- formation to the police and later she identified the defendant. The Chief Constable went on to 1-;ay that the police had received complaints about this sort of thing for two years, and there was no doubt that this was the man. It was fortunate that the defendant had pleaded guilty, as this would save the necessity of the girl going into the witness box. Defendant was .fined £lO, the Mayor (Alder- man Peter Peacock) saying that if it had not been for the tact that the defendant had the money on him, he would have been sentenced to a long term of imprisonment.

div.head: "WORK SHY."
div.p: A "WORK SHY."
Sent To Gaol For Smashing A Window.

At Monday's Borough Police Court, .before the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), Alder- men Bolton and Smethurst. Councillor Wilkin- son and Messrs. S. Wright, W. Roberts, W. Furness, T. Locker and J. Upson. George Donnelly, a stranger to the town, who had been remanded from the Previous week, was again charged with breaking five panes of glass at the works of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles. on October 23rd.—He pleaded guilty. Mr. Boardman, an under-manager at Messrs. Pearson and. Knowles' works, stated that the man asked him for a " sub "of 2s. lie had been employed by the firm twice that week. When he was refused the " sub " he said he would have his money's worth, and then broke five panes of glass in the office windows. The man pleaded that he broke the glass be- cause the firm would not give him his money. "A Tramp, And Looked It!"

Addressing the Bench, the Chief Constable said that the man went about tramping the country, doing as little work as he possibly could, and " doing " as many as he could. He was a tramp, and looked it. He was refused the money because he ran away from his work. Everybody knew that Messrs. Pearson and Knowles were ready to pay "subs." In fact, they " subbed " too often, and paid out pollnds
and pounds before the money had been earned. The man was sentenced to a month's hard labour.
SEPARATION ORDER DISCHARGED

Husband And Wife Who Have Parted A Second Time. A separation order granted to Mrs. Amelia Rawlinson, now residing at 47, Watkin-street, Warrington, in 1906, was annulled at the Police Court on Tuesday, on the grounds that she had since cohabited with her husband. In making the application to the Bench on behalf of James Rawlinson, 4, Cyril-street, Warrington, Mr.. Arthur Browne said that all that he had to prove was that the parties had cohabited since the order was made. On February 2nd, 1906, separation order was granted to the wife with alimony of 13s. a week. Since then they had resumed cohabitation for 44 years. In Septem- ber last she took the furniture away and left her husband. Came Back Of Her Own Accord. In the witness box, James Rawlinson said that after the separation order, had been made, his wife went back to him of her own accord. She left him on September 25th, and on Monday last week she issued a warrant for £2 12s. He was locked up and kept in custody part of the night. Mr. T. S. Steel, for Mrs. Rawlinson, said that he could not resist the discharge of the Order. Ile asked if a _fresh order could be granted, but was told that another summons would have to be taken. out.

div.head: NTERFERED WITH POLICEMAN.
div.p: NTERFERED WITH POLICEMAN.
Solicitor's Motto For "Every Wise Man."

At the Borough Police Court on Monday, .1 passenger by the Cheshire Lines Manchester to Liverpool express, was charged with assault- ing a railway official whilst the latter was in the execution of his duty. P.C. Joynson, of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Police, stated that at 7.30 on Saturday night he was on duty at the Central Station. Several women were making use of bad language and whilst he was ejecting them from the station, a soldier interfered. He tried to reason with the soldier, who, in return struck him across the arm with a cane. He called for assistance to remove the soldier off the station. Whilst doing this he received a blow on the side of his face. He turned round to see who had struck him and 'the defendanepushM his hand down his (the witness's) collar and said, "One dog, one bone." Witness had to let go of the soldier and the defendant was renioN ed from the station. He became very violent arid kicked witness several times on the legs. " Prone to Excitability."

Mr. W. H. Jenkins asked the Bench if be might consult with the defendant !or a few minutes. This permission was grant3l, nd Mr. Jenkins, on behalf of the defendant, then withdrew the original plea of not guilty and plead- ed guilty. He said that the defendant was a maxi of peculiar temperament, and like* everybody else, had his imperfections. He thought that the constable was overstepping the bounds of duty. "Don't interfere with a constable," ought to be the motto of everyone. A wise mitn would never interfere with a police constable under any possible circumstances. The defend- ant was very excitable; he was prone to act unwisely under slight provocation. He was exceedingly sorry and expressed his deep regret. There was really no harm done to the constable. A fine of 10s. was imposed.

div.head: BAD BOY.
div.p: A BAD BOY.
Birching Ordered For Juvenile Thief.

At a Children's Court, held on Wednesday afternoon, before Messrs. S. Wright and A.. J. Jolley, a nine-year-old boy was charged on remand with stealing 18s. 11d., the property of Wilfrid Burgess, newsagent, 761, Knutsford- roa d.

The boy pleaded guilty, and the Chief Con- stable narrated the facts as published in our last issue. He added that it was a very sad ease from the mother's point of view, for she had done everything possible. Mr. J. M. Murray, the Director of Education, pointed out to the Bench that the boy's father was in France. In his opinion it was an ex- tremely difficult case. The boy was ordered to be birched, the Chair- man expr6sing his sympathy with the mother. More Bad Boys.

Three boys were charged with stealing a bicycle, the property of Mr. Davis, fitter, 107, Orford-lane. They admitted the theft. The Chief Constable said that in June last the prosecutor left the cycle at the rear of his premises. He afterwards missed it. He did not inform the police, but made inquiries in the neighbourhood. It would appear that one of the boys saw the bike, having an arrangement with the other two. At first they had no in- tention of keeping the bike, but they kept it. Subsequently the bike was swid for 19s. 6d. The boys' fathers spoke on their behalf. One boy was fined 20s. and the other two 10s. each.

div.head: SUFFERING PONY.
div.p: A SUFFERING PONY.

Father And Son Summoned For • Cruelty. Before Mr. A. J. Jolley (in the chair), Dr. Naden and Mr. W. T. Williams, at the Borough Police Court on Thursday morning, William and Edward Jones, father and son, of 105, Bramhall-street, were summoned for ill- treating a horse—the son by working it whilst it was in an unfit state and the father by causing it to he so worked. Inspector Dee, of the R.S.P.C.A., said that at ten o'clock on the morning of the 27th of last month he was in Winwick-street, when he saw the younger defendant in charge of a bay mare- pony, attached to a hawker's spring cart. He noticed that the animal, which was trotting, appeared to be very lame, and he drew the lad's attention to the fact. "It does limp a little bit," the lad replied. Witness examined the horse and found it to be suffering from a bone-spavin of the off hind-leg, the muscles of the leg being very much drawn. Further ques- tioned, the lad said that the horse had been lame about a week, and that his father was aware of the animal's condition. Subsequently witness saw the father in Priestley-street, and was told, by him, that the horse had done no work for about a month, and that it had hurt itself whilst in the stable-yard. He added that he would have the animal's shoe taken off and that if then it was no better he would have it destroyed. A Lame Kind-Leg.
Acting-Sergeant Armstrong deposed to going to a smithy with Inspector Dee, to examining

the animal, and to filiding it very lame on the off hind-leg. The younger defendant told the Court that his father instructed him to take the animal' out, adding that if he found it to be lame he was at once to bring it back. The father said that what his boy had stated was correct. The cart to which the horse was harnessed was only a light one—as also was the load upon it when the Inspector saw it—and sooner than that the horse should have know- ingly been used whilst in an unfit state he would have utilised a donkey, which was in the yard at the time doing nothing. The reason he suggested that the horse might be used was that he thought a bit' of exercise would do it good. Inspector Dee, in answer to the Bench, said that the pony was an old one and it would never be any different to what it was now. The summons against the boy wag dismissed, and the father, who had been previously con- victed for cruelty to a horse, was fined 10s.

div.head: BROTHER AND SISTER,
div.p: BROTHER AND SISTER,
Loans That Were Followed By County Court Claim.

At the County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge J. Scott Fox, K.C., Mrs. Ann Worrall, ,of Slater-street, Warrington, claimed 3s. from her brother, Henry Scotson, insur- ance agent, Slater-street, Warrington. There was a counter claim for £1 4s. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 6, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 6, 1915.
FIREMEN FETED.
Gold Medals For Long And
Meritorious Service.

Interesting presentations were made in the Recreation Room at the Fire Station on Satur- day evening, after a dinner given in honour of officers and firemen who have retired from active service. At the " smoker " which fol- lowed gold medals were given by the brigade to :
Ex-Superintendent Frank Turner. Ex-Sergeant William Monks. Ex-Fireman Edward Bradbury. Ex-Fireman Albert Blacksbaw.

The Superintendent occupied the chair, sup- ported by the Chairman of the Fire Engine Committee (Councillor Gough), Deputy-Supt. Henry Cook, and engineers and men of the brigade. After the loyal toasts had been honourigi, Councillor Gough made the presentations. It gave him, he said, great pleasure to attend their social gathering and to present gold medals, provided by the men's own subscriptions, to their retiring comrades, Superintendent Frank Turner's Fine Record. Addressing Ex-Superintendent Frank Turner, who has seen 54 years' service, he said : .

TQLI have retired from .active service to the position .of ..'lnspector Of Hydrants. You have been connected with the Fire Department well over half a century, and have seen some re- markable changes in the methods of fire extin- guishing, from manual engines to motor equip- ment; You joined the brigade as fireman, and have risen, step by step, to be the Superin- tendent, which position you held for 31i years. What a record of service! This was recognised by the Town Council with .an illuminated ad- dress and a cheque for .21-00, and you were decorated by His Majesty with the highest honour--the King's Medal: Now the brigade wish to supplement a previous silver medal by asking you to accept their gold medal on your retirement from active service. You have earned it by devotion to duty: the records state you have attended nearly 900 fires. I have very great pleasure, on behalf of the brigade, in presenting you this medal, hoping you may have good health for many years after your faithful service to the town." (Cheers.) A Veteran Sergeant.
Councillor Gough, addressing Ex-Sergeant William Monks, said :

"You are another veteran servant who has done the brigade and the borough and district good service for thirty-two years, being actively connected with the Water Department. Your knowledge of water mains and hydrants made you a useful member, retiring with the rank of Sergeant. I understand the firemen of War- rington are members of families who have served in the brigade for decades. The names of Monks, Cook, Blackshaw and Turner, and a lot of other families, have supplied members of our Fire Brigade for long years. Your father before you occupied the position of Deputy-Superintendent, and another brother is now an officer in the brigade•—a fine family record for your native town. I have great plea- sure in presenting you the brigade's gold medal for services rendered."

div.head: Firemen Who Have Done Their Duty.
div.p: Firemen Who Have Done Their Duty.

TO Ex-Fireman Edward Bradbury (19 years' service) and Ex-Fireman Albert Blackshaw (14 years' service) Councillor Gough said : "Both of you have done your duty well. I know from the Superintendent's reports the brigade have lost valuable men during the past year from various causes. I am, however, pleased to hear from him your services are at his command, if shorthanded, at any fires. When the Brigade loses the services of two experienced men who have worked at most of the large fires in our district—like West's, Pochin's, Garton's, Richmond's, Orford Tan- nery, Rylands Bros., Naylor's, Royal -Court Theatre, Greenhalgh's, Royal Oak Soap Works, and Fleming's, and, outside, Wiges Works (Runcorn), Vulcan Works (Earlestown), and a host of big farm fires—it is a distinct loss to the town and brigade. I have great pleasure in presenting to you the brigade's gold medal as an appreciation and souvenir of your connec- tion with the Fire Brigade." All, he said, had done yeoman service for the safety of the lives and property of the borough and district. At all times, and in every kind of weather, they had answered the call with unswerving loyalty and with such success that the ratepayers were not yet called upon to maintain a professional brigade entirely. As Chairman of the Fire Engine Committed, and also on behalf of the Mayor and Town Council, he thanked them for the very efficient service they had rendered to the town. (Cheers.) Superintendent Turner's Regrets.

Superintendent Turner, who .supported the remarks of Councillor Gough, said, leaving aside his father's record—of which he was proud—he would like to say a few words about the long service of men like Ex-Sergeant Monks with 32 years' service. It was unfortunate such long service in the brigade was unrecognised, but it was the misfortune of auxiliary firemen that no fund was in existence to reward such service. It was regrettable. lie was very sorry to lose the services of three such experienced firemen in the brigade from various causes. • All the recipients suitably responded, except Ex-Sergeant W. Monks, in whose absence his brother, Sergeant A. Monks, responded. On the motion of Superintendent Turner, seconded by Ex-Superintendent Turner, a vote of thanks was accorded Councillor Gough for mak-

ing the presentations and for allowing them the use of the Recreation Room for the occasion. Afterwards an enjoyable evening was spent. Songs and musical' selections were given by Deputy-Superintendent Cook, Firemen W. Rerisford, H. Shaw, R.. Cook, V. Wright, R. Blackshaw and George Vernon. Some reminis- cences from brigade history were given by Superintendent Turner.

div.p: IN THE COURTS.—Continued.

Wigan, and came to Warrington in July, 1910. The defendant was an insurance 'agent, had six children, and had been helped from time to time by his sister. She had lent him £9 165., there had been paid £1 13s. on account, leaving a balance of £8 35., and the claim was in respect of this amount.
' Mr. Arthur Browne interposed to say that he admitted an original loan of £5, and there was a balance of £3 7s.

Continuing, Mr. Steel said that with regard to the counter claim for £1 4s. it was alleged that this sum had been Paid as insurance 'pre- miums by the defendant on the request of the plaintiff. Mr. Steel added that he had no in- timation of this counter claim until October 29th.
Ip. the witness l)ox the plaintiff gave details of the amomits alleged to have been lent to the defendaUt. At the conclusion of Mr. Steel's ex- amination Mr. Browne asked witness:—
Has not this claim arisen through our threatening you with proceedings for disorderly conduct?

His honour: Just answer quietly; ' don't let Mr. Browlie make you angry. The question was not answered. The witness denied that she gave the defend- ant Ihe ,money because she was fond of him. She later admitted that she did not instruct Mr. Steel until after she had received Mr. Browne letter.

The defendant admitted borrowing small amounts of money from the plaintiff from time to time, but these were paid back. Ile furAer admitted borrowing £5, of which he repaid £1 13s. and ulso 2s. 6d. interest.

Evidence was also given by MIT. ScotsonAhe defendant's wife. Judgment was given in favour of the plaintiff to the amount of £7 Is. on the first claim; and also in favour of the plaintiff on the counter claim, with costs.

div.head: "OUGHT NOT TO BE IN THE ARMY."
div.p: "OUGHT NOT TO BE IN THE ARMY."
An Asthmatical Absentee Before The. Bench. •

At the Borough Police Court on Friday, be- fore the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) and a large Bench, a middle-aged soldier was charged with being an absentee, an offence which he admitted. The Chief Constable said that it was rather difficult to understand how the man ever got into the Army. He was an asthmatical subject and ought not to be in. The Bench ordered the man to await the arrival of an escort from his regiment.
THE FOOTBALL MELT.%
SECOND WAR-YEAR SEASON AMONG THE JUNIORS.

place by defeating the Padgate C.L.B. Solan, of the Scouts, scored four goals in succession. The second portion of this game was notable for the splendid exhibition given by the Lads' goal- keeper. The Scouts expected to win by a greater margin.

Orford Juniors lost their position in the League Chart by allowing the Fairfield Reserves to defeat them to the extent of four clear goals. They also had two points deducted for a game they played against the Cadets owing to having no goalposts fixed up.

The Fairfield Reserves are now getting a good team together, and to-day they will be repre- sented by their strongest team of the season. They will make a bold bid to displace St. Elphin's from the head of the table, especially so when the teams meet each other.

The game between Howley United and the Latchford Cadets ended in a drawn game, the first of the season. There is strong rivalry be- tween the clubs, and the Cadets were favourites at the interval, when they were leading by two goals. It was in the second portion that the United were seen at their best, and they suc- ceeded in making the scores level and sharing the points. Already the players are -discussing their chances for the return fixture.

The Mersey Juniors, after playing a hard and keen game against the Bewsey Albions, had again to acknowledge defeat, although it was only the alertness of the Albion goalkeeper that prevented them from scoring.

In to-day's games, the one at Padgate between the Lads' Brigade and • the Mersey Juniors should be a keen encounter, as neither team have won a match, and it should also decide which will be the holders of the wooden spoon.
Mr. E. Bate, the Chairman of the Warrington and District League, has joined the Royal Engineer Field Section, and at present is put- ting in his drills at Old Trafford Park.
INTERMEDIATE LEAGUE.
Two Secretaries Answer To
The Country's Call.

We recently announced that Mr. E. Jackson Mee, the hon. secretary or the Intermediate League, had joined up, and that his place had been temporarily taken .by Mr. A. Malcolm, who, like Mr. Mee; is,an assistant schoolmaster, being engaged at Heatbside. Before Mr. Mal- colm had been permanently fixed in the posi- tion on Thursday this week, he, too, had en- listed. We have been unable to learn officially what transpired at this meeting, but we are asked to request secretaries kindly to send all communications to .

• Mr. W. Bibby, 112, Lovely-lane. We should be glad if secretaries would send reports of matches for insertion in "The Ex- aminer " as early as possible each week, and the names of their teams as soon as they have been selected.

div.head: BOLTON V. ST. JAMES'.
div.p: BOLTON V. ST. JAMES'.

-This match was played in Victoria Park, in the presence of a good crowd; Bolton kicked off, and for a time they hovered in mid-field. Eventually, however, Bolton came away with a fine forward' rush, and the St. James' defence was sorely tried, but their men worked manfully and staved off disaster. Bolton were driven back, but only for a time, for they were soon back again, mainly owing to some good passing movements. The Bolton forwards played a good game, and gave their backs numerous chances. Half-time arrived without score. The second half was commenced at a great pace; first one side and then the other attacking, and neither being able to claim much advan- tage. At last, however, the Boltonites came away with another big rush, and a forward— who had played a good game throughout—com- manding the ball extremely well with his feet, dribbled along the touch and amidst great ex- citement took the ball over the line. He was just •in the act of dropping on the leather to I make good the try, when an opponent who had followed close at his heels, kickedthe ball from 1 under him, and it rolled dead. This was indeed a lucky escape for St. James', and very hard lines for the Boltonites. From the kick out Bolton were soon again on the attack, and St. James' were penalised, Edwards kicking a good goal and thus giving his side a two-points' lead. St. James' made desperate efforts to get on level terms, and attacked desperately, but they were kept at bay. Towards the close Bolton attacked, and St. James' being once more penalised, Ed- wards again did the needful, thus giving his side the victory by four points to nil.

div.head: RYLANDS'S HEAVILY DEFEATED.
div.p: RYLANDS'S HEAVILY DEFEATED.

Itylands' Recs. met Heathside Old Boys on Saturday on the. Rylands's enclosure. Heath- side won the toss. Dumbell kicked off and found touch, the opponents' wing man mulling. The ball was carried backward and forward with- out any headway being made, until Rylands's scrum werd penalised for "feet up." From the free kick the Heathside players followed up and charged the Rylands's full-back's return kick down and obtained a try, the goal kick failing. Four more tries were obtained exactly in the same manner, one being converted. Half-time arrived (after 43 minutes play) : Heathside, 1 goal 5 tries _(l7 _points); Rylands's Recs., nil.

- The second half was started in a most vig- orous style, Rylands's forwards completely out- classing the Heathside pack, but the " Wire- men's " backs, being considerably weakened, failed to make headway. From a forward rush Latimer picked the ball up and dashed over for a try, the goal kick failing. Soon after a curious mistake by the referee occurred. Rylands's full- back fielded the ball, returned, and followed up, the ball was returned immediately, where one of the Ileathside players was standing, and taking the ball in flight dashed over and obtained a try, from which a goal was kicked. Result: Heath- side, 2 goals 6 tries; Rylands's Recs., 1 try.

div.head: JUNIORS.

ORFORD JUNIORS v. ST. JAMES' JUNIORS.
Owing to shortage of players St. James' were unable to play, so Orford Juniors claimed the match.
BEAMONT JUNIORS v. SANKEY.

Played on No. 2 ground, Victoria Park. San- key had a good first half with the breeze at their backs, and playing down the slope, but their attempts to a certain extent were futile, for Sinclair played a sound back game for Beamont. Half-time: No score.

Beamont, soon after the resumption, made matters hot for Sankey, but a good run by T. C6leman, the Sankey back, changed the game altogether, and rough play ensued on the Bea- mont line. Higgins scored for Sankey, no goal resulting. The Beamont forwards played a bustling game, and Makin got possession, scor- ing at ,the.corner. Sinclair kicked a good goal from touch. Sankey retaliated with a'try, Wil- son being the scorer. The goal kick again failed. This gave Sankey the lead 6-5. Beamont at- tacked again, but Sankey's full-back replied by a long kick. One of their forwards happened to be off-side, a kick being given to Beamont. Armitage took the kick and landed a good goal from near half-way. This gave Beamont the victory. Result: Beamont Juniors, 7 points; Sankey, 6 points.

div.head: BEWSEY A.F.C. v. ST. ELPHIN'S.
div.p: BEWSEY A.F.C. v. ST. ELPHIN'S.

The above teams met on the Lovely-lane ground, which owing to rain, was not favour- able to good football. The game opened in favour of the "Saints," and in a few minutes Boyle opened the scoring with a good shot from the wing. Burns added a second point, aid be- fore the interval Morgan added a third. In the second portion the " Saints" had much their own way, and if was owing to bad shooting that more goals were not scored. Humphries shot- a fourth goal for the "Saints." Result : St. Elphin's 4 goals; Bewsey,'

BEWSEY ALBIONS v. MERSEY JUNIORS. On the Arpley ground. Bewsey Albions: Darks; Doughty and Tom- kinson; Rutter, Gibbons and Barlow; White,i Millet, Critchley, Kay and Dutton: Mersey Juniors: Walters; Ashcroft and Guest: Aikenhead, Gray and Treyor ; Willoughby. Walters, Smith, Ashton and Thompson. Refere4, J. Barrow.

The Juniors straightway made an attack on the Albions' goal, but their final efforts were wide of the posts. The Albions retaliated with dash, and Walters had to handle a stinging shot ' from White. The latter regained the ball and banged it between the uprights, registering the first point for the Albions. Each goal was visited in turn, and Guest was a trifle lucky in stopping a low drive from White. Half-time:— Albions, 1 goal; Juniors, nil. The second portion opened with a strong attack by the Albions, which was spoiled by Miller placing wide. Hands against the Albions drove them back, but only temporarily as they 'attacked again more strenuously, and Guest conceded a corner. The kick was well- placed by Dutton, and White scored the second goal. At this stage the Albions were pin vio z much stronger game, and tested the Juniors' defence very much. Critchley met a clearance frpm Walters and sent just over the bar. The Juniors pain a brief visit to their opponents' end, where Walters tested Darks with a good drive, which was well cleared. The Juniors' defence was again sorely tested and Ashcroft made some fine returns. Another visit to the Albions' goal resulted in Ashton testing Darks with a low shot, which was clean-A at the foot of the post. Result :—Bewsey Albinos, 2 goals; Mersey Juniors, nil.
ORFORD JUNIORS v, FAIRFIELD JUNIORS

On the ground of the former club The open- ing exchanges were very even. As the Iz:uric pro- gressed play became very fast, and each custodian was seen to advar toge. The visit( rs gradually gained the upper hand, and after fifteen minutes' -play England scored the first goal for them. The home team played more determinedly, and from a free-kick they gained position in their opponents' half and attacked strongly. They failed in their final efforts. From a goal-kick the visitors at 'length broke through the home defence, and Boyle scored the visitors' second goal. At the interval the score was :—Fairfield Juniors, 2 goals; Orford Juniors, nil. _ _ _

The second portion opened in favour of the visitors, and the home defenders were hard pressed, but they prevailed, and gradually cleared their lines. After a spell of even play in midfield, the home team took up the aggressive, but the defence of Kidd, Cooper and Tunstall proved too good for the many attempts to lower their colours. As the close of play was approaching the visitors added two more goals in quick succession, Lygo doing the needful. The visitors continued to have all the play, but owing to good work by the home custodian they could not add to their score. Result :—Fairfield Juniors, 4 goals; Orford Juniors, nil.

div.head: PADGATE C.L.B. v. STOCKTON HEATH SCOUTS.
div.p: PADGATE C.L.B. v. STOCKTON HEATH SCOUTS.

At Padgate. The Scouts were the first to become aggressive. The home team improved and made ,a raid on the Scouts' citadel, and were finely repulsed by Baguley. After some even exchanges the visitors attacked again, which resulted in Kenwright opening the score. A few minutes later, Farnell added a second point. From the centre-kick the visitors still had the best of play, and Haslam centring from the touch-line, Solan scored the third goal. Follow- ing these reverses, the home team rallied in fine I style, and made several strong attempts to lower 1 the Scouts' eitadel, but they were repulsed by Johnson. The visitors' forwards rushed la- wards the home goal, where Solan accepted a neat pass from Smith and scored the fourth goal. Half-time :—Scouts, 4 goals; C.L.8., nil. The home team made changes in the players' position in the second half, and were seen to better advantage, but Were not capable of breaking down the visitors' defence. The Scouts returned to the attack ad Appleton cleared good shots by Farnell and Solan. Eventually the latter registered the fifth goal. Appleton was prominent with a grand save from Parnell, and then the home forwards paid a short visit to the opposite end, where they were smartly driven back by Foster. Following a Spell of midfield play s Solan scored the sixth 'goal. From now the visitors were all over their opponents, and Appleton saved many shots before Manual beat him with a low drive. Result:—Stockton Heath Scouts, 7 goals; Pad- gate C.L.8., nil.
HOWLEY UNITED v. LATCHFORD CADETS CORPS.

In Victoria Park. A promit4ng movement by the Cadets was neatly checked. The United forwards were set going and advanced to the Cadets' goal, where the defence proved equal to the attack. The Cadets settling down to their

game, penned the United to their goal area, and after fifteen minutes' play Smith scored the first goal. Again the Cadets' forwards combined well, but had to retreat, and the United outside- left made a grand run along the touch-line. His centre was not accepted, and the defence cleared again for their forwards to race to the opposite end and Smith added a second point. At half-time the Cadets led by two goals to none.

Upon resuming, United, with the wind in their favour, began to play a hard game, and owing to the keen rivalry between the clubs there were some exciting struggles. The United succeeded in making the scores equal, and then it was a ding-dong game until the close of play. Each side did its level best to gain the lead, but the respective defences would not yield, and the result was :-.—Howley United, 2 goals; Latch- ford, 2 goals.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES.
FAMFIELD UNITED v. WARRINGTON CENTRAL.

On the Orford-road ground, before a moderate attendance of spectators. Mr. A. Hoult had charge of the game. The United scored in the first minute. Stubbs, meeting- an accurate centre from Bos- cow, sent in a hard drive, with which the visi- tors' custodian was unable to deal. The Unit:ll made another strong attack, and Stubbs hit the crossbar. From the rebound the visitors trans- ferred to the home end, and during a melee in front of goal the ball was sent between the posts, and made the scores equal The game was now more equal and int?,resting, and good combination was shown. the viiit)rs began to show to better advantage and gained the lead. Half-time :—Central,? goals; United, 1 val. The second half opened very evenly aed each end was visited, but the defend!rs were on the alert. After fifteen minute-,' play Ws. ca,or.se equalised with a splendid shot twenty yards from goal. Both teams now played keenly to gain the lead, and the Central proving to be the better stayers, they applied 4avy pressure on the home goal. Gleave, in to-tempting to clear, put through his own goal. ITinal e,:re : Warrington Central, 3 goals; Fairfield United, 2 goals.
EMMANUEL INSTITUTE v. WIDNES ST. MARY'S C.Y.M.S.

Played at Widnes. Play opened in Emman- uel's favour, and they soon opened their scoring, through their right wing, with a fine goal. Shortly afterwards Knight added a second, tak- ing advantage of a misunderstanding between the home backs. The visitors at this period were playing well, especially Knight in goal and the full-backs. The home team were awarded a free kick just outside the penalty area, and after an exciting melee in the goalmouth Bar- rett secured and scored with a shot well out of the reach of Knight. Towards the interval Em- manuel were proving the better team, and after a good run by their left wing, T. Hughes re- ceived a nice pass, with which he made no mis- take, half-time arriving with Emmanuel lead- ing by 3 goals to 1. On resuming, St. Mary's raided the visitors' goal, where Knight made a splendid save. Em- manuel backs were feeding their forwards well, and they on several occasions tested the home goalkeeper. Barrett, the home full-baLtk, re- peatedly drove them back. The game now be- came more even, the C.Y.M.S. putting more energy into their play. The home team forced a corner, from which Yearsley scored. Em- manuel attacked hotly. and Eaton put in a splendid shot, which hit the upright with the goalkeeper well beaten. Emmanuel ran out winners by 3 goals to 2, thus breaking the St. Mary's unbeaten record. For the winners, their backs were in splendid form, and for the losers, Barrett, Yearsley and McHamar were the pick.

div.head: JUNIOR LEAGUE MEETING.
div.p: JUNIOR LEAGUE MEETING.
Winners To Have Medals Instead Of .1
Ball.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington and District Junior League was held at their hea.l- - on Tuesday night; Mr. Simpson pre- siding over a good attendance of delegates. There was some discussion respecting the trophy for the winners of the League, and it was decided that a set of medals should be given instead of a ball, as previously agreed. The Latchford Cadets protested against the result of their match with Orford Juniors stand- ing as a League fixture. At the time this game was played the Orford Club had no goalposts fixed up and the clubs arranged that the game should be a friendly. At the close of play the Orford team having won, wanted to claim the game as a League fixture. The committee de- cided that the points should be deducted and the match rearranged.

div.head: Even So.
div.p: Even So.
"Papa, what is a savage?" "A savage, my son, is a man who occupies two whole seats in a car, while some poor woman with a sick baby has to stand up."

Very Likely. "Yes," exclaimed the poet, who was giving a lecture, "she comes and goes, uncertain, evanescent; now appearing, now vanishing; now charming us with her smiles and casting over our hearts the spell of her presence, lur- ing us and leading us on to believe that she is ours for ever; again hastening from us just when we have come to know the dulcet sweet- ness of her voice; as fickle as a shadow, as—" "What in the world is he talking about?" asked the lady with the purple hat, in a back seat. "A maid servant, I suppose," suggested her neighbour with the turquoise rings and the scent bottle.
