div.head: LOCAL AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: LOCAL AMUSEMENTS.
ROYAL COURT.
Week Of Grand Opera By The Harrison Frewin Company. ,

Only too seldom are our local habitues of the theatre afforded the treat which has this Week, been extended to them in the, visit of. an opera company of recognised standing. The Harrison Frewin company has, at least .the merit, of pre- senting well-knoWn . operas adequately, if its members do not always succeed in realising ones ideal in the singing. and acting of their various. impersonations. The advent of the strong array of *vocal arid histrionic that has . this week been seen and hoord.on. the stage Of the Royal Court Theatre is, in itself, a notable event, and the fact that crowded audiences have ruled almost every night ,in ,all parts, except possibly the gallery-, is. at once a fitting testi- mony of our townspeople's high appreciation of the efforts of the. Harrison Frewin-company to cater for their edification and amusement, and a grateful recognition of the enterprise of the management of Sir Joseph Beecham's popular house. A -glance at the list of operas presented during the week makes plain the fact that in selecting from the company's . ample repertoire the works that have been performed, Mr. Loader has preferred to make Sure of pleasing the great majority of his Patrons to taking the risks )f 'staging little known and untried works, excel- lent though they may be in intrinsic merit. From some points of view it is, therefore, to be regretted that all the 'operas of this week are of the Saturday night order, in the sense that reliance has manifestly .been . placed on their proved popularity. Only when Warrington audiences begin .to demonstrate a real and per- manent interest in opera in general, and in more modern works in particular, would. the experi- ment of further ventures on these lines be justified. Would that this contingency may be realised in the not very distant, future.. "The Bohemian Girl" of Monday afternoon, like the " Maritana " of Wednesday evening was, in the potency of its sheer melodic attractiveness and. the ever-green charm of its incident, quite certain of drawing a large audience. Such indeed has been the case, much enthusiasm being shown in the performance of these favourite works. In them Miss Raymond Amy, Miss Esther Yunson, Mr. Kingsley Lark,, Mr. Geo. A. Fox, Mr. Tom .Griffiths; Mr. Wm. Boland, and. Mr. Edward Arthur sustained the more onerous parts most ably and effectively, following the well-known lines to success that custom seems powerless either to stale or to supersede. In "Ii Trovatore " and " Faust,- performed on Monday, and Tuesday evenings, there are, however, some exactions which give opportunity for individualistic interpretation as well as for the display of exceptional ability. With Miss Myfanwy Newell as Leonora, Miss Dorothea Denstone as Azacena, Mr. Lewys James as Count de Luna, Mr. Geo. A. Fox as Ferrando,.and Mr. John Harrison as Manrico, Verdi's opera was in quite safe hands, each one of these essential and mutually dependent parts being sustained in a manner which was chiefly praiseworthy by reason of the uniformity it dis- played of a high level of ability, if not of actual excellence. It is not too much to say that probably never in Warrington has this work been so efficiently and so completely presented— a pronouncement. which was endorsed by the enthusiastic applause and the vociferous recalls that marked the entire course of its perform- ance. The dellghtful arias, .the harmonious concerted pieces, and the rousing ensembles, in- cluding the moving Miserere music, upon all of which Verdi has so unstintingly lavished his skill, were mostly rendered with charming effect. Nor were the. numerous declamatory and impassioned passages wanting in due ardour and vehemence of expression, the intensely dramatic finale to the first act, Manrico's climacteric aria at the end of the third act, and the finale voicing the startling and tragic denouement which brings the opera to a close are mentioned as a few among many instances of conspicuous good work. . Gounod's masterpiece was, on the whole, dis- appointing, mainly because the Faust of Mr. John Clarke and the Marguerite of Miss Evangeline Florence were in some degree defi- cient in sincerity and convincing power. There was, too, a lack 'of passionate,. tenderness and of the expression of anything like ecstatic rapture at critical mor?,ents,. more especially in the garden scene, while ,a Stiffness and con- straint. in Mr. Clarke's' p.ortral of the part of the enthralled lover was" often noticeable. The parts of Mephistopheles wand Valentine, which were really' both well sung and well impersonated by Mr. Kingsley Lark and MI. Lewys Jaines, gained under these circumstances a prominence that was hardly due to them, and that oeCasionally proved somewhat disconcerting in distracting attention from the central characters. Nevertheless, and notwith- standing these drawbacks, the human factOr which so strongly permeates • " Faust " made its overwhelming appeal to .all, and plenteous applause greeted well-known . songs and . con- certed items, although the ,audience were seldom roused into actual enthusiasm. The choral parts of " Faust " bulk much more largely than is usually the case in grand 'opera. It is due therefore to say that the singing of the music of the. Kermesse, the vocal waltz, the soldier's chorus, and that at- tendant on the death of Valentine, was quite good, the action and the sense of busy, movement in some of the scenes presenting a finely pic- turesque spectacle. On Thursday evening, before an audience filling the theatre to its utmost capacity, Bizet's " Carmen " was presented. The titular role was impersonated by Miss, Myfanwy Newell with a dashing and insouciant, vivaciousness, which was as, admirable as it was appropriate to the part. Her voice was, however, scarcely suitable for an ideal "Carmen," the music being better adapted for vocalisation in a mezzo-soprano range. Many telling solos and some of the concerted music therefore suffered from a certain want of sonorousness and of a fuller tone volume, even when Miss Newell's expressiveness and manner of delivery were everything that could be desired. Miss Newell's dramatic capabilities were always finely exhir bited, especially in the tavern scene and at the entrance to the Bull' Ring—the first of which marks the beginning of Don Jose's fateful dis- trust of the gipsy's constancy, .o hile the second is so largely fraught with tragic consequences of misplaced affection. As Don Jose, Mr. John Harrison confirmed all the good opinions formed of him in "Ii Trovatore " on Monday. A little inclined to over-emphasis in the more dramatic of the recitatives, he yet shone with distinctive lustre, vocally as histrionically, at all critical moments in the portrayal of what must be admitted to be a very trying part. Mr. Griffiths's Escamillo was in all essential respects a powerful delineation, 'and it is a compliment to him to say that, not until his appearance in the second act, was the audience moved to any show of enthusiasm. His breaking in upon the audience with the Toreador's song at this point brought about a vociferous redemand, and throughout the 'further course of the opera Mr. Griffiths's manly bearing and his animated , manner were in direct contrast, as they are intended to be, with the growing Morbidness and hitterness of Don Jose's diSposition. Some good work was done by several of the minor characters. Examples—not the only ones—may be mentioned in the sincere manner in which , Miss Ella Rees sang the beautiful .aria in the third act, and in the rendering of the. terzetto by the card-players in the same scene: The ballet, which figures largely in !'Caren" ',and "Faust," deserves a special word of praise for the ensemble dances which form a spectacu- lar feature of many of the operas 'staged during ,the week. The chorus suffered somewhat, and excusably, in the paucity of its. male voices, but, ift. it was not for this , reason always. adequate, it, in the main, sufficed, There were also,. as is inevitable where so many works are being .essayed, numerous like mishaps in which the -orcheStra was concerned, and some in which interaction between those ,on the stage and the bandsmen was at fault. Bat, tinder the skilful conductorship of Mr. Harrison ,Frewin and that of Mr. David Cochran, who undertook some of, this work, any serious 'halt- ing of the course 'of things was avoided. It is due to say that, in the orchestra itself,. the scores of the composers of the various operas were fully represented by capable instrumen- talists. •

For the smooth working of all, arrangements for the canfori of the numerous 'patrons of the theatre, Mr. H. L. Warburton, the genial act- ng ,xnan agcr,. is, to, be credited anti thanked. - Last evening Wagner's Tannhauser" ;was performed by a cast which' included' Mr. Wm. Bcland in the titular part, Miss Eaymcnd Amy as Elizabeth, Mr H\arry Webster is Wait b •,.!r. and

div.head: Big' Musical Comedy " Hit " Next Week.
div.p: Big' Musical Comedy " Hit " Next Week.

, This week levers of grand opera have had their fill; next week the Royal Court Theatre caters fOr -those who like their music of the light and .airy order and mixed with' plenty of fun, the management having booked:- that premiere, among the moderns, ," The Balkan Princess," than which there are few 'brighter and more humoursome trifles on the • road. There can be little 'doubt that "The Balkan Priuoess" will repeat in Warrington on a smaller scale 'the great "hit" that it Made during its tremendously successful run at the
Prince of Wales' Theatre, London—that popu, lar house that gave birth to so many musical successes. _

We are promised a company worthy of the play, the principal parts being in the hands of artistes of no mean repute, the net result being that "The Balkan Princess" should provide one of the most popultir entertainments seen at the Royal Court for a long time past.
MR. TOM REDMOND, Who takes the part of Count Boethy.

div.head: SPLENDID " BILL " AT THE HIPPODROME.
div.p: SPLENDID " BILL " AT THE HIPPODROME.

Splendid fare is on offer at the Hippodrome this week and large audiences have been nightly availing themselves of the fact to the full, there being no 'vacant seats in any part of the house and many contenting themselves with standing porn only." The principal turn— and it is a splendid one—is provided by' the Harmony Four. a ouartet of the best enter- tainers in the variety world. Their fine voices and their sense of humour, between them, help to provide a show that should not be missed by all who appreciate _sterling melody and mirth. The Harmony Four have made a very big name for themselves and they fully maintain their considerable-sized reputation. J. G. Grahame and Zelina Harrington present a most effective sketch, entitled "The Crook," an effort which "gets right there" at every show. Miss Har- rington takes the titular role, whilst Mr. Grahame portrays a wealthy young American, who, arriving home late at night, finds the woman in his flat, questions her, and, being convinced that she is more sinned against than sinning, has a kindly., word for her, with the result. that she hands over to him an important document; in order to secure which she had burglariously entered his room. The Kavanaghs are one of the cutest pairs of comedy jugglers we have seen for long past and get a warm welcome—and a deserved one !—at every house. Ethel and May extract tuneful music from a variety of instruments in clever fashion, being helped by G. G. Thomas, who formerly con- ducted the orchestra at the world-famed Em- pire in Leicester-square, London. Miss Audrey Cooper sings some fine music finely—providing, in fact, quite one of the most charming turns of the evenings—and Jubb and Jerome imper- sonate, vocalise and dance,. and do all three things equally Cleverly. Walter Lintone is an expert on the concertina, extracting some Par- ticularly sweet music from the instrument, which, owing to its associations with the bean- feasting spirit, has of late years fallen from its high estate. The current issue of "The Gau- moat Graphic" goes to the completion of a really fine show. " Billy In The Ring " Next Week.

Next week the, risible faculties of the patrons of the Hippodrome will be putting in some over- time, for the "top line" on the bill happens to be the "Famous Craggs," in their latest and greatest comedy sketch, "Billy in the Ring " "a screamer that brings the roof down nightly." George Newburn, "the star mimic of star artistes" will provide Another fascinat- ing "turn," and Conway George promises some unique vocal and humourous variations. Camp- bell and Brady, "the talkative juggler and the dancing girl," will provide a show that bristles with skill and prettiness, and the Maro Duo will put in some comedy work on the triple- bars. " One of the best items on the programme will be provided by Mooney and Holbien. who are two- comedians of note—real " top-holers in the mirth and merriment line.

div.head: FAMOUS NOVEL FILMED AT THE
div.p: FAMOUS NOVEL FILMED AT THE
"STAR."

"The Eagle's Nest," a fine film of Western life, was the chief attraction at the Star Kinema gn the first three days of the week. It is full of exciting events, and the plot is of a novel character, and in every way the Wm provided a good hour's entertainment. The qther pic- tures were by no means less interesting. A scenic 'picture entitled -" Volandour," pictured some of the beauties of: Holland, and " Pathe's Gazette" was up to its usual high. standard. The comedy side of the programme. consisted of two films, "When Samuel Skidded," and "Baby's Fault." -
For the latter part of the week "John Halifax, Gentleman," is the great attraction, and the film being as interesting as the novel, it is well worth seeing. Next Week's " Star " Films.
The big films at the Star Kinema next week will be "A Garret in Bohemia,"• on the first three nights and "The Dawn of a To-morrow" on the last three nights.

div.head: " CABIRIA."
div.p: " CABIRIA."
Great Film Coming To The Grand Electric Theatre.

" Cabiria." described as the world's greatest film, will :be shown at the Grand :Electric theatrd, Bridge Foot, every, evening of the week commencing Monday, November 15th. The main part of "Cabiria " was produced in Turin by the famous Itala Company, who made cinematograph history in 1910 by pro- ducing "The Fall of Troy." At Turin a 'glass.g covered studio, a quarter,of a mile equare, was 'specially constructed for • certain portions of the film. .Other portions of the story were enaeted in Sicily and •Tunie, the identical spots on which the great .historical scenes originally took place. The ,preparations began over four years ago. The .discovery of Maciste, the -giant slave, who takes a prominent part in the film, has quite a, romantic flavour. This Italian, among the strongest men in the world, was found carrying bales, of cotton, in the port of Genoa. At first his histrionic. abilities were not great, but by careful training-'—he rehearsed the first scene in which he appears over fifty times before the produc,r would pass his per- formance----he has attained Such artistry that one cannot think of him as other than the -huge negrci 'slave. All the supers employed as soldiers went through a three. months' course of physical training to prepare for the many

strenuous battle scenes. As showing the ex- treme particularity of the producer, it may be mentioned that the actor who plays the part Of Archimedes allowed his hair and beard to grow for six months,: so that: he 'Might dispense with wigs, .Scc. " Cabiria"'.:hag been pUblicly .exhibited .in the. United States and Australia,' and in both countries it made a-great impression. At, one -theatre alone, in Neiv ,York, the net profits amounted to 415;000. -It 'would be a grave mistake, however, to eraphasiSe the spectacular in the film above the dramatic; the spectacular is all the more impressive be- cause an artistic master-hand has subordinated it to the dramatic, and poetic moinents. Of the play.

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Further Accommodation For Wounded Soldiers.

div.head: MR. IVIATHER AND THE L.G.B. INSPECTOR.
div.p: MR. IVIATHER AND THE L.G.B. INSPECTOR.

A meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held on Wednesday morning, Mr. A. J. Jolley being in the chair. The House Committee reported that they had .been asked if the Board was prepared, if the necessity arose, to provide further accommoda- tion for Wounded soldiers in that part of the house now devoted to aged and infirm inmates. They had decided to accede to the request.
Mr. Mather pointed out that it was the duty of all public bodies to do what they possibly could in connectiou with the war. . • .
Mr. Billinge stated that there was nothing in the minute as to the terms for the accommoda- tion of the soldiers. _

The Chairman replied that the War Office was anxious to procure increased accommodation for a number of men, and it was suggested that the Board should, if the emergency arose, give over a portion of the aged and infirm block for the use of the wounded. The suggestion was made because their house numbers were down, and there was ample accommodation for the aged and infirth in other parts of the house. This was not a permanent thing, and the committee was agreed that it was the proper thing to do. In reply • to a question by the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, the Chairman replied that after the alteration had been made they would have accommodation for 320 Men.
'1 he minutes of the committee were approved

LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOAFib REPORTS. On the Clerk announcing that be had received extracts from the report of the Local Govern- men Board Inspector. Mr. Mather submitted that the report ought to go to the Local Government Board before it was submitted to.the Board of Guardians. The Chairman replied that it was the duty of the Inspector to act as an intermediary between the Local Government Board and the local authority. It very often happened that when anything was at fault an agreement was arrived at between he Inspector and the local authority without the Local Government Board interven- ing. Mr. Mather maintained that if the report was not sent to the Local Government Board, there was no record at the offices as to what was being done.

The Chairman said that many people grum- bled about "red tape," but this suggestion en- couraged "red tape." Ultimately it was decided that a copy of th.‘ report should be sent to each member of the Board.

div.head: CONTROVERSIAL MATTER.
div.p: A CONTROVERSIAL MATTER.

The Clerk announced that he had received a letter from the Lewisham Board of Guardians, which recommended that "during the continu- ance of the present war, in view of the severe strain on national resources, the members of the House of Commons will set a noble example in economy and self-denial to the nation by per- forming their duties gratuitously, and that those who are members.of the Cabinet will accept sub- stantial reductions in their salaries; that the Government be urged to economise in all Gov- ernment departments, apd that copies of this resolution be sent to the Prime Minister, Major Sir E F. Coates, and all Boards of Guardians throughout England and Wales." The Chairman remarked that this was too controversial a subject to discuss. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell said it would be a splendid thing to get the Government to set the example instead of preaching. Nothing was done in the matter.

div.head: LATE MR. F. T. BENNIE.
div.p: LATE MR. F. T. BENNIE.

Mr. F. Bennie, of 80, Liverpool-road, War- rington, a gentleman well-known in the borough, passed aWay on Thursday. he deceased had been ailing for the last twelve months, but had managed to get about up to a week or so ago. when complications set in from his complaint, which necessitated his • being confined to bed, and from which he did not, unfortunately, re- cover. The late Mr. Bennie was engaged in business as a public works contractor practi- cally all his life, and amongst his commercial associates was highly esteemed and admired for his integrity and geniality. For the last few years he did not take an active part in the affairs of the borough, although he always 'had • its welfare at heart, he being content with in- teresting himself with those in the immediate neighbourhood in which he resided. He was a Freemason, having acted in the past as Wor- shipful Master of the Lodge at Ashton-in- Makerfield, besides being a member of the "Lodge of Lights." Fiffy-eight years of age, he was. prior tt his illness, the President of the local "Jolly Anglers' Association," being par- ticularly fond of the piscatorial branch of sport. He was also President of the Bank Quay Bowling Club, by whose members he was highly respected and esteemed. • The deceased gentle- man leaves a widow and four daughters to mourn their loss. The interment will take place on Monday at the Warrington Cemetrey.

div.head: CHURCHMEN'S BATTALION.
div.p: CHURCHMEN'S BATTALION.
Special Battalion To be Raised 133 Church Lads' Brigade.

Field-Marshall Lord Grenfell has addressed the following letter to the clergy in connection with the raising of a special Battalion of Churchmen by the Church Lads' Brigade : "Dear Sir,—Now that a special recruiting effort is being made I feel there is a great op- portunity to recruit a second Battalion (Reserve) of the Churchmen's Battalion, 16th (S.) Battalion K.R.R.C. (C.L.8.). "I am particularly anxious that we should be-able to do this, as by this means we shall be able much more effectively to keep up the present traditions of the battalion—frequent communions, prayers on parade, silence for private prayers, &c. "If we do not get enough recruits for the Reserve, when casualties occur, they would be replaced from other units, which would natur- ally make the maintenance of the religious exercises more difficult.

`f I have lately inspected and taken leave of the 16th Battalion on its going to the Fronts and I can say it would be hard to find another Service Battalion so well set up, smart, and with so fine a record as to conduct, there having been absolutely no crime lip the battalion, thus showing what C.L.B. training has done in the past when put to the test. "May I ask you to make now a special endeavour in this Recruiting Campaign to filt. up the ranks of our Reserve, for such an opportunity .for. Churchmen is entirely unique. "Headquarters will gladly send any papers or give any advice which may be required.— Yours faithfully,
" GRENFELL, ' "Field-Marshal."
Aldwyeh House, Catherine-street, Aldwyeh, London, W.C.

div.head: AGRICULTURAL JUMBLE SALE.
div.p: AGRICULTURAL JUMBLE SALE.

In aid of the British Farmers' Red Cross Fund and the Agricultural Relief of the Allies Fund, a jumble sale of agricultural implements, &c., is to be held in the Brewery Field, Wilderspool. on Thursday, November 18th. Donations and gifts of stock, produce, agricultural implements, be welcomed, as it is hoped to make the sale a real success, and one that will prove of substantial financial help to the worthy objects on behalf of which it has been promoted. Mr. Harry Gandy, of Bridge Foot, Warrington, is kindly undertaking the secretarial duties, and he will be delighted to hear from donors.

MO THE MAYOR, ALDERMEN AND .1 BURGESSES OF THE BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON, BEING THE URBAN SANITARY AUTHORITY FOR THE SAID BOROUGH; TO THE INHABITANTS OF THE SAID BOROUGH; AND TO ALL OTHERS WHOM IT MAY CONCERN. WHEREAS the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington (here- inafter called the Corporation), being the Urban Sanitary Authority for the said Borough, have made application to the Local Government Board for the issue of a Provisional Order under Sections 297 and 303 of the Public Health Act, 1875, to partially repeal, alter, or amend the Warringtdn Corporation Gas Act, 1877, so as : • (1.) To provide for the abolition of the standard of illuminating power of gas sup- plied by the Corporation and the substitu- tion therefor of a calorific standard; (2.) To increase the pressure at which gas is required by the said local Act to be sup- plied by the Corporation; and (3.) 'or the several purposes of the Application or for purposes connected with, incidental to, or consequent on those pur- poses to make any such alteration or amend- ment of the said Local Act, or of any other Local Act or of any Act confirming a Provi- sional Order made in pursuance ot any of • the Sanitary Acts or of the Public Health Act, 1875, and in force in the said Borough as may be necessary or desirable; • AND WHEREAS it is proposed that a Pro- visional ()icier should be issued in compliance with the saia Application; NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that A. W. Brightmore, Esq., D.Sc., M.lnst.C.E., one of the Inspectors of the said Board, will attend at the Town Hall, Warrington, on Wednesday, the Tenth day of November, 1915, at half-past Ten o'clock in the forenoon, to hold a Local Inquiry into the subject-matter of the said Application and the proposed Provisional Order. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN that any person interested may attend at such Inquiry and be heard with reference to the said Application and the proposed Provi- sional Order, AS WITNESS my hand this Twenty-sixth day of October, 1915, at the Office of the Local Gov- ernment Board, Whitehall,' London. THOS. PITTS, Assistant Secretary.

REPORTED KILLED. RIFLEMAN A. HEESOM. "lie Was A Good Soldier, Dying An Honoured Death." Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Heesom, of 128, Knuts- ford-road, Latchford,. have this , week received the, following letter from Captain H. 3tl. Griffiths, King's Royal Rifles, respecting their son, Arthur Heesom, whom we reported :as missing in our last issue "I received your letter of the 20th, and I beg to inform you that, your son has been 're- ported missing from the 25th September ,and has not been heard of -since. I much regret: to tell you that I am of the opinion that, he was killed on that date. Please accept my sincere Sympathy, in this your great loss-, and I trust' it may help you to know that your son was very well liked by us all and did his duty always cheerfully. He ',Was a good Soldier,. dying a death we all honour." Joined When War Broke Out. : Riflenian Heesom was twenty years of age and enlisted immediately after the outbreak of war. As previously reportedf he was Wounded some time back and had only been again a short while in the ,firing line. He was exceedingly popular wherever he went for his genial man- ner and kindly disposition earned him a host •

DIED OF WOUNDS. PTE. JOSEPH THOMPSON. As we announced lost week, Private Joseph Thompson, Royal Scots Fusiliers, son of Mr. Thompson, . 11, Norris-street, has died from wounds received in the last great advance in
the West. He was twenty-three years of age, was educated at St. Ann's School, and was employed by Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons. He was ,a regular attendant at the Gospel Hall Church.

WOUNDED. LANCE-CORPORAL K. BAGULEY. Figures` In Casually List For Fourth Time. Lance-Corporal Edwin Baguley, a married Man, of 9, Shepherd's-row, off Orford-street, and a member of the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, has. recently been w6unded for the

LANCE-CORPORAL E. BAGULEY. Wounded. third time since he went out to the Front. He has also been previously gassed. His hurts this time consisted of gun-shot wounds in the head and leg, but he has now sufficiently recovered to be sent back to camp. An Old Local Footballer. Lance-Corporal Baguley, who is twenty-seven years of age, has been in the Army eleven years, and immediately war was declared he was sent from the depot, Orford ;Barracks, to the Front, alone with his regiment. He was at one time an einployo of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Ltd., at the Bewsey Forge, and he played football with the works team. Lance-Corporal Baguley has two brothers serving in the Army. One is in training, while another, a Company-Sergeant-Major, is serving at the Front. • MISSING. PRIVATE JOHN THOMPSON. Private John Thompson, 6th South Lancs. Regiment, 5, Dickinson-street, who went out to the Dardanelles, has been reported missing, as stated in last week's "Examiner." He is a

married man and the brother of Private Joseph Thompson, Norris-street, who has died of wounds. He, as a boy, attended the Wycliffo School and worked at the Corporation Gas Works. He, is thirty years of age, and, like his brother, was a lember of the congregation of the Gospel Hall Church. • GASSED. PRIVATE MARTIN HUGHES. Spent His Birthday In The Trenches. This trouble is caused through the acid .used ih the galvanising and can be prevented by giving the wire two coats of the best white lead paint. APPLE KERRY PIPPIN. The rage for size and colour is so much on the increase that apples like the above are in danger of being neglected. For private use there is no comparison between say the highly. coloured Worcester Pearmain and Kerry Pippin. The Newer is certainly the more valu- able for sale, but the latter is far superior when flavour is taken into account, while it is just of the -size that most people like for dessert. Very few apples can equal the Kerry Pippin for flavour in its season—September—and now that the planting season is with us.those who do riot already grow it should procure trees of it. It is a good apple for those who have but small gardens, as in bush form it is very free bearing, and on a light warm soil it takes on a lovely colour on the side exposed to the sun„ COARSE PEARS. Size now seems the order of the day, this applying to pears in,A marked degree. These huge overfed pears that one so often sees at fruit shows are very misleading to the general public, and do much harm. Exhibitors can hardly be blamed, as they only show what will catch the judge's eye, well knowing that if they only selected and exhibited fruits for quality they would not find a place in the prize list. Not till there are classes set apart for quality

only will there be any change. A big coarse pear is the worst of all fruits, big specimens of other fruits not showing such a marked differ- ence in quality. " Gude things are made up in sma' parcels," and this is well exemplified in such sterling and consistently flavoured pears as Olivier des Serres, Winter Nelis, Seekle and • Passe Colmar. STRAWBERRY RUNNERS. Those who failed to make fresh plantations of strawberries in the early autumn should lay in the runners in some good soil until the spring, by which time they will have formed a mass of roots and can be transferred to their permanent quarters, when they will at once start away. and if carefully attended to during the summer in the way of mulching with short stable manure, and if the weather is dry, an occasional soaking of water, will m-akii strong crowns which will bear heavy crops during the follow- ing season. In my young days this plan wo9 the one always followed in the North, and no gardener at that time ever dreamt of planting in the autumn. This, however, is now changed the rule being to make fresh plantations as soon as strong, well-rooted runners are to be had in the autumn, thus gaining a season as regards cropping—Wick, in "Farm and Home." THE LOGANBERRY AS A PRESERVE. For this purpose I think the loganberry Is more valuable than for dessert, as the fruits cans be gathered when not dead ripe, and when Pre- served have a delicious flavour. The loganberrY is not so sickly sweet as the .raspberry nod strawberry, and for this reason is, when Pre- served, preferred by many. • • The Difference. In England to call a woman homely mea that she is fond of anything about home no° is unpretending; in the -United States it means not handsome. To be clever in England means to be dexterous and with America the tern' signifies good-natured or honest. They saY crackers; we say biscuit; their mail is eur post; •a baggage check in England becomes brasses in the States; while we say luggage for • baggage. A tramp in the United States is a vagabond, but in England any traveller may . . be so called.
